Introduction

Swargiya Mahabir Prasad Srivastava was born on Kartik Shukla 2, 1644, according to that, on October 18, 1887, in the village Bijhauli, tehsil Handia, district Allahabad. He passed the High School (1606) and Inter Examinations (1608) from the Kayastha school of Allahabad and the B.S.-C. examination (1610) from Moore College. Due to not being in good financial condition, he took a job. From Kartik month of year 1679, he started writing the 'Vigyanbhashya' of 'Surya-Siddhanta' which was continuously published in the monthly magazine of the Science Council. This ended in year 1667. The Science Council published it in book form in two parts.

He received the Mangalaprasad award and the Chunnulal award for this text.

Upon completion of the first edition of this text, it is being re-published at the request of the readers.

This book, equipped with the 'Vigyan Bhashya Tika', is a priceless treasure of ancient Indian literature and a glorious book of Hindi. 'Surya-Siddhanta' is useful and collectible for all libraries and inquirers.

Introduction

Many texts of ancient literature have been published on behalf of Dr. Ratnamukari Swadhyay Sansthan—the texts of Swami Satyaprakash and Dr. Usha Jyotishmati, such as Bakshali-Manuscript, Shulba-Sutras (in Sanskrit and English). In this tradition, we are publishing the Science Commentary of Surya-Siddhanta by Swargiya Shri Mahavir Prasad Srivastava. This honor has been received from the Science Council, Prayag, for which we are indebted to the officers of the council.

It would have been difficult for us to complete the arduous task of publication of this book if we had not received financial assistance from the respected Raisahab Chaudhary Pratap Singh ji and the trust established by him in Karnal. We are extremely grateful to Chaudhary Saheb. We are currently publishing the first part, which includes Madhyamadhikar, Spashtadhikar, and Triprashnadhikar. In the second part, this book will be completely finished.

Role

Swami Dayananda gave a comprehensive curriculum of study and teaching to graduates of the Vidya-Layas in 1874 in his immortal text Satyarth Prakash. This course has historical significance because before this arrangement by Rishi Dayananda, there was no comprehensive system of courses in this country. In 1858, three universities were opened in the country—Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay. In 1888, two more universities (after the death of Maharishi Dayananda) were established in Prayag and Lahore. Such examinations of Sanskrit, like that of Kashi, had not begun. Therefore, we can surely say that the entire curriculum method of Rishi Dayananda is the first attempt in this direction. After studying grammar, the Rishi said that he taught Manusmriti, Valmiki Ramayana, Mahabharata, Shad Darshanas, Brahmanas, Upavedas (Ayurveda, Dhanurveda, Gandharvaveda; Arthaveda-Shilpa etc.). Then he wrote that in two years, learn astrology, the theory of the sun, which includes algebra, numbers, geography, astronomy, and geology, as is.

The primary source of astrological subjects is the hymns of the Vedas. The name of Sukta 164 of the first Mandala of Rigveda is Asyavamiya Sukta. The mantra-darshita of this Sukta is Rishi Dirgatamas. This Sukta is the inspirational source of astrology-

Twelve are not the wheel that circulates in the mind of the wise.

O son of fire, do not be deceitful here for seven hundred and twenty-five.

(RV 1/164/11)

The cycle of the sun which has twelve rays, which constantly moves, never tires, does not age, does not die. It has 720 sons (360 days and 360 nights). In the Atharvaveda, they are in the nineteenth section of two Suktas (Suktas 7 and 8), whose sage is Gargya. In this Sukta, the calculation of 27 constellations is given. Taking inspiration from the Vedas, Lagadha Muni composed Vedanga Jyotish, whose verses are found in Rig Jyotish and Yuj-Jyotish. Lagadha's time is considered to be before 600 AD. There is another word for Jyotish for this, Kaal-Vidhan-Shastra (Yuj-Jyotish 3). Lagadha also used the word "Ganit" in this sense, and the glory of this part of Vedanga is expressed as follows—

Source page 7

7

As the splendor of the crest of peacocks and the jewels of snakes are as such, so is the mathematics of the Vedangas.

Yuj: Jyotish, verse 4

The splendor of the crest in the body of the peacock and the glory of the jewel on the head of the snakes are the mathematics of the Vedangas, that is, the mathematics of astrology.

After the Vedangas, many principles of astrology were practiced in the field of Jyotish. Five of these principles are of special importance. Varahamihira discussed them comparatively in his famous work "Panchasiddtantika". The five principles are counted in the following verse—

Polish-Romak-Vasishtha-Sora-Patamahasru Panchasiddhanta:

Latdev analyzed the first two of these. According to Varahamihira, the calculation in the Polish theory is true, and the Romak theory is also almost the same. The true theory of sunlight, i.e., the solar theory or the sun theory, is even clearer than these two. The remaining two, Vasishtha and Patamaha, are false (misled). One edition of Panchasiddtantika was published by Professor Thibaut and Mahamahopadhyaya Sudhakar Dwivedi along with the English translation. The name of Sudhakar ji's Sanskrit commentary is “Panchasiddtantika Prakashika” (Prayag, 15 December 1888).

In the same tradition, Shri Mahavir Prasad Srivastava, an old councilor of the Science Council, Prayag, took up the arduous task of the science commentary of the Sun Theory. This lifetime work of his ended in 1640 AD. The work began in 1622, its first chapter (Madhyamadhikar) was published in 1624. The twelfth chapter was printed in 1631. Work stopped due to lack of funds. The last two chapters were printed in 1640. Thus, this commentary ended in Bhai Tritiya Samvat 1667 B.E. i.e., 1640 AD. This book was published in the science-monthly magazine in small parts, and some copies of the book were also prepared separately. This science commentary of the Sun Theory has been unavailable for the last about 20 years.

The Swadhyay Sansthan has attained this honor, by the immense generosity of the officers of the Science Council, Prayag, which obtained permission for its publication. The Swadhyay Sansthan has taken charge of the organization of the publication of precious books of ancient literature. We are publishing this book in two parts. The pictures included in the book were taken by the Block Science-Parishad

Role of the Commentator

[A brief excerpt of the introduction written by Sw. Shri Mahavir Prasad Srivastava]

Astrology is the principal part of the Vedas because from it the time of sacrifices is determined. Therefore, in ancient times in Bharata, the study-teaching of astrology was considered meritorious work. It also has another name, Kalavidhyashastra or Kalajnan. According to Kashyap Samhita, there were 18 Acharyas who were the originators of astrology, whose names are:-

1—Surya, 2—Pitamah, 3—Vyasa, 4—Vasishtha, 5—Atri, 6—Parashar, 7—Kashyap, 8—Narad, 9—Garg, 10—Marichi, 11—Manu, 12—Angira, 13—Lomash, 14—Paulish, 15—Chyavan, 16—Yavana, 17—Bhrigu and 18—Shaunak.

The principles and texts of these 18 names are unknown. Many are the doers of both Samhitas and Siddhantas, some only in one subject, and the text of some names is not available in both subjects.

The ancient principles that have been discussed since the time of Varahamihira are 1—Paulish, 2—Romak, 3—Vasishtha, 4—Saur, and 5—Patamah Siddhanta, which Varahamihira has collected in his book named Panch-Siddhantika (approximately 550 AD), in which he also states that the Paulish Siddhanta is clear, the Romak-Siddhanta is close to it, but the Surya-Siddhanta is the clearest, the other two are very corrupted. On page 2 of Panchsiddhantika-Prakashika Tika, M. M. Sudhakar Dwivedi quotes Suryarun-Samvad and says that the knowledge of the sages Gargadi which Maharshi Paulish said is the Paulish Siddhanta, which arose in the city of Romak due to Brahmashap, which the Sun God revealed to the Yavana caste of Romak is the Romak Siddhanta, which Vasishtha gave to his son Parashar is the Vasishtha Siddhanta, which the Sun gave to May Daitya is the Saur-Siddhanta, and which Brahma gave to his son Vasishtha is the Patamah-Siddhanta.

Where this Surya-Runa dialogue is taken from is not stated. According to this, the preceptors of both the Rumak theory and the solar theory are the Sun God, the first

However, Brahmagupta (628 AD) considered only the Romaka theory as foreign (memory external), not the solar theory. Chapter 2-6 of the current solar theory states that at the end of Satya Yuga, an asura named Maya performed penance of the Sun God to learn astrology, and then he appointed his part-man for this task. This same part-man made the entire solar theory, which the Sun God himself had told the sages in previous ages, known to Maya-asura, from which the sages then obtained it.

If the scriptures, Brahmin texts, and Upanishads are studied impartially, it will be revealed that even in that prehistoric period, the experiences of sky-gazing are filled everywhere and much debate was held on them. If this were not the case, from where does the fact that they occur in different constellations of the Ayan biṃdu come, and how could they know the relationship between seasons and months and dates and constellations! Even in medieval India, there was no lack of wise and microscopic astrologers and mathematicians. By reading the texts of Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Brahmagupta, Manjal, Keshav, Ganesh, etc., they can know what subtle things they wrote about the events of the sky. Now, Shankar Balakrishna Dikshit, Prabodhchandra Sengupta, etc., have also proven through the comparative study of the texts of Eastern and Western astrologers that Indian astrology is completely independent of the astrology of Hipparchus or Ptolemy.

It is clear from Aryabhatiya that Aryabhata created the Aryabhatiya text by churning the ancient Indian astrology and by self-observing the Sun, Moon, planets, and constellations.1

Mihir possessed the Siddhanta texts of the Yavanas and the manner of their explanation suggests that they were introducing new ideas or at least ideas and words that were not common in both in their texts, and it is certain that some of these ideas are later than those of Talmi. To refute this view, the strongest evidence I know is that Varahamihira showed ignorance of the motion of the ecliptic or the motion of the vernal equinox, although he knew that in his time it occurred at the beginning of the south motion of the constellation Cancer or in the Pushya constellation, and in ancient times it occurred at half of Ashlesha.1 If he had been familiar with the texts of Hipparchus or Talmi, he would have certainly accepted their writing on the precession of the equinoxes. Brahmagupta also did not pay attention to this, which shows that the matter of the precession of the equinoxes was not emphasized by medieval Indian astrologers, although he had experienced it through direct observation of the sky in ancient times that the constellations of Uttaraayana and Dakshinayana had changed because the Maitrayini Upanishad mentions that Dakshinayana occurred when the sun remained from Magha to half of Dhanishtha and Uttaraayana occurred when the sun remained from Shravishtha-ardha to Ashlesha. In Vedanga Jyotisha, it is clearly stated that the beginning of Uttaraayana occurred when the sun came to the beginning of Shravistha. Varahamihira, while discussing this, state that in our time, Dakshinayana is in Punarvasu, and if it is different from this, one should determine it by observation2.

It is clear from the above numbers that the Indian value of the sidereal year is not more than 3 minutes 27 seconds larger than the actual sidereal year, and Brahmagupta's value is the closest to it. In fact, this value is about a quarter minute less than the value of the mean-centre year, so they are almost exactly the same. This is why the motion of the apogee of the sun is generally considered negligible in our texts. In comparison, there is more error in the values of the sidereal year of Meton and Babylon. The values of the sidereal year of Thaalmi and Kepler are six or seven and a half minutes more than the actual sidereal year. Therefore

The direction of these matters has been shown in various places in the Scientific Commentary.

The composition period of Sūrya Siddhānta—there is a great difference of opinion among scholars regarding this. The composition period stated in this book does not make sense by logic because if it had continued in the same way for so ancient a time, twenty-one lakh, sixty thousand years, then why does the question arise that when will the fourteen years of exile of the Pandavas be completed, in the court of Maharaja-adhiraj Duryodhana in the Mahabharata era, where great scholars existed at that time? Even from Bhishma's answer, it is not understandable that he had knowledge of the astrological calculations of a text like Sūrya Siddhānta at that time. However, there is no doubt that the original form of this text is much earlier than Varahamihira, and it is possible that the form seen in Panchasiddhāntika is not the original form, but Varahamihira made some amendments to it. But it is surprising that Aryabhata (476 AD) did not mention it anywhere in his text, from which it is estimated that it was composed around the time of the composition of Aryabhatiya. The form of Sūrya Siddhānta given by Varahamihira is different from the current Sūrya Siddhānta, in which the matters of precession have been added from behind because if the discussion of precession had been in Sūrya Siddhānta before Varahamihira, it must have been included somewhere in Panchasiddhāntika and not been satisfied by writing only that the precession point was in the Nakshatra of Ayana in ancient times, now it is in Punarvasu. Even in the time of Brahmagupta (628-665 AD), the form of Sūrya Siddhānta did not have the matter of precession because in such a situation, Brahmagupta would have certainly discussed it. This point must have been found some time before Bhaskaracārya, but still not in that form as seen now because Bhaskaracārya himself has expressed doubt about its purity. Therefore, it is proven that the original form of the current Sūrya Siddhānta is the same as that given in Panchasiddhāntika and existed even before Varahamihira, or Varaha Sūrya Siddhānta is its modified form and later astrologers have periodically refined it.

The opinion of Western scholars—Western scholars have greatly pondered the relationship with the time of composition of this, for which it is our utmost duty to thank them. Mr. Bentley has done a lot of work in this matter. He calculated the positions of the Sun, Moon, and other planets for different times according to the Sūrya Siddhānta and new observations, and fixed the time of composition of the Sūrya Siddhānta when the portions of the planets according to both calculations become equal. This will be clear from the bracket on page 14 where the inaccuracies of the planets are shown.

From this Bentley derives the result that the Sūrya Siddhānta was written in the late phase of the 11th century. In appearance, it seems very logical and there is no doubt that the author has shown great novelty in it, but in reality, this method is not acceptable without proper examination. I understand sufficiently this point in the words of the publication committee of Burgess's translation:-

The times that Bentley has taken for the relationship of the other planets with the zero error are very close to the times we have calculated, which we have derived by calculating backward from the errors of 1860 AD, and which are given with the commentary of the 67th verse.

Upon comparing these two brackets, it will immediately be seen that Bentley did not derive his decision from the inaccuracies of the absolute positions of the planets, but from the comparison with the position of the Sun. However, he did not consider the inaccuracy of the Sun's position. The Hindu zodiac is sidereal and does not depend in any way on the motion of the Sun. Like other planets, the Sun was not at the position assumed in 3102 B.C., and therefore the motion of the Sun considered in this method is different from the reality because the sidereal year is considered 3 minutes larger. Therefore, why not consider the inaccuracy of the Sun and why consider the sidereal motion of the planets in comparison to this inaccurate motion? It is apparent that Bentley should have considered the position of the Sun completely and should have shown that the same result follows from the calculation of other planets, and if not, what was the cause of the inconsistency? "But what is the real matter about our theory? We get that in it such polaritudes of the planets have been given whose positions, when tested according to the method above, it seems that these polaritudes were not determined with the idea that their actual celestial positions could be known at a specified time. Rather, they give such evidence that an attempt was made in the 10th or 11th century AD to know the positions of the planets exactly in comparison to the position of the Sun. This is also doubtful in terms of time because there is a great variation in those times, in which error is considered zero. In the history of Sanskrit literature, this fact is as certain as anything that the Sūrya Siddhānta existed much earlier than that time. The instructions and quotations from other astronomical texts also show that there were many recensions of this book and we have also seen above (in shloka 6) that there are not exactly the same polaritudes given in the current text that were considered in the Sūrya Siddhānta. Therefore, what else could be that the calculation of the seed which was done for the revision in the 10th or 11th century was merely done by changing four or five shlokas in the original.

The time of the zero inaccuracy of the sun in our brackets is 250 AD. There is no need to emphasize the inaccuracy of this date, because it depends on the purity of the position of the sun which was determined first and then directed from that point which is called the initial point of the celestial circle. It was impossible to observe with the naked eye whether the center of the sun was when, according to the mean motion, the star Zeta Pisces was ten lunar phases before the conjunction of Revati, and it is clear that the Hindus have made big mistakes in the other points of the zodiac determined from this point, and if even a fraction of an error is made in determining the position of the sun, a difference of 425 years may occur in the time of zero inaccuracy.

The time of Sūrya Siddhānta also comes around the time of the conjunction stars' polar longitudes given by Brahmagupta and others by comparison. Some polar longitudes are obtained in these. These are those which are integral in all three texts, some of which the authors themselves have purified. From their comparative study we can know the superior and inferior limit of the Sūrya Siddhānta period. In Varaha's Panchasiddhāntikā as well (according to Thibo), seven polar longitudes of the conjunction stars are given which we consider the polar longitudes of that ancient Sūrya Siddhānta which existed before Varaha (see pages 20-21).*

The constellations written below are chosen for the depiction of the ancient Sūrya Siddhānta time, for which the longitudes of Brahmagupta are greater than the polar longitudes of the Sūrya Siddhānta are shown:-

Ansha kala kṛttikā 4 48 Rohini 1 28 Punarvasu 5 3 Magha 3 0 Po Phaalguni 3 0 Chitra 3 0 Yoga 20 16 Madhyamamana 3 23

The mean of the excess of the polar longitudes of these six stars is equal to 3 degrees 23 arc. If an increase of one degree of longitude is considered to have happened in 72 years due to the motion of the ecliptic, then this increase must have happened in approximately 244 years. However, we know for certain from Brahmagupta's time that it is 628 AD. Therefore, the time of Sūrya Siddhānta comes 244 years before this or 384 AD. It can be understood in a gross sense as 400 AD. This is the superior limit of this time. To find the inferior limit, we should look at the polar longitudes of the stars written below whose longitudes are greater than those of Brahmagupta by 1 degree 15 arc.

Thus, it can be concluded that the composition of Sūrya Siddhānta took place from 400 AD to 725 AD. Bentley and Burgess also compared the polar stars in Sūrya Siddhānta with the proven polar stars from the modern astronomical measurements to determine the time of Sūrya Siddhānta in this way, but it does not seem so accurate, because the kind of error that the Sūrya Siddhāntakar made regarding the arcs, Brahmagupta and others must have also made. Thus, the upper limit of the period of composition can be extended further. However, the lower limit can be brought up to 1100 AD as proved by Bentley.

The view of Bentley is also supported by the matter of the motion of the ecliptic. In the time of Bhaskara-Charrya, the ecliptic motion written in Sūrya Siddhānta was not as much as in the current Sūrya Siddhānta. It is apparent that the correction of the ecliptic motion was made after Bhaskaraacharya. However, the time of Bhaskaraacharya is 1150 AD.

The author of Sūrya Siddhānta—it has been shown that the polar coordinates of Sūrya Siddhānta do not match the polar coordinates of the Greek astrologers Hipparchus, Talmi, or other Western country astrologers. Therefore, this treatise was not written based on the observations of those people. Its tradition is explained by Vivsvān, that is, by the Sun (see Chapter on Mean Motions verse 8-6), just as the tradition of the Yoga path described in the Bhagavad Gita is explained (see Bhagavad Gita Chapter 4 verse 1-2). Maya is not foreign. He was a resident of India and obtained this knowledge, and the sages also learned from him. This seems to be the secret of the story given in Sūrya Siddhānta. Due to the Brahmashāpa, the story of the Sun God arising in the luminous city is fabricated and is found only in one or two handwritten books.

Source page 23

( 23)

is, therefore, it is projected which no one has accepted. If the Sūrya Siddhānta had been obtained by Trideśi, Brahmagupta would surely have written it, because for the Romak Siddhānta, which is undoubtedly foreign, he has written it clearly. There is no trace in the Prakashika ṭīkā of M.M.P. Sudhakar Dwivedi that gives the origin of the Surya-sūrvāda, so it cannot be said who wrote it and on what basis. The writing in Nityānanda1 that it was written when the 3600 years of Kali Yuga had passed, i.e., in the year 421 or 466 AD, when Aryabhata wrote his Aryabhatiya, is a delusion. Perhaps because of this delusion, Muniśvara also considered Aryabhata the author of the Sūrya Siddhānta. Alberuni's statement that it is a delusion that Latāchārya or Laṭsiṃha made it2 is because neither Varāhamihira nor Brahmagupta considered Latāchārya the author of the Sūrya Siddhānta. According to Varāhamihira, Latāchārya is an interpreter of the Romak and Polish theories. Latā's measurements3 are from the sunset time of Yavanpura. Thus, it is apparent that all the estimations regarding the time of composition and author of the Sūrya Siddhānta are not proven. Based on internal evidence, it can only be said that its growth started around 400 AD and ended by 1200 AD. Initially, Varāhamihira must have expanded (amended) it. Then other modifiers tried to make it Up-to-date by taking advantage of the observations of Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, Manjula, etc. This amendment continued until Rangnath ji wrote its commentary and bound its verses. Some more verses are found in Madhav Purohit's commentary, don't know if they were written on the basis of an old text or just added.

Scientific Commentary—some people interpret the second verse of the ninth verse to mean that the scripture that the Sun God taught to the sages is that same scripture without any change, only a difference in the time of saying. But if this were the meaning, what was the need to say that there is a difference in time? What was said in the first verse was sufficient. Therefore, the more reasonable meaning of this verse is that if there is any difference in the Jyotiḥ-shastra previously stated and the one being stated at this time, it is due to time, and there is no essential difference. How can there be a difference due to time? The reason is that the Jyotiḥ-shastra is an experimental science and some subtle errors remain in the experiment, which is called experimental error. This error accumulates in Jyotiḥ-shastra year by year and after hundreds of years it takes a very large form; therefore, it has to be revised from time to time, which is called seed-transformation. From this perspective, this sentence was said by Suryāṁśa Puruṣa, for which there are 21 verses named 'Bijopanayana' in the last chapter of the Surya Siddhānta, which Rangnath Ji and Pan. Indranarayan Dwivedi Ji have not considered as a commentary and have explained the reason for not considering it as a commentary, which is that how the seed-transformations are done by the Sun God in the scripture spoken by the Sun God. But Rangnath Ji, while explaining the 6th verse in his gūḍhārtha-prakāśikā commentary, also state that some difference occurs upon taking time. His sentences are as follows:

And also by the movements of time, if there are some celestial bodies, then in the time between the ages, the scriptures were revealed by the compassionate ones for the purpose of the planetary movements, as in the subsequent scriptures, the meaning of which is. Scientific Commentary—When a healthy person is sitting comfortably, the time it takes to inhale and exhale air (life air) naturally is called Pran. This is the smallest unit that could be measured at that time. There was no means to measure less time than this at that time; therefore, it was called abstract. Now such clocks are made by which the measurement of that unit is easy, which are called abstract. In one lunar day, 60 clocks = 60 X 60 shadows = 60 X 60 X 60 Pran or 21600 Pran exist. Similarly, in 1 day, 24 hours = 24 X 60 minutes = 24 X 60 X 60 seconds or 86400 seconds exist. Therefore, there are 4 seconds in 1 Pran. Everyone knows how easy it is to measure a second when the hand of the clock is attached to it. There are also such clocks by which the fifth or tenth part of 1 second can be easily known. However, the tenth part of 1 second is the same as the fortieth part of 1 Pran. Therefore, some units below Pran can also be called concrete nowadays.

Pran is also called Asu. In the Siddhānta-Shiromani of the famous astrologer Bhaskaraacharya ji, the second definition of Pran is given in the words of Chandas-shastra—the time taken to pronounce one Guru letter is called Pran ten times that time. A Guru letter is that which has a conjunct letter after it, such as Sanuswar, Visargant, Dirgha, and the short letter.

There is also a name for a unit of weighing, which is like four tole.

This word reveals that the 12 months that make up a year are the solar months. The year of Chandra, Nakshatra, or Sawan months is not.

It is shown that in 1 day there are 21600 prana or 86400 seconds, so in 1 prana there are 672000 nimesha or 45 nimesha and 1 second has 113 nimesha.

Nakshatra Ahuratra—Nakshatra means star, star-group and the 27th part of the cycle on which the sun appears to revolve once in a year. Due to the daily motion of the Earth, all stars in the sky rise in the east, move towards the west, set in the west, and then rise in the east. Note down the time of rising of any star by looking at the clock and see when that star rises again. If the clock is correct, the time between these two risings is approximately 23 hours 56 minutes and 4 seconds. This is called Nakshatra Ahuratra or only Nakshatra day. This is always the same, it does not increase or decrease, if the very subtle motion of the stars is not considered. Therefore, astrologers calculate time from this.

Sawan day — the time from one sunrise of the sun to the next sunrise is called Sawan day. It is 4 minutes larger than Nakshatra day. The Sawan day's

2. Siddhanta Shiromani Ganitadhyaya Madhyamadhikar, Kala Manayaadhyaya Shloka 16, 17.

Source page 31

The value is not the same. Therefore, the value of the mean Sāvan day is the time known by clocks.

The Indav Tithi or Chandra Tithi—the time when the moon reaches very close to the sun while revolving in the sky is the new moon. The time between one new moon and the next new moon is called the lunar month. Its mean value is 26.530587646 of the mean Sāvan day. After the new moon, the moon moves further towards the east from the sun, and when it moves 12 degrees further, the first tithi (pariva) passes. When the difference is between 12 and 24 degrees, it remains duija. When the moon is ahead of the sun from 24 to 36 degrees, it remains tīja. When the difference is between 178 and 180 degrees, it is the full moon. When the moon is ahead from 180 to 162 degrees, it is the 16th tithi or pariva (pratipada). Duija remains from 1620 to 2040, etc. After the full moon, the moon moves back by 2 hours (48 minutes) each day from sunset. The 14, 15 days from the full moon to the new moon are called the dark fortnight. The new moon is also called the 30th tithi, which is why 30 is written for the new moon in Panchangs.

Sārmāsa—the path along which the sun travels while revolving in the sky is called the ecliptic. Its twelfth part is called the Rāshi. The center of the solar system, at the time it enters one Rāshi and moves to another Rāshi, that time is the transit of the second Rāshi. The time between one transit and the next transit is called Sārmāsa. The 12 solar months are different in magnitude; the reason for this is that the motion of the sun is not always the same. When the motion of the sun is fast, it completes one Rāshi quickly and the solar month is shorter. Conversely, when the motion of the sun is slow, the solar month is larger.

The number of types of months is equal to the number of types of years; a lunar year of twelve lunar months, a Sawan year of twelve Sawan months, and a solar year of twelve solar months. Our astrologer tradition has believed this. However, the direct meaning of the second part of the 13th verse is that there is a year of 12 months, which is called the divine day. Therefore, the year of twelve months mentioned is not other months, only solar months. This proves that the Surya Siddhanta discusses only the solar year and considers the solar year as the year, not others.

Source page 32

Chapter on Mean Motions

It is stated that the North Pole of the Earth is the abode of the gods and the South Pole is the abode of demons. Therefore, the North Pole is called Deva-loka and the South Pole is called Asur-loka. At the time when the sun comes to the equator, day and night are equal. This phenomenon occurs only twice a year. The sun remains north of the equator for 6 months and south for 6 months. In the first half, the day is longer and the night is shorter in the northern hemisphere and the day is shorter and the night is longer in the southern hemisphere. In the second half, it is exactly the opposite. However, when the sun remains north of the equator, it is visible on the North Pole (on Mount Sumeru) for 6 months and not visible at the South Pole at this time. Therefore, this half is called the day of the gods and the night of the demons. When the sun remains south of the equator for 6 months, the gods are not seen at the North Pole and the demons are seen equally at the South Pole for 6 months. Therefore, this half is called the night of the gods and the day of the demons. Therefore, our 12 months are like one yuga of the gods or demons.

Scientific Commentary—the 14th verse states that there is a divine year of 360 days for gods or asuras. The 13th verse states that one day of the gods is like one solar year, so it is clear that one year of the gods is equal to 360 solar years. According to the 15th verse, a Chaturyuga is a period of 12000 divine years or 12000 X 360 (i.e., 432000) solar years. Chaturyuga is also called Mahayuga. In one Mahayuga there are four Yugas: Satya Yuga; Treta, Dvapara, and Kali Yuga, which is why it is also called Chaturyuga. In Satya Yuga, Dharma has four stages, in Treta three stages, in Dvapara two stages, and in Kali Yuga one stage. Similarly, in one Mahayuga, Satya Yuga has four parts, Treta has three parts, Dvapara has two parts, and Kali Yuga has one part. Therefore,

Divine years in solar years, Satya Yuga, Treta, 4800 1728000, Dvapara, 3600 1296000, Kali Yuga, 2400 864000, Mahayuga 1200 432000

Both sandhyas of Satya Yuga are equal to the sixth part, so one sandhya (period) is equal to the twelfth part. The sandhya at the beginning of the Yuga and the sandhya at the end are called Adi Sandhya and Ant Sandhya. Their values are as follows:-

In divine years in solar years, the beginning and end sandhyas of Satya Yuga are 400 144000, of Treta 300 108000, of Dvapara 200 72000, of Kali Yuga 100 360000

Just as there are two sandhyas in the morning and evening in one Ahoraatra, there are two sandhyas in each Yuga, one at the beginning and one at the end.

तेषां तु परिवर्तन पौष्णान्ते भगणास्मृतः ॥२७॥

Translation—(25) The planets, moving with the swift constellations, always fall behind in their respective orbits by the same amount while moving towards the west; (26) Therefore, they appear to move towards the east and their daily motion also appears different according to the circumference of the orbits; Therefore, the lunar cycle also completes in this different time, that is, (27) in a short time of swift movement and in a long time of slow movement. The cycle that is completed at the end of Revati is called bhagaṇa.॥25-27॥

Scientific Commentary—the principle of the motion of the planets is explained in these three shlokas; therefore, these are of great importance. From these, it is revealed in brief what the ancient Indian astronomers thought about the planets. It is stated in the 25th shloka that all the stars seen in the sky are moving towards the west with the planets; but due to the very fast movement of the constellations, the planets lag behind and appear to move in the easterly direction. The speed of their movement towards the east is the same, but because the extent of their orbits is different, their motion also appears different. The secret of this will be revealed in the following figure—suppose that the inner circle in the given figure is 10 inches and the outer is 15 inches, and suppose that two ants moving at a speed of 1 inch per second orbit the inner and outer circles from the positions of x and y, which are in a straight line with the center; then it is clear that the ant moving on the outer circle will complete one orbit in 15 seconds and the ant moving on the inner circle will complete one orbit in 10 seconds. This proves that when moving with the same linear motion, the revolution of orbits of different sizes will take different times. But in the 27th shloka

Source page 39

It has been said that fast-moving planets complete their orbits in a short time and slow-moving planets in a long time. There seems to be some opposition here, but this is not an opposition; because the motion stated in the first verse is the planimetric motion and the motion in this verse is the angular (Angular velocity). One revolution is of 360 degrees; therefore, one inch of the outer circle makes an angle of 360/15 = 24^° at the center and one inch of the inner circle makes an angle of 360/10 = 36^°. Therefore, although the rectilinear motion of ants is the same at 1 inch per second, although their angular motion is different per second. The outer ant moves at 24^° per second and the inner at 36^°. Therefore, it is clear that the fast-moving ones will complete their orbits in less time and the slow-moving ones in more time.

In the 27th verse, the definition of revolution is also given. When the planet moves towards the east, starting from the end of the constellation Revati, and after completing one revolution, it comes back to the end of Revati, then it completes one revolution (constellation group which is 27). Therefore, revolution is also called a circuit.

Source page 40

According to this principle, it must be assumed that there is a special relationship between the distances of the planets and their periods of revolution. The farther a planet is, the longer its period of revolution (time taken to complete a revolution) is. This relationship is stated very briefly here. Its full explanation will be given in the twelfth chapter called Bhūgolāyādhya, comparing the principles of Indian and Western astrologers.

When the linear motions of all the planets are assumed to be equal, it can be easily proven what is the mutual relationship between the distances of the planets; because it is not difficult to know how many days each planet takes to complete one revolution. When it is known that Saturn takes a revolution in a coarse manner in 30 years and the Sun in 1 year and their linear motions are equal, then it is self-evident that the orbit of the Sun is 30 times the orbit of Saturn; because in 30 years the Sun travels 30 times its orbit and Saturn is able to complete its orbit only once. Therefore, the orbit of Saturn = 30 X orbit of the Sun. That is, the distance of Saturn from the Earth is 30 times the distance of the Sun. Similarly, the distances of the other planets can also be known.

It has been known from the current observations that the relationship between the mutual distances of the planets is not so simple, nor are their linear motions the same. Now it is proven that the distance of Saturn from the Earth is almost 10 times the distance of the Sun from the Earth.

विकलानां कला षष्ट्या तत् षष्ट्या भाग उच्यते ।
तत्त्रिंशता भवेद्राशिः भगणो द्वादशेव ते ॥ २८ ॥

Translation—A skill of 60 zodiacs, a part or fraction of 60 zodiacs, a quantity of 30 parts or fractions, and a revolution of 12 zodiacs॥28॥

Scientific Commentary—these are the units for measuring angles. The entire zodiac cycle is called revolution. If twelve equal parts are made of this revolution, each part is called rashi. The thirtieth part of rashi is an degrees, the sixty-th part of degrees is arcminutes, and the sixty-th part of arcminutes is arcseconds. Revolution and rashi are used only for that celestial cycle in which the sun appears to revolve around the earth in its plane and other planets revolve somewhat shifted. However, degrees, arcminutes, and arcseconds are also used in measuring other angles. Nowadays, the way to write degrees in short is that a small circle slightly to the right of the digit indicating the magnitude of degrees.

Source page 41

They write, for writing the arts, they draw a crooked line slightly to the right of the number and a similar two slanted lines for the obliquity; for example, if one wants to write 5 degrees 16 minutes and 50 seconds, they write 5°16'50".

There is a proportional relationship in the units of measuring angles and time. The time it takes the Sun to complete one revolution is one year, the time it takes for one zodiac sign to move is one month, the time it takes for one degrees to move is one day, the time it takes for one arcminutes to move is approximately one hour, and the time it takes for one arcseconds to move is approximately the same as a moment.

Translation—(26) The Sun, Mercury, and Venus moving in the retrograde direction in one (Maha) yuga, the revolutions of Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter are also the same number of revolutions as the Moon's 5,77,53,336 revolutions, the 22,96,832 revolutions of Mars (31), 176,37,060 revolutions of Mercury, and 3,64,220 revolutions of Jupiter. Scientific Commentary—It would be good to state here what is the old tradition for writing numbers among us. Some words have been fixed to write the numbers one, two, three, four, etc., in verse. Those or their synonyms are placed in order according to the rule 'ankānām vāmato gatiḥ', that is, the word indicating the number written in the unit place is written first, then the word indicating the tens place.

Source page 42

The word indicating the number being referred to, and the word indicating the place in the hundreds, are kept in sequence. For example, if 325 is said, the word indicating 5 is written first, such as Panch, Ishu, Margana, etc., and after it, the word indicating 2 is written, such as Dvi, Ashvi, Yama, etc., then the word indicating 3 is written, such as Tri, Agni, Shikhi, etc. In this way, 325 can be written as Panchaavashikhi or Ishuyamagni. This is the same procedure for writing numbers in Sūrya Siddhānta, Brahmasphuta-Siddhānta, and Siddhanta-Shiromani. The ways of writing numbers in the Aryabhatiya of the first Aryabhata and the Mahā-Siddhānta of the second Aryabhata are different from this.

The number of revolutions of the planets in one great age are given above according to the Sūrya Siddhānta. According to the theories of Aryabhata and Brahmagupta, there are some differences in the values of the great age revolutions, and the values of the revolutions that are known with the help of sūkṣmayaṃtroṃ nowadays do not match any theory but have only a slight variation. On the next page, we give a comparative view of the values of the Sūrya Siddhānta, the Brahmagupta-Siddhānta, and the modern revolutions, from which it will be apparent how little the difference is between the revolution periods calculated by our ancient astrologers and the revolution periods calculated by the modern sūkṣmayaṃtroṃ. The time taken for a planet to complete one revolution or orbit is called the revolution period. The method for calculating this is as follows according to the theory: divide the number of revolutions of that planet in one great age by the solar years of the great age, then 1 revolution period (in solar years) will be obtained. Now, you can write this either in decimal fractions or in Sawan days. The easiest way to calculate the revolution period in Sawan days is to divide the number of Sawan days in the great age by the great age revolution, the remainder is the number of Sawan days. Make the rest into hours, minutes, etc. Just as there are 60 minutes in 1 hour, so it can be imagined that there are 60 vipala in 1 pala and 60 prativipala in 1 vipala.

In these verses, the new words used are graha-shighra, chandrocch, and pata. To know their position, one must first know where the sun is. The period of revolution of their epicycles is the same as the time it takes for Mercury or Venus to revolve around the sun according to present opinion. Therefore, the period of revolution of the epicycles of Mercury or Venus should be understood as the time it takes for these constellations to revolve around the sun, not the zodiac, but around the sun. The epicycles of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are separate from the epicycles of the other two planets. Their period of revolution is considered the same as that of the sun. This means that the epicycles of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are the points that complete a revolution of the entire constellation cycle in 1 year. But the sun also completes one revolution of the constellation cycle in 1 year; therefore, the epicycles of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn remain near the sun. Special discussion will be made about these epicycles in the second chapter.

Mandaucch or uchch—it is stated above that the moon completes 4,88,203 cycles in one Mahayuga, therefore, according to the theory of the Sun, one Bhagankal is 3232 Sawan days, 5 ghadi, 37 pal, and 1306 vipal. The moon's high is that point of the lunar orbit which is at the farthest distance from the other points of the lunar orbit than the Earth. When the moon is at this point, due to being very far, it appears extremely small in size and its motion is also very slow. In the lunar orbit, there is also a point at 1800° from the lunar high which is very close to the Earth. When the moon comes to this point, its motion becomes the most intense and due to being very close, its size also appears very large. Due to this irregular motion of the moon, it is not easily possible to tell what its position will be at any time. Above this also

Source page 46

In the sky, a place does not remain fixed but keeps moving towards the east with a slow motion. The Moon completes one orbit in approximately 3232 Sawan days. The higher or apogee of other planets also move towards the east with even slower speeds. This imagination is not used nowadays. It has been proven by mathematics that the Moon and the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun, and the path of revolution is not circular but elliptical. Before saying anything about this, it is necessary to state some properties of the ellipse. The ellipse is a figure (Figure 3). The upper axis is called the major axis and the lower axis is called the minor axis, and the point where these two axes meet is called the center of the ellipse. At the center, the minor axis and the major axis have two equal parts. There are two such points on the major axis at equal distances from the center, which if connected to any point P, A, or B of the ellipse, then P + A = B + BA = PN + PI. These two points are called the focus of the ellipse. If the Moon's orbit is assumed, then the position of the Earth will not be there. From point N, the distance of the Moon's orbit is maximum at point U and minimum at point B, so point U will be the higher or apogee of the Moon and point B will be the lower of the Moon. If the position of the apogee is known, the position of the lower can be easily known, as it always remains at 180° from the higher.

Similarly, the Earth, Mars, Mercury, Venus, etc., also revolve in an ellipse around the Sun, and the Sun remains at the focus of these orbits. Why the motion is very slow at a high place and very fast at a low place is due to the variation in the force of attraction. When the planet is at a high place, the force of attraction is very small due to the very large distance, which slows down the planet's motion, and when it is at a low place, the force of attraction is very large due to the very small distance, which makes the planet's motion very fast. Many rules have been known regarding this, which are famous by the name of Kepler's laws; these will be discussed in due place in the second chapter named Chapter on True Positions.

Node—the path on which the Sun moves and revolves the sky in 1 year is called the circle of declination. Similarly, the path on which the Moon moves and orbits the Earth is called the lunar orbit. The circle of declination and the lunar orbit are not in the same plane and are not parallel; therefore, these two orbits appear to meet at two points; just as the strings of two flying kites meet at one point even though they remain very far from each other.

Source page 47

It seems and due to the variation in the motions of those kites, this point does not appear in the same direction. These points are called the nodes of the Moon. The Moon moves in its orbit and remains north of the ecliptic for half the period of revolution and south of the ecliptic for half the period of revolution. When it reaches its node, it either moves towards the north or/or the south of the ecliptic. The node to which it moves towards the north is called the Ascending node and the node to which it moves towards the south is called the Descending node. The Ascending node is also called Rahu and the Descending node is also called Ketu. When the Moon is near these nodes at the time of the full moon or new moon, a lunar eclipse or solar eclipse occurs; that is why it is imagined that Rahu and Ketu are demons caused by the eclipse. Some people consider the tip of the Earth's shadow as Rahu and the tip of the Moon's shadow as Ketu; but this is an illusion.

The positions of these nodes are also not fixed but seem to shift towards the west. The time taken for them to complete one revolution while shifting towards the west is called their period of revolution. Similarly, one should understand the positions of other planets. The reason why they shift towards the west is explained by very subtle mathematics in Physical Astronomy, which will also be explained in this Scientific Commentary in the appropriate place. In Figure 4, if the arc is understood as the path of the sun, i.e., the ecliptic, and the arc is understood as the lunar orbit, then the points R and Q are called the nodes of the moon. When the moon moves ahead of the node in the direction of the arrow, it becomes north of the ecliptic and remains north up to the arc part, therefore the node is called the northern node. Upon reaching point Q, the moon moves south of the ecliptic, therefore Q is called the southern node. The Indian astrologers call the northern node of the moon Rahu and the southern node Ketu. The angle between the ecliptic and the lunar orbit is the angle between the planes of the ecliptic and the lunar orbit, which is approximately 50. This angle of deviation of the moon is discussed in the 68th verse of this chapter.

In relation to the revolution of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus, Bhaskaraacharya says that the number of revolutions of the Sun is equal to the number of years in a Kalpa. Therefore, the period of the Sun's revolution is a year. Mercury and Venus remain sometimes a little ahead and sometimes a little behind the Sun, like a follower. Therefore, their revolutions are also the same as the Sun's revolution.

This method is given to know the period of the Sun's revolution—

Draw a circle on a plane and mark the directions in it. When the Sun is in the Uttarayana position, on the day when it rises a little south of the east, find the Sun by passing through the nail embedded in the center of the circle. After this, one should calculate the rising of the Sun for one year. The Sun will rise 365 times in a year. The last rising will be a little south of the rising place of the first day. Write the difference between these two. Find the Sun by rising on the second day. On this day, it will rise a little north of the east. Also know how much north it rises from the rising place of the previous day. Then, by the ratio, find out that when such a much north moves in 60 hours, then how much time has passed for the first difference. In this way, 15 hours 30 minutes 22 minutes 30 seconds and 365 Sawan days, the Sun rises in the same place as it did at the beginning of the year. Therefore, this time is the period of the Sun's revolution. Then, by the ratio, find out that when there are such Sawan days in 1 year, then how many Sawan days are there in 1 Kalpa years, etc.

What is used nowadays to know the vernal equinox is very much found in the method explained by Bhaskaraacharya ji. The difference is that Bhaskaraacharya ji asked to divide on the horizon circle, and nowadays it is divided on the meridian circle, so that no error can occur due to the lengthening and apparent deviation of light; the second difference is that the instruments of today are very subtle, but in the method explained by Bhaskaraacharya, it was done with a naked eye.

The derivation of the lunar revolution should also be known by dividing the spherical instrument in which the constellation circle, declination circle, obliquity circle, lunar orbit, planetary orbit, etc., remain, and knowing it. There does not seem to be a need to describe this in great detail. It is written only because ancient astronomers also tested the things given in the text by division and accepted what turned out to be correct.

Method of knowing the period of the moon's culmination

One should find the true motion by eclipsing the moon with the sphere instrument every day. On the day when the motion is least, there is no difference in the positions of the mean and true moon. This is the position of the moon's high point. Similarly, while observing daily, when the moon's motion becomes very small again, that same place should be considered the high point. This place remains some ahead of the first place. Knowing how far ahead it goes, one should calculate by the ratio how much the daily motion of the high point is and in how many days one revolution period is completed.

Method of knowing the period of lunar eclipse—while eclipsing the moon daily, one should see on which day the southward deviation of the moon becomes zero. At the time when the deviation is zero, the moon is at the position of the lunar eclipse. Similarly, when the southward deviation of the moon becomes zero in the second revolution, it should be understood that it has reached its node. The position of the node is some west of the first place; that is why it is said that the motion of the node is opposite, i.e., towards the west. Then one should know by the ratio that when the node moves this much in so many days, how much it will move in one day. This should be understood as the daily motion of the node. Similarly, one should also know how many revolutions occur in one kalpa.

Regarding the epicycle apogees of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—when they are ahead of the Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, or Mars, the planets remain some ahead of the mean position, and when the Sun is behind, the planets remain behind the mean position; therefore, the scholars imagined that the epicycle apogees of these three remain with the Sun and attract the planets towards themselves, i.e., towards the Sun; therefore, their revolution periods are the same as that of the Sun.

They complete the orbit. This orbit is called the sidereal revolution. Therefore, in one great age, the number of sidereal revolutions is equal to the number of sidereal-night.

The preceding part of the above shloka explains the method of knowing how many times a planet rises in the eastern horizon in one great age. Subtract the number of revolutions of the planet from the number of Nakshatra revolutions of a great age by the number of revolutions of the planet in one great age; the remaining number will be the number of times that planet will rise in the eastern horizon in one great age. Suppose we want to know how many times the sun rises in the eastern horizon in one great age. It is stated in the 26th shloka that the sun makes 43,20,000 revolutions in one great age. If this is subtracted from the Nakshatra revolutions of a great age of 1,58,22,37,828, then the remainder is 1,57,76,17,828. The sun rises in the eastern horizon 1,57,76,17,828 times in one great age. However, it is stated in the Scientific Commentary of the 12th shloka that the time between one rise and the next rise of the sun is called a Sawan day. Therefore, according to the 34th shloka, there are 1,57,76,17,828 Sawan days in one great age.

Similarly, the number of rises of the planets can also be known. Its derivation is as follows: If a star rises with the sun on a certain day, then the next day that star rises 3 minutes 56 seconds before the sun. Because in this time, the sun moves one degree towards the west. On the third day, that star will rise 2 times the time difference from the sun, that is 3 minutes 56 seconds earlier, i.e., 7 minutes 52 seconds before. On the fourth day, it will rise three times earlier than that, and on the 16th day, it will rise fifteen times earlier, i.e., 56 minutes and 1 minute less 1 hour earlier. In this way, after lagging behind, on the 361st day, i.e., after 360 sidereal days, that star will rise 24 minutes less, 24 hours earlier, and after 366 sidereal days, the whole 24 hours, i.e., 1 day earlier, when the sun and that star will be together again. Therefore, in the time it takes the constellation to complete 366 revolutions, the sun rises 1 time less and completes one revolution in that time. Therefore, the sun rises 366-1 times in one revolution period (in 1 solar year). Similarly, one should understand about the rises of other planets.

Sūrya Siddhānta—the time when the Sun and the Moon are in conjunction is called Amavasya. At this time, the Moon and the Sun are very close. The time from one Amavasya to the next Amavasya is called Chandra-masa. Therefore, if one wants to know how many Chandra-masas are in one Mahayuga, one should first know how many times the Sun and the Moon are in conjunction in one Mahayuga. For this, it is sufficient to find the difference in the Mahayuga revolutions of the Sun and the Moon. Because it is easily known that if two boys start revolving around a round field and if one boy makes 5 revolutions and the other 3, then if both start running from the same place at the same time, they will meet each other 5—3=2 times in an hour. For this, the example of the movement of the hands that tell the hours and minutes of a clock is very appropriate. At twelve o'clock, both hands remain together, meaning their conjunction remains. After this, both start revolving and meet for the first time at 1 hour and 561/9 minutes. The second time they meet at 2 hours and 10110/9 minutes, the third time at 3 hours and 1640/9 minutes, the fourth time at 4 hours and 2150/9 minutes, the fifth time at 5 hours and 2730/9 minutes, the sixth time at 6 hours and 3280/9 minutes, the seventh time at 7 hours and 3820/9 minutes, the eighth time at 8 hours and 4340/9 minutes, the ninth time at 6 hours and 4620/9 minutes, the tenth time at 10 hours and 5440/9 minutes, and the eleventh time exactly at twelve o'clock. For these eleven conjunctions, the minute hand had to make 12 revolutions and the hour hand had to make 1 revolution. The annual motion is calculated as follows:—the number of revolutions in a Kalpa is divided by the solar-year of the Kalpa, a different number of revolutions is obtained. Translation—(48) Add up the number of solar years that have passed after the end of Satya Yuga up to the end of Satya Yuga from the solar years mentioned above. (46) Keep this number in two places, multiply it by the number of lunar months of Mahayuga and divide by the number of solar months of Mahayuga, the remainder will be the number of eras from the beginning of creation to Ishtaka. Multiply this by 30 to make lunar days (tithis) and add the number of days that have passed in the current month up to Ishtaka, so that the number of days that have passed from the beginning of creation to Ishtaka will be known. (50) Keep the number of these days in two places. Multiply one by the number of Mahayuga decay-days and divide the product by the number of Mahayuga days, the remainder will be the number of decay-days from the beginning of creation to Ishtaka. Subtract this from the number of days kept in the second place, the remainder will be the number of Sawan-days up to the half-night of Lanka, which is one less than the number of half-nights. Because all the planets were together at the beginning of creation and how many revolutions they make in one great age and how many Sawan days there are, this has also been stated; therefore, by knowing how many revolutions occur in the Sawan days of the great age, in the Sawan days up to the auspicious time, the position of the planet comes out. The method of knowing the number of Sawan days up to the auspicious time, which is called Ahargana, is explained in the above three shlokas.

Translation—(51) One should know by counting from the Sun the day-lord, month-lord, and year-lord from the number of Sawan days. Divide this number by 7, the remainder is the day-lord starting from the order of days of the Sun. (52) If this (number of Sawan days) is divided sequentially by the numbers of months and years, and the quotients are multiplied sequentially by two and three, and one is added to each product, and the sums are divided by 7, then the remainder is the month-lord and year-lord in the order of days of the Sun. (51-52)

Scientific Commentary—The name of the day is given on the name of the planet which is considered the lord of the first hour (hora) at the beginning of the day. The planet which is the lord of the first hour is also considered the lord of that day. Similarly, the day that falls at the beginning of the Sawan month is considered the lord of that Sawan month, and the day that falls at the beginning of the Sawan year is considered the lord of that Sawan year. For example, the lord of the first hour of Sunday is Ravi, the lord of that day is Ravi, the lord of the month that starts with Sunday is Ravi, and the lord of the year that starts with Sunday is also Ravi.

*Sawan should not be considered as Shravan. The month of 30 Sawan days and the year of 12 Sawan months is called Sawan year.

Source page 64

To know which planet is the lord of which hour(hour), one should understand the sequence in which the lords of the hours change. Saturn is farther from the Earth than all the planets, then Jupiter is nearest to it, Mars is nearest to Jupiter, Sun is nearest to Mars, Venus is nearest to Sun, Mercury1 is nearest to Venus, and the Moon is nearest to Mercury. The lords of the hours change in this sequence. If the lord of the first hour is Saturn, then the lord of the second hour is Jupiter, the third is Mars, the fourth is the Sun, the fifth is Venus, the sixth is Mercury, the seventh is the Moon, the eighth is Saturn, and so on in sequence. However, the name of the day should be Saturday on the day when the lord of the first hour is Saturn. Therefore, the lord of the second hour of Saturday is Jupiter, the lord of the third hour is Mars, etc. In this way, the same sequence of lords restarts after every seven hours. Therefore, the lord of the 22nd hour of Saturday is Saturn, the 23rd is Jupiter, the 24th is Mars, and the lord of the hour after the 24th should be the Sun. But this 25th hour is the first hour of the next day whose lord is the Sun, so after Saturday comes Sunday. The lord of the second hour of Sunday is Venus, the third is Mercury, the fourth is the Moon, and so on in sequence, the lord of the 11th and 18th 25th hours is also the Moon. But the 25th hour is the first hour of the next day, so the next day falls under the name of the lord of this hour, which is Wednesday. In this way, the naming of other days has also been done2.

The reason why after Saturday comes Sunday and after Sunday comes Monday and after Monday comes Tuesday is now clear. In the order of the planets, Saturn is the fourth planet from the Sun, the Moon is the fourth planet from the Sun, Mars is the fourth planet from the Moon. Therefore, this rule has been established that the lord of each fourth planet, counted from Saturn, is the lord of the next day.

1. Earth is farther than Mercury and Venus, but in our astrological texts, Venus is considered farther. The reason for this is that the planet which is as far as much, completes its revolution in the same amount of time. This is also the belief of our astrologers, but they have taken this distance from Earth, and modern astrologers have taken it from the Sun.

2. This order of days is found in all countries. But the origin of their names, as done here, is worth finding out whether it is the same elsewhere or not.

The Maspati—if the first day of a Sawan month is Sunday, then the first day of the next Sawan month will be the 31st day from Sunday because the Sawan month is 30 days. But the 31st day from Sunday is Tuesday, which is the third day of the fifth week. Therefore, the lord of the second Sawan month is Mars. The first day of the third Sawan month is 31 days from Tuesday, which is the third day of the fifth week starting from Tuesday, which is Thursday. Therefore, the lord of the third Sawan month is Jupiter. Similarly, the lord of the fourth Sawan month is Saturn, the lord of the third day from Thursday, and the lord of the fifth Sawan month is the lord of Monday from Saturday, which is Som, and the lord of the sixth Sawan month is Mercury and the lord of the seventh Sawan month is Venus. This sequence will continue from the eighth Sawan month. Therefore, the first day of the Sawan month that comes on the third day in the order of days and its lord is the lord of that Sawan month. Now if one looks closely, it will be known that the order of the Maspatis is as follows according to the order of the planets—Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Moon, Mercury, and Venus; then Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, etc. If this cycle begins from the Moon, then their order will remain the same as the order in which they are considered sequentially distant from the Earth.

The lord of the year—the day from which the monsoon year begins is considered the lord of that year. If the beginning of the first monsoon year is on a Sunday, then the beginning of the second monsoon year will be on the 361st day from Sunday, which is the fourth day of the week after 51 weeks, which is Wednesday. Therefore, the lord of the second monsoon year will be Mercury. The beginning of the third monsoon year will be 361 days after the second monsoon year, so it will be the fourth day from Wednesday, which is Saturday, whose lord is Saturn. Therefore, the lord of the third monsoon year will be Saturn. Similarly, the lord of the fourth monsoon year will be Mars, the fourth day from Saturday. The lord of the fifth monsoon year will be Venus, the fourth day from Tuesday. The lord of the sixth monsoon year will be the Sun, the fourth day from Friday. The lord of the seventh monsoon year will be Jupiter, the fourth day from Monday. And the lord of the eighth monsoon year will be the Sun, the fourth day from Tuesday. In this way, the same sequence will begin from the eighth monsoon year. The sequence of these lords is as follows: Sun, Mercury, Saturn, Mars, Venus, Moon, Jupiter; then Sun, Mercury, Saturn, etc. Therefore, if the sequence is matched according to the days, the coming monsoon year's

By knowing this rule of the names of the days and the relations of the astrologers and the month-makers, the derivation of the 51st and 52nd shlokas can be easily understood.

The number of days that have passed is the remainder when the day (Sawan day) that has come until the desired time is divided by seven. Since the creation began on Sunday, Sunday is the first day of the week and Saturday is the previous day, i.e., the seventh day. Therefore, if 5 remain, it should be understood that it is Jupiter's day, whose midnight completes that day because Jupiter is the fifth day of the week. As in the previous example, when the number of the day is 7, 14, 40, 41, 31, 603, when divided by seven, the remainder is 1. Therefore, the day for which the day was calculated is the first day of the week, Sunday. However, this day is until the midnight before Basant-Panchami, so Basant-Panchami will be Monday.

To know the month-makers, the desired day should be divided by 30, and the remainder is the number of Sawan months from the beginning of creation. Multiply these Sawan months by two and add one and divide by seven, because the order of the month-makers changes on the third day according to the days, and the same order begins again after seven months. The remainder is the lord of that month that is running on the same day of the week. As in the above, when the day is divided by 30, there are 23, 81, 34, 71, 53 Sawan months and 13 Sawan days. When the number of these Sawan months is multiplied by two and one is added, it is 47,62,66,42,107. When divided by 7, the remainder is 3. Therefore, the first day of the running Sawan month was Tuesday. Therefore, the lord of this month is Mars.

To know the year lord, divide the Savana months which are taken from 360 or above by 12, which gives the number of Savana years passed. Multiply these by three and add one and divide by seven because the order of the year lords changes according to the day and the same order begins again after seven years. The remainder (of weeks) is the lord of the Savana year of that same day because the week begins with Sunday.

As in the example above, when the ahargana is divided by 360 or the Savana months are divided by 12, the number of past Savana years is 1,68,44,55,621.

Source page 68

Multiplying this by three and adding one gives 5,65,33,67,734. Dividing this by 7 leaves a remainder of 1. Therefore, the start of the Sawan year was on a Sunday, and the lord of this year is Ravi.

This is the method for finding the year lord according to the Sūrya Siddhānta. In all the calendars of today, the year lord (varshapati) is considered the lord of the day when Chaitra Shukla Pratipada occurs, and the minister of the year is considered the lord of the day when Mesha Sankranti occurs. Meghesh is the lord of the day when the Ardra constellation appears, etc., and the result for the entire year is calculated with this idea. The rule in the Makaranda Sārini is different from the Sūrya Siddhānta:--

Translation—(53) Multiply the number of *ahargana* by the great revolution of any planet and divide the product by the great Sawan days. The revolutions that result are the ones that the planet has completed according to its mean motion (from the beginning of its creation). Multiply the remainder by 12 and then divide by (great Sawan days) to find the number of quantities that the planet has completed in the current revolution. Scientific Commentary—These verses explain the method by which the mean positions of the planets at a desired time are known. Great Sawan days: *ahargana*:: Great revolution: desired revolution

If 's' is taken as the great divisional savana day, 'a' as the desired degree, 'b' as the great revolution, and 'ba' as the desired revolution, then in short, it will be written as:-

This is a fraction, which when simplified, the integer that results is the number of revolutions of the planets that have been completed up to that time, and when multiplied by 12 and simplified, the integer that results is the elapsed amount, and then when multiplied by 30 and simplified, the numerator of the current amount will be obtained. Therefore, if 2 degrees 3 minutes 5 aspects are subtracted from the 12 zodiacs, then 6 degrees 26 degrees 55 aspects will result, which means that it is at the 26 degrees 55 aspects of the tenth zodiac after the 6 zodiacs of the zodiac.

It is necessary to discover when this practice began. There are many smaller divisions in the cycle of years, the beginning of which also starts from Prabhava. Their discussion will be in the final chapter called Mānavādhyāya.

Translation—(56) The method of knowing the mean positions of the planets has been stated with detail so far; but for practical purposes, this work should be done briefly from the auspicious age. Scientific Commentary—The method for finding the mean positions of the planets described in the 45-50 shlokas of this chapter is not practical due to the expansion of mathematics, as is clear from the examples given. Therefore, there is no need to calculate the years from the beginning of creation to the end of the Satya Yuga. The mean positions of the planets should be known by knowing the calculation up to the Ishatkal from the time the current age began, according to the succeeding lines of the 48th shloka and the 46-50 shlokas.

At the time when Surya Siddhanta taught Maya to Purusha, according to the second verse of this chapter, it is the time of the end of Satya Yuga. Therefore, in the 57th verse, there is an indication of making Ahargana from the beginning of Treta, and it is also shown that at this time all the planets were in the same mean position at the beginning of Aries. According to this rule, it is convenient to derive Ahargana from the beginning of Kali Yuga itself in Kali Yuga, which is also prevalent nowadays. Just as all the planets were in the same mean position at the beginning of Aries at the beginning of Treta, so in the beginning of Kali Yuga also at the beginning of Aries.

Sine—if the length of any side of a right-angled triangle is divided by the length of its hypotenuse, the resulting quantity is called the sine of the angle opposite to that side. Figure 8 has a right-angled triangle with sides a, b, c; therefore, the sine of the angle a = a/c and the sine of the angle b = b/c. Of the right-angled triangle

The length of the chord is greater than the length of the side; therefore, the sine of the angle opposite to the side will be less than one, so it is written in decimal fraction. This is the practice of today. In ancient times when the promotion of decimal fractions did not exist, the sine of the angle was written in integers.

To know the sine of an angle, a circle is taken in our theories, whose radius (semi-diameter) is 3438 units and the circumference is 21600 units, so that each unit is equal to one art. Because the circumference is like a circle in which there are 360 degrees or 360 X 60 = 21600 arts. Then two radii are drawn from the center to the circumference such that the angle between them is the same as the angle whose sine is to be known, and a perpendicular is drawn from the point of intersection of the radius and circumference to the other radius. The meridian—the circle of the Earth that lies midway between the North and South poles at an equal distance and divides the Earth into two equal halves is called the equator; the half of the geography north of the equator is called the northern hemisphere and the south is called the southern hemisphere. The celestial poles (the point in the sky that is just above the North or South Pole of the Earth, the North Star is usually about 10 degrees from the North Pole) appear on the horizon from this line. Here, the latitude is zero and the longitude is 60^°. Therefore, the equator is also called the meridian. In Figure 10, V is the equator. If a circle (Parallel of latitude) is drawn on the Earth parallel to the meridian from a place 'S', its magnitude is called the meridian of 'S'. From the equator

However, this definition is not simple and practical. In the 64th verse, the discussion of longitude is further. This is also a simpler definition of longitude; therefore, it is appropriate to explain it here as well.

As many places on the same north-south line have the same noon or midnight at the same time, as in places k, s, p, and kh. But the places that are to the east of this line have noon or midnight earlier, and the places that are to the west have it later. As much earlier the noon is at s from a (the meridian), we call that the time difference of longitude of s. We can express this in units of time; if we write it in minutes, we will call it longitudinal degree or longitudinal-nadi, and if we write it in hours, we will call it longitudinal hour or minute. From this definition, we have the facility to easily reveal the time difference of longitude of k, s, p, and kh all from the same thing, whereas in sums, their longitude differences will have to be written differently.

In this way, the time that is behind the meridian by as much as on the line C will be called the western longitude of C.

The noon or midnight happens because the Earth rotates on its axis from west to east once every 24 hours or once every 60 minutes like a top, due to which celestial bodies like the sun, moon, stars, etc., revolve from east to west.

The translation -(63) one knows by mathematics when the fully eclipsed moon will begin to emerge from the darkness (from the middle night, how many hours behind), and one should observe by sighting what time (how many hours behind the middle night of one's place) the fully eclipsed moon begins to emerge from the darkness at one's location. If the observed time (known by instrument sighting) is more than the mathematically determined time, then it should be understood that one's location is east of the meridian and (64) if the observed time is less than the mathematically determined time, then it should be understood that one's location is west of the meridian. Similarly, by observing that time, it can be known that at what time the full image of the moon goes into darkness. The difference between the mathematically determined and the observed times is called the longitude of one's place or the longitude in hours (because time is usually written in hours). Multiplying this longitude in hours by the circumference (65) and dividing the product by sixty, the resulting value is the east longitude yojanas (if the place is east) and west longitude yojanas (if the place is west). The longitude of the planets should be calculated from this longitude (according to the method stated in verses 60-61). 63-65

This is the time when the total or partial eclipse begins. This is also called the totality period.

Emergence = (1) opening of the eyes, (2) appearing, (3) the full moon emerges from the darkness. Therefore, the emergence period is the time when the full image of the moon begins to emerge from the darkness.

Touching period is the time when the moon's image begins to enter the darkness, that is, the time when the actual eclipse begins.

Salvation period is the time when the entire image of the moon comes out of the darkness.

Figure 13 shows the center of the Sun, the center of the Earth, and the tip of the shadow of the Earth. The moon revolves around the Earth in its orbit. When the center of the moon reaches the point in the orbit where 1 is written, the moon's image touches the Earth's shadow, so this position of the moon is the position of the touching period at the time of eclipse. At this time, the moon's image appears to enter the darkness. When the moon reaches the position indicated by the number 2, its entire image is in the darkness. This is the state of the totality period or the occultation period. When the moon reaches the position indicated by the number 3, the moon begins to emerge from the darkness. This is the state of the emergence period. And when the entire image of the moon comes out of the darkness, as indicated by the number 4, then it is the state of the salvation period.

Among these four events, the event that occurs in the sky is also seen on the ground at the same time. However, the sunrise or noon in all places on the ground, from which clocks can be accurately corrected, does not occur at the same time, as demonstrated in the scientific commentary of 60-61 shlokas which define the definition of longitude, therefore the time of seeing an event in clocks of different places is different. How the time difference is known from the time difference yojana, it should be understood from the scientific commentary of 60-61 shlokas. It is clear that the sun completes the revolution of the Earth in 60 hours, so it revolves in 60 hours around the circumference of the meridian of any place, so the part of the circumference that is the difference from the meridian of that place will be complete in the time difference of that place. Trairashika expresses this as:-

60 hours: time difference hour:: Circumference: time difference yojana.
