Third method—by comparing the moments of the appearance and disappearance of the breaking stars with the local times of different places, the longitude can be known with subtlety if the time of the breaking of the stars can be determined beforehand and there is no error in their recognition.

Fourth method: Knowing the longitude by sending news by electricity—If there is such a relation between two places that news can be sent from one place to another by electricity, then the longitude of these two places can be easily known because the time taken for the electrical news to reach is so short that any inaccuracy that may occur is not like an error.

Suppose one wants to know the longitude of Lucknow from Kashi. The observers of both cities should keep the same type of clock, as if the clock of one tells the time of Sawan, then the clock of the other also tells the time of Sawan. Both clocks should be reconciled with their local time so that each clock can accurately tell the local time of its place. Since Kashi is to the east of Lucknow, the local time of Kashi will be ahead of the local time of Lucknow, and the difference between these two is the longitude of Kashi from Lucknow. At the time when the clock of Kashi shows 'S1' time, a signal should be sent from Kashi. At the time when this signal reaches Lucknow, the time on the clock of Lucknow should be seen. If the time in this clock is 'S2' and it is assumed that the signal reached Lucknow at the same moment it was sent from Kashi, then the longitude of Kashi from Lucknow will be proved by the equation written below:-

d1 = s1 - s2

But the value of the difference in longitude that will be obtained from this equation will be some less than the actual longitude because some time must necessarily pass for the electrical signal to reach from Kashi to Lucknow. If the value of this time is 'y' and the actual longitude from Kashi to Lucknow is 'd', then the form of the aforementioned equation will be:-

d = (s1 + y) - s2 = d1 + y (7)

Source page 94

Because at the time the news reaches Lucknow, the time in Kashi will be 'S1 + y'. To know the value of 'y', one should send a signal from Lucknow to Kashi and then know the local time of both. Suppose that at the time the signal was sent from Lucknow, it was 'Sa2' time in the Lucknow clock, and at the time the signal reached Kashi, it was 'Sa1' time in the Kashi clock, and if it is assumed that the signal does not take any time to reach, then the difference between these two will be the longitudinal difference of Lucknow, which is as follows:-

d2 = sa1 - sa2

But the value of d2 will be some more than reality because it must take some time to reach the signal, which will be like 'y', so the actual longitudinal difference

d = sa1 - (sa2 + y) = (sa1 - sa2 - y) = d2 - y (2)

(1) and (2) adding the same sides of the equations

2d = d1 + d2

(d1 + d2) / 2 (3)

which means that the time difference that arrives when sending the longitude from Kashi to Lucknow should be added to the longitude known when sending the reverse signal from Lucknow to Kashi. Then, adding both and dividing by two, the actual longitude will be found. According to the local time in Kashi, at night, it is 12 hours 73 minutes and 12 seconds, which is 12 hours 26 minutes 12 seconds, and in Bombay, the tendency of the day which is 26 minutes west of Ujjain from Ujjain occurs 26 minutes or 11 minutes 36 seconds before 12 o'clock at night. This means that the time tendency of other places in India should be understood at the same time when the midnight occurs on the meridian of India. Therefore, the position of the planets which is mathematically proven at the time of midnight of Lanka or Ujjain is the time at which the day tendency occurs in other places. That is why if one needs to find the planet at the time of midnight of a place, the difference or addition of the longitude should be done.

This opinion is of the Sūrya Siddhānta that the transit of the day occurs at the midnight of Ujjain in all places. Acharyas such as Brahmagupta,1 and Bhaskaracharya have considered the transit from the time when the sun rises in Lanka because according to them, the beginning of creation happened at the time when the first sun appeared in Lanka and the beginning of the first day also happened at this time. This rule is generally prevalent nowadays, yes, followers of the Vaishnava sect3 consider the transit of the day from the midnight and consider the same date during the day for religious acts as the time that remains in the previous half-night, hence their Ekadashi is usually on the day of Dwadashi. Most calendars also give the planet at the time of true midnight.

In these two views, the belief in the direction of the day from midnight is simpler and more comprehensive. All places located on the same north-south line have either midnight or noon always, but they do not occur together at sunrise except in two days of the year. Sunrise is the sine of the sun's declination and the latitude of the places.

Scientific Commentary—it is clear that the mean position of the planet at midnight does not remain at any other time because the planets are constantly moving. Therefore, to know the mean position of a planet at any auspicious time before or after midnight, it is necessary to know how much the planet will shift at that time. This can be easily known from Trāiraśika—

60 clock: Auspicious time:: Daily motion: Motion in the auspicious time ∴ Motion in the auspicious time = Auspicious time × Daily motion/60 clock Therefore, the position of the planet at the desired time = Position of midnight ± Auspicious time + Daily motion/60 clock

If the auspicious time is before midnight, the minus sign should be kept, and if it is after, the plus sign.

Therefore, the name of this chapter is kept as Chapter on True Positions.

(2) These forms, if (of the planets) are in the east with their right and left hands, pull the planets towards them according to the distance as they are tied to them by ropes of air to the east if they are in the east, and to the west if they are in the west. (3) The air named Pravaha also pushes these planets towards their poles. This is the reason why the planets pulled towards the east or west

Source page 103

A variation occurs in the motions. (4) If the planet is to the east of the high point and not more than 6 degrees or 1800 from it, it pulls the planet towards the east from the mean place, but if it is more than 1800 away (due to being to the west of the planet), it pulls the planet towards the west. (5) The clear position is obtained by adding as much as the planet has moved towards the east from its respective high points in the mean place and by subtracting as much as it has receded towards the west from the mean place. The added quantities are called the cube quantity and the subtracted quantity is called the negative quantity. (1-5)

Scientific Commentary—in these five and the next 6—11 shlokas, our Acharyas have attractive imaginations from which it is proven that they worked with how subtle descriptions. They saw that a planet, while revolving, reaches a place where its true motion becomes extremely slow at some time. They determined the position of the planet's apogee by this very thing. The position of the apogee is also not fixed, but it moves with very slow motion, so it is considered to move on the rāśicakra (circle of the zodiac), which is based on the revolution. The ordinary motion of the planets on the rāśicakra is to the west of the east. When the planet reaches its apogee, due to its extremely slow motion, its mean motion is less than the mean motion. Therefore, when the planet moves ahead of the apogee, it does not reach the place where it should be with the mean motion during the day, but remains behind. In this way, a difference arises between the mean and true positions of the planet. This difference increases daily, and when the planet moves 60^° ahead (towards the east) of the apogee, this difference is the most. After this, this difference begins to decrease, but the planet remains behind the mean position until it moves 180^° ahead of the apogee. At 180^° from the apogee, the mean and true positions of the planet become one. It is natural to imagine that when the planet is 180^° less than the apogee and remains towards the west, the apogee pulls it towards the mean position. Therefore, by performing a negative calculation in the mean position, the true position of the planet is obtained. As the planet moves further away from the apogee, the true motion increases accordingly; therefore, it was understood that the attraction of the apogee increases and decreases according to proximity.

At the time when the planet reaches apogee from 1800, its motion is very high. This is the inferior position of the planet. Therefore, by performing calculations in the mean position of the planet, the true position is found. When the planet goes beyond 1800 from apogee, it is to the east of the apogee planet within 1800. Therefore, here too, the planet seems to be pulled towards the apogee. For this reason, it is imagined that if the planet is towards the apogee, i.e., towards the east, it pulls towards the east, and if it is towards the west, it pulls towards the west.

When the planet is at its apogee, its true motion is very slow. At this place, the mean and true planets are together. But because the mean planet moves faster than the true planet, it moves ahead, and the true planet lags behind. At this place, the motion of the true Sun is very high and it is much faster than the mean Sun, so the true Sun remains ahead of the mean Sun after moving beyond the nadir. Si and ci are the positions of the true Sun and mi and mi are the positions of the mean Sun. Here too, the true Sun appears to be shifted towards the high side and is ahead of the mean Sun, so to know its position, addition to the position of the mean Sun is required.

The reason for the difference between the mean and true positions of the Sun and the Moon can be explained by such imagination, but there is even more variation in the mean and true positions of the five planets—Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn. Therefore, the imagination of the apogee was also made along with the imagination of the epicycle apogee. The way this was imagined is estimated by Bhaskaracharya as follows1:-

When the Sun is ahead of the Sun by Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, then the true planets are ahead of the mean planets, that is, they appear to be moving towards the Sun. But when the Sun is behind them, then the true planets are behind the mean planets, that is, they appear to be moving away from the Sun. Therefore, the scholars imagined that the epicycles of these three planets remain with the Sun. Therefore, it is natural to assume that these planets, along with their epicycles, also pull towards the Sun. If this imagination were further extended, then Newton's theory would be known in taking the Sun itself as the epicycle or the attractive force of these planets.

The matter of the node has already been written. What is written about the node of the Moon is also applicable to the nodes of other planets. When a planet comes to the northern node, it appears on the ecliptic. When it moves further from here, it becomes north from the ecliptic. Until it reaches 1800 degrees further from the southern node, i.e., 1800 degrees from the northern node, the ecliptic remains north. In such a situation, the northern node remains to the west of the planet. That is why it is stated in the next 7th verse that the node (northern node) located to the west of the planet up to 1800 degrees pulls the planet towards the north, and the position of the node to the east up to 1800 degrees pulls it towards the south. This is also invisible, and it appears that the planet is pulled towards the north or south by the ecliptic. Therefore, divine power is also considered in this. However, the real reason is that the orbits of the Sun and the planets are not in the same plane, due to which the orbit of each planet appears to intersect the orbit of the Sun at two points.

In the next 6-11 verses, it is stated that the planets whose size is larger pull less due to their apogees, epicycles, etc., and those that are lighter pull more. This estimation is the result of subtle depiction and is completely in accordance with the theory of attraction.

Based on these eight verses of Sūrya Siddhānta, some scholars say that the inventor of the law of attraction cannot be called Newton, but rather our own ancient astrologers. When considered impartially, it is proven that the revered Acharyas made the estimations with their imagination and reasoning, which are highly commendable considering the condition of that time. They certainly understood that there is a force causing the variation in the motion of the planets, but it was not known how this force works, whether it is only in the epicycles, apogees, and nodes of the Earth and the planets, or in all substances of the world, and by what operation of mathematics it can be proven. Newton is the inventor of this universal law of attraction. There is no doubt that if the study and teaching of astrology proceeded in India in the same way as during the time of Bhaskaraacharya, Ganesh Daivagya, etc., or as during the time of Copernicus, Tycho Brahe, Kepler, Newton, etc., in the 16th and 17th centuries in France, Germany, and England.

Kepler made these three laws from the subtle representations of the planets in the years 1664-1674 (1606-1616 AD). He did not know what forces cause the motions of the planets according to these laws. No proof of these laws could be established for 75 years. After this, Newton proved that universal gravitation is the cause of all this. The three laws on which Newton proved this are called the laws of motion, are famous by that name, and are:-

First Law—If no external force is applied, every object either remains in its state of rest or moves in a straight line with uniform motion.

Second Law—The change in motion is according to the force applied and this change occurs in the direction of the force applied.

Third Law—To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction, meaning that for every action, there is a reaction in the opposite direction, i.e., the same action but in the opposite direction.

These laws are self-evident. For more information, one should read any book of Dynamics.

From Kepler's first and second laws, Newton proved that every planet moves due to a force directed towards the Sun and whose magnitude is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the Sun and the planet. From Kepler's third law, Newton proved what is the relation between the increase in the motion of one planet and the increase in the motion of another planet, and from this he derived the theory of universal gravitation, which is:-

Every particle of matter attracts every other particle by a force that varies according to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

Now it has to be proved that if a line is drawn from a fixed point to a moving particle and it covers the same area in the same time, then the direction of the force with which that particle is moving is towards that fixed point. This is briefly based on Differential Calculus and kinematics

दक्षिणोत्तरयोरेवं पातो राहु स्वरंहसा ।
विक्षिपत्येष विक्षेपं चन्द्रादीनामपक्रमात् ॥६॥
उत्तराभिमुखं पातो विक्षिपत्यपराद्धगः ।
ग्रहं प्राग्भगणाद्धस्थो याम्यायामपकर्षति ॥७॥

Translation—(6) The planets like the Moon etc. displace north or south by their velocity due to the deviation from their node or Rahu ecliptic. (7) When the node is less than 6 degrees or 180° from the planet, it removes the north from the ecliptic, and when it is less than 6 degrees from the planet to the east, it removes the south from the ecliptic.

Sūrya Siddhānta—the simple meaning of these two shlokas is that by looking at the positions of the planet and its node, one should understand whether the planet is exactly on the ecliptic or is shifted some north or south from it. If both the planet and the node are at the 'same place', it should be understood that the planet is on the ecliptic. If the planet is ahead of the node, i.e., east, but not more than 180^° away, then it will be shifted north from the ecliptic, and if the planet is behind the node, i.e., west, but not more than 180^° away, then it will be shifted south from the ecliptic. The reason for this is not the attraction or repulsion of Rahu, but rather that the orbit of a planet is not in the plane of the ecliptic, so the planet does not always remain on the ecliptic. The two points where the planet's orbit and the ecliptic seem to meet are called the node. When the planet is at these two points of its orbit, then it appears on the ecliptic, otherwise the ecliptic

Source page 118

It is according to what is said above as North or South. The distance of the planet from the meridian of the ecliptic is called the deviation of the planet. This occurs on the circle that makes a right angle with the meridian (ecliptic pole).

बुधभार्गवयोः शीघ्रात्तद्वत्पातो यदास्थितः ।

Translation—(8) When the nodes of Mercury and Venus are in accordance with the rules written in the above (6, 7 shlokas), they remove the planets from the meridian to the North or South by attraction in the epicycles.

Scientific Commentary—The rules stated in the 6, 7 shlokas apply only to the Sun, Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. To know the positions of the two planets Mercury and Venus, one should see which direction and how far they are from their epicycle nodes. If the epicycle node is to the East but less than 180°, the planet will be North of the ecliptic, and if it is to the West but less than 180°, the planet will be South of the ecliptic.

Translation—(12) There are eight types of motions in the planets called arc, arc of arc, crooked, slow circle, straight, quick, and quick. (13) Among these, the very quick, slow, slow, and straight motions are straight, that is, when the planet has these motions, it appears to go from west to east in the circle and the arc and crooked motions are called arc motion because when the planet has such motions, it appears to go from east to west in the circle in reverse. When the planet has straight motions, then it is called straight and when there are curved motions, then it is called crooked.

Scientific Commentary—the reason why these different motions occur in the planets is not explained anywhere in our theories, because the reason cannot be well explained until the Earth is considered stationary. Yes, if the Earth is also considered to revolve around the Sun like other planets, which has also been proven by many experiments, then it is easily understood how these eight motions appear in the planets; although in reality the planets are continuously moving from west to east revolving around the Sun. If you plant a flag in the field and make a circle with a distance of 4, 7, 10, 15, 52, 65, 162, and 300 furlongs with a height of three feet for each circle; appoint one horseman near each circle; you stand near the flag and command the horsemen to stand near their respective circles in such a way that they all appear in a straight line, and then all the riders begin to circle the circle with this speed so that the nearest one completes one revolution in 88 seconds, the one some distance away in 225 seconds, the third in 365 seconds, the fourth in 687 seconds, the fifth in 4332 seconds, the sixth in 10756 seconds, the seventh in 510 minutes, and the eighth in 1003 minutes, when they complete the revolution, just as the horsemen will know that you are circling them in seconds, so the planets in the solar system appear to revolve around the sun in days. The only difference is that the riders will circle on a surface, but the planets also shift some north and south.

If you do not stand near the flag but ride on the third horse of the flag and begin to circle with the previously said speed, you will see the flag and the horsemen, the same scene that is visible to the inhabitants of Earth when they circle the sun of the planets. Sometimes it seems that the planets are moving forward, and sometimes it seems that some are moving backward, and sometimes they also appear to be stationary.

From the example of the riders, you must have known that if a rider circumambulates the flag while sitting on the third horse, the peculiarity of the motions of the horses on both the outside and inside is seen, like the peculiarity in the motions of other planets when riders on the horse of Earth see the motions of other planets. Translation—(14) I respectfully state that the rules by which the planets attain the apparent equality in these motions, that is, they appear directly in the place of the node, are the rules by which they come to be seen, and I say these rules are known by mathematics.

Sūrya Siddhānta - this verse is of great importance. It proves that our ancient Acharyas used to determine the true positions of the planets so that there would be no difference in mathematics and direct observation. For this, subtle rules were made in the Chapter on True Positions. However, as I have explained in the Scientific Commentary of the 6th verse of the Chapter on Mean Motions, whether the instruments are gross or subtle, some experimental error remains in determining them, so a difference occurs in time, which requires periodic revision. This is called 'seed' correction. For example, suppose a clock slows down by one second per day, then in 60 days it will be 1 minute and in 1 year it will be 6 minutes behind. But in practice, it will be said that the clock is very pure; because the difference of 1 minute in 60 days or 1 second per day is not like (the difference). If this difference always occurred and the clock was not revised, then in many years such a difference would occur that it would be impossible to consider it as not like (the difference), and revision would have to be done. Just as a difference of 1 second per day in a clock can take a very large form in some time, similarly, in the periods of revolution of the Sun, Moon, etc., the difference of even 1 moment becomes very large in hundreds of years. This is why the seed correction has to be done. The practice of making revisions in between was accepted by our ancient Acharyas, whose incarnations I will give below; but there has been a difference of opinion on this subject for some days. One side says that there is no right to make any commentary or revision on the ancient texts; whatever is in them should be accepted as is. The other side says that revision is entirely appropriate. The arguments of both sides, as I have found them, are given below:-

Sūrya Siddhānta—it is stated in the fourth and fifth verses of this chapter that up to 1800, the apogee or epicycle apogee, which is situated behind its planet, pulls towards it, i.e., towards the east, according to the proximity, by which the position of the true planet can be known by performing a calculation in the mean planet, etc. In the above 26th verse, it is stated how the distance of the mean planet from the apogee or epicycle apogee should be calculated. The difference between two points of a circle can be shown in two ways. If the difference between the points m, ma, mi, and mi is not measured in the direction of the arrow in figure 15, then it will be um; uma, umi, and umi in sequence. But if the difference between these points is measured in the opposite direction from u, then the difference between u and m is 360°—um, the difference between ma and m is 360°—uma, the difference between mi and m is 360°—umi and the difference between mi and m is 360°—umi. The direction indicated by the arrow in the figure is called the opposite or apasvya direction in Sanskrit texts, nowadays it is called 'positive' or 'direction opposite to the clock'. People living to the north of the celestial equator see the sun, moon, and planets, etc., moving in this direction in their orbits. The opposite direction is called vilom, pratilom, savya, and nowadays 'negative' or 'clock direction' in Sanskrit. Due to the daily motion of the Earth, people living in the northern hemisphere see the sun, moon, stars, etc., moving in this direction. In Sūrya Siddhānta, the method of knowing the difference between the planets from the epicycle apogee or apogee, which are in sequence the fast kendra or slow kendra, is stated to be measured in the opposite or negative direction. Therefore, it is said that the mean planet should be subtracted from the epicycle apogee or apogee. However, many other scholars like Brahmagupta, Bhaskaraacharya have written to measure the difference between the mean planet and the apogee from the opposite direction and the difference between the epicycle apogee and the mean planet from the opposite direction. The reason for this is that the mean planet moves in the opposite direction because it is more rapidly moving from the apogee, and the epicycle apogee moves in the opposite direction because it is more rapidly moving from the mean planet; therefore, the mean planet moves in the opposite direction from the epicycle apogee. Whether the difference between the mean center or the fast kendra is measured, both have the same meaning. Bhaskaraacharya's method is natural and some of the Sūrya Siddhānta are misleading.

Source page 150

When the mean center and the epicycle center of the planet are known, then it is necessary to know their sine and cosine, because they are further required. Those who are familiar with modern trigonometry can know directly because they know how the cosines, sines, etc. from zero to 3600 can be known. But in ancient times, to find the sine of any angle from zero to 3600, they first looked at which position (quadrant) it is in. If the mean center or epicycle center is within zero and 60°, then in the odd position, above 60° but less than 180°, then in the even position, above 180° and less than 2700, then in the odd position, and above 2700, then in the even position. In short, the first and third positions are called odd positions and the second and fourth positions are called even positions.

To know in which position the planet is, the mean center or epicycle center should be divided by 60°. If the remainder is zero or 2, then it should be understood as an odd position, and if 1 or 3 is, then it should be understood as an even position. The remainder that is left is called the arc part. Subtracting this remainder from 60° gives the part that is to be subtracted. If it is an odd position

Calculate the sine of the portion of the past and the mean portion of the present. This is called the versed sine. But if the portion is odd, it is called the quotient of the sine of the portion of the present and the sine of the past.

This matter can be understood easily from figure 28. The given circle is the orbit of a planet. 'U' is the position of the apogee or apogee. Mi, Mi, Ma, M are the mean positions of a planet. Therefore, moving in the opposite direction, Umi, Umi, Uma and Um are the mean centers of the planet in the first, second, third and fourth positions or in the odd, even, odd and even positions. In the first position, Umi is past and Mi is future; therefore, the sine of Umi, i.e., Mi, is called the versed sine of Mi, and the sine of Mi, i.e., Mi, is called the quotient of the sine. In the second position, Pm is past and Mi is future, therefore, the sine of Pm, i.e., Mi, is called the quotient of the sine of Mi, and the sine of Mi, i.e., Mi, is called the versed sine. In the third position, 'Ni Ma' is past and 'Ma Pu' is future, therefore, the sine of Ni Ma, i.e., Ma Ja, is called the versed sine, and the sine of Ma Pu, i.e., Maka, is called the quotient of the sine. Similarly, in the fourth position, Pu is past and Mu is future, therefore, the sine of Pu, i.e., Ma Ka, is called the quotient of the sine, and the sine of Mu, i.e., Ma Ja, is called the versed sine.

In short, it should be said that the difference between the mean planets is the versed sine of the line drawn from the line, i.e., the lower line, passing through the mean point. The difference of the mean planet from the line that forms a right angle with this line, passing through the mean point, is called the quotient of the sine. If the radius is equal to 3438 units, then the measurements of Mi, Ma Ja and M Ja in these units will be the versed sine, and the measurements of Mi Ki, Ma, and M Ka in these units will be the quotient of the sine.

Sūrya Siddhānta—the difference that occurs in the mean and true positions of a planet due to the apogee is called the mean motion, and the difference that occurs in the mean and true positions due to the epicycle apogee is called the quick motion. This changes according to the distance of the apogee or epicycle. The greatest difference between the mean and true positions of the planets is due to the apogee, and the greatest difference due to the epicycle is called the quickest motion. This is known by sighting, i.e., by the gnomon instrument. The circle drawn by taking the sine of the true mean motion as the semi-diameter is called the mean circumference. Similarly, the circle drawn by taking the sine of the quickest motion as the semi-diameter is called the quick circumference or the running circumference. If a circle is drawn and the Earth is taken in the center and the mean planet is considered to be moving on the circumference, then the circumference is called the planet's orbital circle or orbital circle. If 360 equal parts are made of this orbital circle, the extension of the mean circumference of the Sun will be at the end of the samapodas. Similarly, one should understand the magnitudes of the mean and quick circumferences of other planets. This can also be written that the mean circumference of the Sun is 360 of the orbital circle. In Figure 26, if the position of the Earth, the orbital circle of any planet, and its mean and true positions are shown, and if the value of the latter is the ultimate, then the sine of the mean motion, which is the linear distance between the lines in between, is called the ultimate mean motion. The smaller circumference drawn by taking the sine of the mean as the semi-diameter and the sine of the mean as the mean is called the mean circumference. If the extension of the orbital circle is considered as 360 parts, then the circumference of the mean circumference is the arc corresponding to the number of parts. Similarly, one should understand the length of the quick circumference. This magnitude also varies according to the opinions of different teachers. The reason for this is that the value of the ultimate mean motion is not always the same; it is changing gradually. The ultimate mean motion of the Sun decreases by 3 degrees in one thousand years. At this time, the ultimate mean motion of the Sun is 1055'. In Sūrya Siddhānta, the ultimate mean motion of the Sun is 2013'41". There is also an inaccuracy due to the imprecision of sighting.

Translation—(44) Subtract the epicycle from the epicycle to find the fast kendra and the śīghraphala. Add half of this śīghraphala to the madhyama planet (if the fast kendra is less than 6 degrees) and subtract (if the fast kendra is more than 6 degrees); whatever results from adding or subtracting is called the first correction yukta madhyama planet. Subtract the mandocca from this first correction yukta madhyama planet, consider the remainder as the maṃda kendra, and make the maṃda phala. Half of this maṃda phala, whatever results from adding or subtracting to the first correction yukta madhyama planet, is the second correction yukta madhyama planet. Subtract again from the mandocca and consider the remainder as the dūsarā maṃda kendra, and make the dūsarā maṃda phala. Whatever results from adding or subtracting to the madhyama planet is called the maṃda true planet. Subtract the śīghraphala from the śīghrocca to find the fast kendra and śīghraphala, and whatever results from adding or subtracting this śīghraphala to the maṃda true planet is called the true planet.

In short, the rule is as follows:—

(1) If the sign of the quick fruit is reversed and added to the mean centers (according to algebra), the first Sanskrit mean center will come. Its mean fruit is the first Sanskrit mean fruit or the first mean fruit. (2) If the sign of the second mean fruit is reversed and added to the first Sanskrit mean centers, the second Sanskrit mean center will come. Its mean fruit is the second Sanskrit mean fruit or the second mean fruit. (3) If the sign of the second mean fruit in the quick center is reversed and added, the Sanskrit quick center will come, whose quick fruit is the second quick fruit. (4) If the second mean fruit and the second quick fruit in the mean planet are added without reversing the sign, the true planet will come.

The rule for knowing the true planets in Sūrya Siddhānta is this. Other commentators have acted in some different ways, for which there is no need to compare. Such intricate rules were made only so that the position of the true planet might be known exactly. Therefore, all those new methods by which the position of the true planet could usually be known exactly were brought into use. This is why there is a difference in the opinions of the commentators. Not all real positions can be known by just these rules; anyone can test this nowadays; therefore, it is my view that it is extremely necessary to use those methods by which this can be correct. From this perspective, I will also write in the Scientific Commentary about those new methods from which similarity may arise in astronomy and mathematics. (46) Multiply the sun's meridian (mean position) by the daily true motion of the planet and divide the product by 12 quantities of arc, that is, 21600 arcs, and add or subtract this from the planet's true position (if the sun's mean position is positive) or subtract (if the sun's mean position is negative), so the planet will be visible in the true midnight.

Scientific Commentary—at the time when the mean sun comes on the meridian circle, that time is the mean noon and at the time when the true sun comes on the meridian circle, that time is the true noon. Similarly, at the time when the mean sun is in the nether (the part of the meridian circle that is below the horizon) there is the mean midnight and at the time when the true sun is in the nether there is the true midnight. From this it is apparent that the true midnight will be as much earlier or later as the true noon will be in the nether as the true sun will be in the nether as the mean sun. But the difference between the true and mean sun is called the mean motion; therefore, in the time it takes for a segment of the meridian circle similar to the mean motion to cross the meridian, the true midnight will be as much earlier or later.

As much as the planet will move in this time, by adding or subtracting the mean midnight time in the true midnight time, the true midnight time will be the true midnight time. To make a subtle calculation, it should first be known how long the arc of the ecliptic or the violation of the meridian will take for the mean motion, but even not doing so results in very little inaccuracy. Therefore, in short, all that is to be done is that in the time it takes to violate the meridian of the geocentric cycle, the planet moves forward at the same speed as its daily motion, so in the time it takes to violate the ecliptic of the mean motion, what will be the speed of the planet.

Translation—(47) By subtracting the daily motion of the apogee of the moon from its mean daily motion, and taking the action told in (48 46 shlokas), the apparent daily motion of the moon is obtained by subtracting or adding from the mean daily motion. (48) The mean daily motion of other planets should be known in the same way as the action of knowing the mean motion of a planet by the mean daily motion of other planets, which is—multiply the mean daily motion by the difference of the versed sines and divide the product by 225; (46) Multiply the latitude by the revolution angle and divide by (if the latitude is in fractions, by 260 and if it is in degrees, by 21600), the latitude will be in degrees. If the mean center is in the second and third positions (in the order of positions), then add, and if it is in the first or fourth positions (in the order of positions), then subtract. By doing this, the apparent daily motion of the sun and the moon and the mean daily motion of other planets are known.

Scientific Commentary—By subtracting the daily motion of the apogee from the mean daily motion of a planet, the daily motion of its mean center is found. This is called the center motion of the planet. However, the motion of the apogee of other planets, except for the moon, is so small that leaving it out will not cause any error, so the mean daily motion of other planets is considered the center motion, only the procedure for knowing the center motion for the moon is prescribed. Just as by giving the correction of the mean fruit in the mean planet, the mean true planet is obtained, similarly by giving the correction of the motion of the mean or the motion of the mean fruit in the mean daily motion, the mean true motion is found. For the sun and the moon, this becomes the apparent daily motion. For other planets, the action told in the next 50—52 shlokas should also be done. The origin of this rule is as follows:—

The distance the true planet travels in a day is the true daily motion of the planet. Therefore, to know the true daily motion, it is sufficient to know only that any

(52) When the planet is far from its epicycle (more than three zodiac signs difference) then the ropes from which it is drawn become slack. Due to this, the planet is pulled in the opposite direction and the motion becomes a curve, that is, it is reversed. (53) When the final epicycles (from which the second epicycle is extracted) of Mangala, Budha, Guru, Shukra, and Shani are in succession 164, 144, 130, 163, and 115 degrees (54) then their circular motion begins, and when the epicycles are in succession which come from subtracting 3600 from the above epicycles (that is, 196, 216, 230, 167, and 245 degrees) then the circular motion ends, that is, the planet becomes rectilinear again. (55) Due to the increase of the larger circumference of the epicycle, the circular motion of Shukra and Mangala stops at the same time when the epicycle is in the seventh sign, Budha and Guru when the epicycle is in the eighth sign, and Shani when the epicycle is in the sixth sign.

According to Kepler's law, to know the true position of a planet, it first has to be seen where the planet, which is elliptical in shape in its orbit and whose focus is the Sun itself, is. Then it has to be known where that planet will appear from the Earth at that time.

Suppose the orbit of a planet is elliptical and R is the position of the attractive Sun, which is at the focus of the ellipse. The beginning of the revolution of the planet is considered from the time when the planet is at the nearest distance from the Sun, i.e., at A, and if the planet appears at point G at a distance of 'D' from that time, then A-G is called the apogee of the planet, which will be denoted by the letter S hereafter.

Just as the time between one sunrise and the next sunrise is called sāvana day, similarly, the time from the time a planet rises in the east to the time it rises again on the next day is called that planet's ahorātra. If the planet is in the direct motion, its ahorātra will be more than the nakṣatra-ahorātra, and if it is retrograde, it will be less. The method of knowing how much more or less the planet's ahorātra is than the nakṣatra-ahorātra is explained in this verse. According to how much the planet moves forward or backward during the day, the planet's ahorātra will be more or less than the nakṣatra-ahorātra. The shadow of the gnomon of the finger is as large as the meridian time, that is called the equinoctial shadow. Due to the daily motion of the earth, the planets, constellations, sun, etc., which appear to revolve on a circle and complete one orbit in a day, that circle is called the diurnal circle of that planet, constellation, or sun. These diurnal circles are parallel to the ecliptic. The diameters of three diurnal circles are shown in Figure 42 with the lines of Va, Vi, and Vu. The diameter of the Vi diurnal circle coincides with the diameter of the ecliptic. In this way, the same stars or planets appear to move as if they were on the ecliptic. On the day of the vernal equinox, the sun also (if its motion of declination is assumed to be constant for a short time) appears to move on this diurnal circle. If a planet is like the north declination and the Sagittarius, then the diameter of that planet's diurnal circle will be Va. Similarly, if the planet's south declination is like the Aquarius, then the diameter of its diurnal circle will be Vu.

From the figure it is revealed that the lines of the horizon in the meridian country are cut into two equal parts by the diameters of all the great circles. In the meridian country, as long as the sun, star, or planet remains above the line of longitude, it is seen or rises, and as long as it remains below this line, it is not seen or sets. Therefore, in the meridian country, where this line forms the horizon, the sun, the moon, the stars, all—no matter the declination—remain rising for 12 hours and setting for twelve hours. In this twelve hours, for 6 hours, they rise from the eastern horizon and reach the meridian circle, and for 6 hours, they descend from the meridian circle and go to the western horizon. (The slight difference caused by the refraction of light is not considered here for convenience). In places to the north or south of the meridian country, only those planets or stars that lie on the equator remain visible for half a day and not visible for half a day, which means the diameter of their great circle is similar to the equator.

Translation—(64) One constellation enjoys 800 zodiacs and one tithi enjoys 720 zodiacs. The number of constellations that have passed, which is the enjoyment of a constellation, is obtained by dividing the enjoyment of 800 zodiacs by the enjoyment of one constellation, and the remainder is the motion of the next constellation. If one wants to know when the planet came into the current constellation, dividing the passed zodiacs by the planet's daily motion yields the number of days, hours, etc. Subtracting the passed zodiacs from 800 and dividing the remainder by the daily motion will show when the planet will remain in the current constellation.

Translation—By adding the true positions (nirayana bhogashas) of the Sun and the Moon and finding their art, and dividing by 800, the number of past yugas is obtained. If this past navigable art is multiplied by 60 and divided by the sum of the true daily motions of the Sun and the Moon, then it will be known how many hours before the current yuga began and how many hours after it will end.

An example will be sufficient to understand the rule. Suppose you want to know which Yuga was current at the time of the Aries solstice of 1681 A.D., and when it began and when it ended?

There are 5025 solar years and 18,35,423.080625 mean Sawan days from the beginning of Kali Yuga until the time of the Aries solstice of 1681 A.D. The beginning of Kali Yuga occurred at midnight of the Guru in Ujjain, so 1681 A.D. Aries solstice occurred 0.080625 days after the midnight of Saturday in Ujjain. It will be good to clarify the Sun and Moon at the time of midnight for convenience.

The way in which the true position of the Sun has been calculated, similarly, the positions of both the Sun and the Moon should be clarified. The essence of the calculation is:-

The position of the Sun is the position of the Moon, the sum of both is Saturday (midnight) 356°55'16" 65°38'53" 65°34'6" Sunday (midnight) 0°53'56" 108°16'56" 106°10'55" Daily motion 58'43" 120°38'3" 130°36'46"

Subtracting the sun's true position from the moon's true position at the midnight of Saturday does not decrease, so subtracting the sun's position from the sum by adding 360^° to the moon's position gives 65^° 43’ 37’’. Similarly, the difference in the positions at the midnight of Sunday is 107^° 22’ 57’’. The difference in their daily motions is 110^° 36’ 20’’.

There is a date of 720 art or 120. Therefore, when 65°43’ 37” is divided by 120, the remainder is 7 and 11° 43’ 37”. From this it appears that the eighth date, which is Ashtami, is currently at the time of midnight, and 11° 43’ 37” has passed, with 16’ 23” remaining. In this chapter, some hold that the number of shlokas is 50 and some hold that it is 51. Those who consider the number of shlokas to be 50 say that in the 11th and 20th shlokas, there are 6 steps instead of 4 in each. Those who consider 51 believe that each shloka has four steps. Therefore, both opinions are identical in my understanding. At this time, I have four reminiscences of Sūrya Siddhānta, but regretfully, the order of the numbers of shlokas is not the same in two of them. The order of the numbers is also messed up in the book edited by Indra Narayan Dwivedi, so for convenience, I have considered the 11th and 35th shlokas as three lines or six steps each. Considering the 20th shloka as having 6 steps causes the problem that the rules are not complete in any subsequent shloka, but the latter half of one shloka and the first half of another shloka have to be combined. Considering the 35th shloka as having 6 steps, this inconvenience remains only in shlokas 36-42.

In this chapter, many methods of obtaining information about direction, country (place), and time from the sun's zenith are described. Only one instrument is used for the zenith, which is called gnomon. A straight pointed rod of a hard metal or ivory was placed vertically on level ground, and all work was done from its shadow. This is called the gnomon. The Yantradhyaya describes other instruments, but in this place, only the gnomon is discussed. It is clear that the image of the sun appears very large, and the tip of the shadow of the gnomon cannot be determined with much subtlety, so the things that can be known from the gnomon are some gross ones. Nowadays, more subtlety can be achieved by sighting with a telescope, but in ancient times, the gnomon was very useful. Our astrologers have shown great skill in obtaining the subtlety that could be achieved by sighting with it. There is no doubt in this at all.

Some such things have also been invented with the help of the gnomon instrument, without which knowledge of direction, country, and time remains coarse, so there is a need to discuss them as well. Therefore, in the Scientific Commentary, the parallax of rays (refraction of light), the cause of the motion of the ecliptic, the deviation of the axis (nutation), the aberration of light, and the equation of time will be described in detail.

(1) Draw a circle with the diameter of one and a half angulas according to the gnomon on the surface of the stone leveled by water, or on a level platform made of vajralepa (sarkhi lime etc.). (2) Establish a cone of twelve angulas in the vertical form at the center of this circle. Mark the points where the shadow of this cone touches the circle before and behind the meridian. (3) Make two points on the circle at those locations. These two points are called the forenoon and afternoon points. Draw a north-south line between these two points with a plumb line. (4) Draw east-west lines between the north-south directions with a plumb line. In this way, draw lines of directions such as northeast between the two directions with a plumb line.

Sūrya Siddhānta—the easiest way to know whether a plane is level is to fill water one or a one and a half inches deep by hiding it with wet soil around the edges of the plane and see with a straight plumb line whether the water depth is the same or different everywhere. If the water depth is the same everywhere, then it should be understood that the plane is level. Nowadays this work is done with a Spirit level.

Vajralepa – in the beginning, many types of spices were mixed in lime to make such a mortar that became as hard as thunder. Such mortar is called Vajralepa. There is one method for making Vajralepa in the Barahi Samhita:-

Timi - If two circles are drawn intersecting each other, the part between them becomes fish-shaped. This is called timi.

In Figure 44, the place of the gnomon is in the center of the circle. When the shadow of the gnomon before noon is the same as the shadow of 'k', its tip reaches the point on the circumference of 'k'. When the shadow behind noon is the same as the shadow of 'kh', its tip reaches the point on the circumference of 'kh'. Just these points 'k' and 'kh' are taken as centers, and two circles of equal diameter are drawn from them, which form an area in the shape of timi. The line joining their general points is the North-South line. The direction of North should be indicated by 'u' and the direction of South by 'd' on the points where this line cuts the first circle. Then, taking 'u' and 'd' as centers, two more arcs of equal diameter are drawn, and their general points are joined by a straight line. This will be called the East-West line. 'p' should be written for the West direction and 'pu' for the East direction. Then, taking 'u' and 'p' as centers, two arcs of equal diameter are drawn, and the point where the circumference will be cut between their general points is the direction of the NW angle and the point where it will be cut between 'pu' is the direction of the fire angle. Similarly, the direction of the North-East and South-West angles can also be known.

Proof—At the time of rising, the point on the eastern horizon where the sun appears, rises towards the south, and the shadow of a vertical stick or gnomon moves towards the north, becoming smaller. At noon, the sun comes to the meridian. At that time, the shadow is the smallest and in the exact north direction. After this, the sun begins to descend slightly towards the north, and the shadow moves from the north towards the east, becoming larger. The time before noon when the gnomon's shadow makes a larger angle towards the west from the north is the same time behind noon when the shadow makes the same larger angle towards the east from the north. From noon the same

Source page 247

Forward and backward in time, the length of the shadow is also equal*. Therefore, when the length of the shadow is equal to half the diameter of the stretched circle, the line that divides the angle formed between them into two equal parts will be the North-South line. To draw this bisecting line, it is ordered to draw arcs of equal diameter and make a shadow, which is according to the method of geometry. According to this rule, lines indicating other directions can be drawn. The line joining the points fixed by the noose of the shadow at the forenoon and afternoon on the circle is also the East-West line, but in order to work with the tilted gnomon in the future, it is necessary that all the lines drawn indicating directions pass through the center of the gnomon. Therefore, it is ordered to make a shadow from the North-South points of the circle and draw the East-West line.

Source page 253

Translation—(6) In one yuga, the constellation-circle oscillates like a pendulum 600 times towards the east. Multiplying this 600 by the number of days of the great yuga (10) and dividing by the number of days of the season, multiply the result by 3 and divide by 10. Whatever remains is called the precession angle. By imprinting this on the positions of the planets, one should know the revolution, shadow, declination, etc., of the planets.

Scientific Commentary—The common point on the ecliptic where the sun comes from the north of the ecliptic and the tropics is called the vernal equinox. When the sun reaches 60 degrees beyond the vernal equinox, its northward movement stops and it begins to return towards the south. At this time, the onset of the southward motion begins. Therefore, the point where the sun turns to the south is called the summer solstice. The time when the sun continues to move towards the south from the beginning of the southward motion, which is similar to 6 months, is called the southward motion. After 3 months from the beginning of the southward motion, the sun comes again on the vernal equinox. This point is called the autumnal equinox because the autumn season begins at this time. The sun continues to move towards the south for 600 further, then turns back to the north. The point where the sun begins to return to the north is called the winter solstice. The onset of the northward motion begins from this time. The southward and northward points are called the apogees. In Figure 36, the order of V, D, SH, and U are vernal equinox, southward motion point, autumnal equinox, and winter solstice. The circle that occurs on the apogees, celestial poles, and latitudes is called the solstitial colure. In Figure 36, the circle of V, D, SH, U is the solstitial colure.

The declination point does not always remain in the same place in the sky but is moving towards the west, therefore the constellation or star group that has Uttarayana or Dakshinayana nowadays does not have it in the ancient times. Vedanga1

Source page 254

In astrology it is written that when the sun was at the beginning of the Nakshatras Śravishtha or Dhanishtha, the beginning of Uttarayana started, and when the sun reached the half of the Ashlesha Nakshatra, the beginning of Dakshinayana started.

In Barahmihira's Barahi Samhita, while discussing this, he writes that in ancient times, Dakshinayana was at the half of Ashlesha and Uttarayana at the beginning of Śravishtha, but now as soon as the sun enters the sign of Ka, Uttarayana happens when the sun enters the sign of Makara. If this is not the case, one should ascertain by observation.

Nowadays, the beginning of Dakshinayana starts at the beginning of the Ardra Nakshatra and the beginning of Uttarayana starts at the half of the Moola.

Thus it is proven that the Uttarayana point was at the beginning of Dhanishtha in the time of Vedanga Jyotisha and now at the half of the Moola. Therefore, it is clear that the motion is towards the west. Because of this, the Spring Equinox point or Autumn Equinox point is also moving towards the west. The westward movement of the Spring Equinox point is called precession of equinoxes by European astronomers, so the phenomenon that our astrologers have written as Ayana-Chalan is called precession of equinoxes by Western astronomers. Bhaskaracharya Ji2 has equated Ayana Chalan and Vishuvatkranti-Valay-Patachalan.

There is a great difference in the opinions of our ancient astrologers regarding Ayana Chalan. The view of Sūrya Siddhānta is that the beginning point of the Nakshatra cycle moves or oscillates by up to 27 degrees on both sides of the Spring Equinox like a pendulum (Figure 46). Cause of luni-solar precession

It has been proven that the change in direction along the axis on which the Earth rotates once every 24 hours is due to the movement of the ecliptic point. The reason for the deviation in the direction of the Earth's axis is that the Earth is not a perfect sphere, but is somewhat flattened at the poles and bulged at the equator. Therefore, the resultant attraction of the Sun and the Moon does not pass through its center. In Figure 52, let s be the Sun, k be the center of the Earth, dh be the axis of the Earth extended to the sky, va be the equator, a be the point where the Sun's attraction is acting, and aa be the direction of the Sun's attraction. If the Earth were a perfect sphere, a and k would be at the same point, so the plane of the equator would not tilt towards the Sun. The figure also reveals that half of the meridian, which is towards va, is near the Sun, and the other half, which is towards v, is far from the Sun. Therefore, the Sun's attraction will be weaker towards v, which results in the meridian plane tilting towards the Sun, causing the 'axis of the Earth dh to wobble'. It also appears that the plane of the equator, as it tilts, will eventually meet the plane of the ecliptic, where the Sun resides, and the axis of the Earth will start to form a right angle with the ecliptic, and the pole and the south will become one. However, this is not the case. Because the Earth is rotating on its axis at a very high speed, the angle between the planes of the equator and the ecliptic will always remain approximately the same, and the pole and the south will continue to revolve in a circle around each other.

Scientific Commentary—Much has been written regarding the equinoctial shadow on pages 204-205 and in the commentary of the seventh verse of this chapter. On the 205th page, it is stated that when the tangent of a place's latitude is divided by the gnomon, it gives the equinoctial shadow of that place. Therefore, it is necessary to state here that the value of the equinoctial shadow according to this verse is gross. Because on the day of the vernal equinox of Aries or Libra, when the shadow of the gnomon is measured at noon and the equinoctial shadow is known, the Sun is not exactly on the vernal equinox at noon but is some ahead or behind. The conjunction of the Sun coming exactly on the vernal equinox at noon happens after many years. On this day, the precession of the Sun changes by approximately one zodiac sign per hour. Therefore, one should know the precession of the Sun at noon by knowing the pure time calculation of the vernal equinox of Aries or Libra and after performing the correction, know the pure equinoctial shadow. It is also stated in pictures 42-43 that the height of the pole from the uttara point of the horizon is equal to the latitude. This may cause readers to doubt which definition of latitude is correct. Therefore, it should be decided here that these three definitions of latitude are the same.

From pictures 7 and 10 it is clear that the angular difference of any place from the equator on the north-south line is its latitude, and the angular difference of the place from the pole on the north-south line is its longitude. If the plane of the equator is extended towards the sky, this is called the prime vertical circle, and if the plane of the north-south line is extended in the sky, it is called the meridian circle. Similarly, when the line joining any place from the center of the Earth is raised, the point it reaches in the sky is called the astrolabe of that place. Therefore, it is proven that the difference between the astrolabe of a place and the prime vertical circle is also a latitude, and the difference between the astrolabe and the celestial pole on the meridian is the longitude. Therefore, the latitudes of the kha dhanu sthāna and the longitudes of the kha dha dhanu sthāna in pictures 40 and 43 were obtained. However, the dha vi dhanu or u kha dhanu is equal to 60 degrees. Therefore, if the common arc is removed from each, then the remaining kha vi and u dha will be equal, that is, the difference between the prime vertical circle and the astrolabe is the same as the difference between the uttara point of the horizon and the northern celestial pole. Similarly, it can also be proven that the dha kha dhanu is equal to the vi dhanu, that is, the height of the prime vertical circle from the south point of the horizon is also equal to the longitude. It is also clear that the prime vertical circle of any place in the northern hemisphere is always to the south of the prime vertical circle, so the kha vi remains the latitude and the vi da remains the longitude in the northern hemisphere.

Now it remains to prove that the difference between the gnomon and the subsolar point is equal to the latitude.

(14) To find the meridian altitude of the sun, multiply the shadow of a day's noon, which is also called the radius, by the shadow hypotenuse of the meridian and divide, and make an arc of the quotient, then the meridian altitude of the sun will be found. Sūrya Siddhānta - The circle drawn perpendicular to the horizon from a point (star, center of the sun, etc.) to which the science extends is called the Vertical Circle. The difference between that point and the x-coordinate from the x-coordinate is called the zenith distance of that point, and the difference from the horizon is called the altitude of that point. The prime vertical circle is also a vertical circle. But its special feature is that it is at the points east and west of the horizon. The meridian circle is also a vertical circle at the north and south points. Therefore, when the sun is on the meridian circle, the difference of the x-coordinate from it is its meridian altitude. If the sun is also on the equator circle, then this will be the same as the latitude. If the sun is not on the equator circle, then it will be either north or south of the equator circle. The difference of the sun from the equator circle at the meridian time is the sun's declination, which is called the north or south declination according to whether the sun is north or south of the sun's equator. Similarly, the sun can also be north or south of the x-coordinate. If the sun is north of the x-coordinate, the shadow will be towards the south, and the difference between the sun and the x-coordinate will be called the northern altitude. But if the sun is south of the x-coordinate, the shadow will be towards the north, and the altitude of the sun will be south. If the sun is in three zodiac signs like Taurus, then subtracting this arc from 6 signs will yield the true sine portion of the mean solar time. If the sun is in three zodiac signs like Libra, then adding this arc to 6 signs will yield the true sine portion of the mean solar time. And if the sun is in three zodiac signs like Capricorn, then subtracting this arc from 12 signs will yield the true sine portion of the sun. By performing the inverse operation several times in this true sine portion, the mean sine portion will be obtained.

Scientific Commentary - in 14-15 shlokas, the method of knowing the latitude by adding or subtracting the meridianal portion and the declination of the sun is explained. In the 17th shloka, the method of finding the revolution by knowing the latitude and the declination is given. Therefore, this is the second form of the first method, and just as addition or subtraction is required there, so is it here too. The reason for this can also be understood from the three equations in relation to figure 56.

The rule of addition and subtraction will be easily understood from this equation -

a ± n = k

In which 'a', 'n', and 'k' indicate latitude, declination, and revolution respectively, the sign of the number will be written at the time when the directions of latitude and declination are different, otherwise the sign of minus will be used. The direction of latitude in a circle is understood as North, but in this rule, its direction is understood as South because in the northern circle, the direction of the equator from the cross is South.

Where sin (portion of the sun) is the sine of the portion of the sun, ecliptic of the sun is the ecliptic of the sun, and 1367 is the ultimate ecliptic of the sun. This is the form of the last part of the 17th verse and the first half of the 18th verse.

If the value of sine is to be used in decimal fraction according to the current custom, then an even simpler form will be—

ja (sp) ja (vs) = ja (svp) (2)

Now it has been well proven that the revolution of the sun is not 240 but its mean value is approximately 23°27’ at this time and it is decreasing by about half a degree every year. Therefore, if one wants to know the portion of the sun's revolution nowadays, one should calculate by considering it as equal to 23°27’.

Example—on one day, the revolution of the sun at noon is 16017’ south and this is in the sign of Makara, then tell the true sine portion.

sin (portion) = sin (revolution) / sin (great revolution) = sin16° 17' / sin23° 27' = .2804 / .3676 = .7047
∴ portion = 440, 48 ′

Source page 290

Since the Sun is in the latitude of Makara, this portion should be the sine portion of the Sun after subtracting 12 degrees or 3600. Therefore, this is the sine portion of the Sun for this day

= 360 ° - 44 ° 48 ′ = 315 ° 12 ′

It is also clear from the picture 36 of page 200 and experience that the time it takes for the Sun to go from the vernal equinox to the south point, that is, to go from the sine Aries to three signs, the corresponding time in which its northern revolution increases from zero to 23°27’. When the Sun goes from the south point (from the beginning of the sine Cancer) to the autumn equinox, its northern revolution decreases and becomes zero from 23°27’. The solar declination increases from zero to 23°27’ when the Sun goes from the autumn equinox, that is, the sine Libra, to the post meridian (until the beginning of the sine Makara), and then it decreases and becomes zero from the beginning of the sine Makara to the vernal equinox.

The rule given above for finding the portion only tells that how far the sun is from the vernal or autumnal equinox. If the sun is between three zodiac signs, i.e., between Aries and Pisces, then the obtained portion is the distance of the sun from the vernal equinox, so this is the sine portion. If the sun is within three signs from the beginning of Cancer, then the obtained portion is the distance of the sun in the opposite direction from the autumnal equinox. But the autumnal equinox is 6 signs away from Aries, so the obtained portion has to be subtracted from 6 signs, then the sine portion of the sun from the vernal equinox is obtained. If the sun is between three signs from Libra, then the obtained portion is the distance of the sun in the opposite direction from the autumnal equinox, so 6 signs have to be added, then the sine portion of the sun from the vernal equinox is obtained. And if the sun is between three signs from Capricorn, then the obtained portion is the distance of the sun in the opposite direction from the vernal equinox. Therefore, by subtracting this portion from 12 signs, the distance of the sun in the opposite direction from the vernal equinox (portion) is obtained.

It is stated above that the sun's apogee decreases by about half in the year. It would be good to give the formula so that the apogee can be easily known at any time.

Therefore, it is said to do the unperformed action, that is, consider the mean Sun that comes by giving the inverse correction of the apogee once and then do the correction of the apogee. Agra should only be understood as the angle by which the Sun, planet, or star differs from the east or west point on the horizon circle. In Figure 43, the position of the rising planet is at point G of the horizon circle, and the east point is P, so the rising agra of the planet is P dhanu. Similarly, the setting agra of the planet is P dhanu because P and G are the positions of the planet at the time of setting and the west point. If a perpendicular is dropped from points G or P to the east-west line, its value will be treated as the rising agra. In Figure 42, P is a straight line, the agra of the rising planet. Except for the time of rising, in any other time, the difference between the point where the Sun will fall on the vertical circle and the east or west point will be called the istakalik agra.

Nata kala—the time taken for a planet or star to come on the meridian from some time is called the west sidereal time of that planet or star, and the time that remains after passing the meridian of that star or planet is called the east sidereal time of that star or planet. If the sidereal time (hour angle) and declination of a planet or star are given, its position can be easily determined. The magnitude of the sidereal time is known by the angle between the polar circle of the planet or star and the meridian. The polar circle is perpendicular to the equator, so the sidereal time is also known by the arc from the equator to the pole of the star or planet.

In figure 57, kha dha ra, kha dha sa and kha dha rā angles are the hours of the sun while the sun is at the points ra, sa and rā in sequence. This place is east of the meridian circle, so it is the hours of the sun east. When a planet or star is on the meridian circle, its hour is zero. The hour is generally written in degrees. If the east hour of a star or planet is 15^ o, it should be understood that it will arrive on the meridian circle in 15 imes 4 minutes or 1 hour (sidereal).

The advanced time is called the advanced time when the hour is subtracted from half the day time. The east advanced time is the time from the rising time of the planet or star to the auspicious time, and the west advanced time is the time from the auspicious time to the setting time. The west advanced time is the time when the planet or star is west of the meridian circle. The advanced time or its abbreviation advanced should be understood as different from the declination as the hour is different from the minute.

Translation—When the shadow of the desired time is multiplied by the hypotenuse and divided by the shadow hypotenuse, sine is obtained. Subtracting the square of sine from the square of the radius and taking the square root yields the gnomon. Multiplying the gnomon by the radius and dividing by the sine of colatitude gives the hole. Multiplying the hole by the sine of declination and dividing by the versed sine gives the sine of inclination. Subtracting this from the node gives the remainder, which is understood as the versed sine, and forming an arc from the versed sine body, the east or west time of day is known.

Scientific Commentary—The summary of these three shlokas is:—

(1) shadow x radius / shadow hypotenuse = sine (2) √(radius^2 - sine^2) = gnomon (3) gnomon x radius / sine of colatitude = hole (4) hole x radius / sine of declination = sine of inclination (5) node - sine of inclination = nto-versed sine

These are the opposites of the rules written in shlokas 34-35, so their derivation is the same. Yes, here, the value of the sine of the shadow, i.e., the sine of the ntaansh, should be known as in the rule mentioned in the 13th shloka. It has already been stated that the angle between the gnomon and the shadow hypotenuse is the ntaansh, so when the shadow is divided by the shadow hypotenuse, a decimal fraction * and when this result is multiplied by the radius, the value of the sine of the ntaansh of the arts is obtained.

The line on which the tip of the shadow moves—

इष्टे हि मध्ये प्राक्पश्चाद् वृत्ते बाहुत्रयान्तरे ॥४१॥
मत्स्यद्वयान्तरयुते स्त्रिस्पृक्सूत्रेण भाभ्रमः ।

Translation—On the day when the line of the tip of the shadow of the gnomon is to be drawn, determine three points of the shadow tip before and behind the meridian of that day. Make a triangle from the first and second points and the second and third points. Extend the lines passing through the general points of each triangle so that they meet. Taking the point where they meet as the center, draw a circle passing through the three points of the shadow tip. This circle will be the apparent line of the shadow tip on that day.

Scientific Commentary - In reality, the path of the tip of the shadow is not circular but is in the shape of a hyperbola. Therefore, this rule is impure, which has been accepted by Bhaskaraacharya, Ranganatha ji, etc. Therefore, there is no need to think much about it.

(45) At the time when the ascendant is to be known, the apparent Sun and the actual Sun should be known. The portion of the Sun that is on the zodiac is called gataansh, and the portion of the zodiac that remains for the Sun to enjoy is called bhogyansh. By multiplying the rising signs of the zodiac by gataansh and dividing by 30, and by multiplying gataansh and bhogyansh by 30 and dividing by 30, bhogyasu are known. (46) From the time the sunrise has passed until the auspicious time, the bhogyasus should be subtracted. The rising signs of the subsequent zodiac are to be subtracted from the remainder.

Source page 346

We should subtract the rising signs of the amounts beyond this from the rest. Similarly, by subtracting the rising signs of the following signs, when the remainder is such that the rising signs of the further amounts do not decrease, this is called the impure amount (the amount that does not decrease). But if one wants to know the ascendant from the setting signs, then the rising signs of the signs that have already risen before sunrise should be subtracted in the time of sunrise, in reverse order, that is, first subtract the setting signs, then subtract the rising signs of the amount that is behind the sign of the sun, then subtract the rising signs of the sign behind that, and so on, (47). Finally, if some remains, it should be multiplied by 30 and divided by the rising signs of the impure amount. If the operation is done from the setting signs, subtracting the quotient from the impure amount, and if this operation is done from the setting signs, adding the quotient, it is known that which point of the ecliptic is the ascendant in the horizon at that time.

Translation—(88) Know the segment between the arc of light between the instantaneous Sun and the meridian circle from the rising of the Sun and Lanka in the east or west. If it is the eastern meridian, subtract it from the instantaneous Sun, otherwise add it, then the mean ascendant can be found.

Scientific Commentary—The point of the declination circle that lies on the meridian is called the mean or the decimal point. The point of the declination circle that is very close to the cross is called the tritibha. The tritibha is found by subtracting 3 signs in the rising sign or adding three signs in the setting sign.

The time it takes for the rise of signs in Lanka is the same time it takes for them to cross the meridian. This is the same for all places. For example, the rising portion of the Aries sign in the Nirayana in Lanka is 26°18’. Therefore, the rising of Aries in Lanka was 1758. In the same time, the Aries sign crosses the meridian in all places. Similarly, one should understand about the other signs.

The reason for this is that the rising portion of a sign in Lanka is the segment of the ecliptic for which it takes the same time to rise as it takes to come above the horizon. It also takes the same time to cross the meridian for this segment of the ecliptic. Therefore, this sign will also take the same time to cross the meridian.

The method of knowing the time from the ascendant can only be practically used when the identification of the signs and constellations is good. Therefore, it is necessary that there is complete information about the signs, constellations, and other famous stars. In the eighth chapter of Sūrya Siddhānta, there is a discussion of some constellations and stars in the chapter named Yutyaadhikar, so there it will also be stated which are the famous stars from which the time in the sign can be easily known.

Here, it is sufficient to state that knowing the time from the mean ascendant is more convenient. If it is known what was the declination of the sun at noon and which star, whose declination is known, is on the meridian circle at night, then it can be easily known how much time has passed since noon because the difference between the declination of the star and the declination of the sun is the same in the degrees, in which that star comes after noon on the meridian circle.

If the declination of a star is not known, the gross knowledge of time can be obtained by just identifying the star groups of the ecliptic. For this, it is also necessary to know which constellation the sun is in. It has already been said that the 27th part of the ecliptic is called a constellation and the entire ecliptic is a

Source page 359

The Earth seems to revolve in the constellation during the day, therefore a constellation violates the meridian in 60 ghaḍī = 23 ghaḍī or two and a quarter ghaḍī or the meridian, or 6 constellations violate the meridian in 20 ghaḍī or 8 hours. From this calculation, the time known will not differ from the actual time by more than half an hour.

Example—if the Sun is in the constellation of Punarvasu, at what time will it be on the meridian of the śravaṇa constellation?

In the Nakshatra table of 213 pages, Punarvasu is the 7th Nakshatra and Shravana is the 22nd Nakshatra. Therefore, there is a difference of 15 Nakshatras between these two.

The difference between 6 constellations is 20 degrees or 8 hours.
