It will be on the meridian 133 hours behind or at 1:15 in the night from midnight the śravaṇa nakṣatra meridian.

Nowadays, time is not known from the sundial but from clocks that run on the force of a chain, whose time is somewhat different from the sundial, so those who calculate the ascendant from the clocks prevalent nowadays and tell the results of astrology do not have exact knowledge of the ascendant. Besides the Panchang of Mahamohopaladhyaya Bapudevji Shastri of Kashi, no other Panchangs have come where this point is well discussed. Therefore, it is very necessary here to state what the relationship is between the sundial and the chain clocks.

True time, mean time, and time-equation—

In Chapter on Mean Motions pages 7, 8, it is stated that the time from the time a star rises until it rises again is called Nakshatra day and the time from one sunrise of the sun to another sunrise is called Sawan day. However, knowing the exact time of rising is very difficult because for this work, there should be a horizon where there are no trees, etc., which is generally impossible for everywhere because such a plain is found very rarely where there are no trees in the east or west direction for many kosa. Even if such a horizon is found, the rising of the sun or star happens some time before the proper time due to the bending of the rays of light, the magnitude of which varies according to the different conditions of the atmosphere.

Source page 360

is. Therefore, for very fine calculations, the time is not tested from the time of sunrise but from the time of noon. Therefore, the definition of Sawan or Nakshatra day is made as follows today:-

The time from the moment the center of the Sun comes to the meridian circle until the moment its center comes to the meridian circle is called 'Spatha Sawan day'.

The time from the moment the Spring Equinoctial point comes to the meridian circle until the moment this point comes to the meridian circle is called 'Nakshatra day'.

The motion of the Spring Equinoctial point is generally the same. Therefore, the Nakshatra day is always the same*. However, a lot of difference occurs in the magnitude of the Sawan day because the daily motion of the Sun constantly changes. This can be easily found by clocks that indicate the Nakshatra period. If a clock is made such that when the Spring Equinoctial point comes to the meridian circle, it shows exactly 12 o'clock, such a clock is called Nakshatra clock (Ghatika Yantra). With such a Ghatika Yantra, it is easily known how much difference occurs in the magnitudes of the Sawan days. For example, four Sawan day magnitudes are given for 1606 AD:-

1606 AD(Nakshatra period) hour minute second 1st January's true noon to 2nd January's true noon 24 44 24.6 2nd April's true noon to 3rd April's true noon 24 3 38.5 3rd July's true noon to 4th July's true noon 24 4 7.5 2nd October's true noon to 3rd October's true noon 24 3 37.6

Due to the deviation of the axis, the position of the vernal equinox becomes mean or western before the true position (see page 247). However, this does not cause such a small difference in the magnitude of the sidereal day that it is not a loss to consider it as such.

†Ball's Spherical Astronomy page 215

Source page 361

From this it appears that the value of the Sawan day is not the same. The value of the Sawan day from the noon of January 1st to the noon of January 2nd is 46 4 seconds larger than the value of the Sawan days of the second and third April, etc. It is impossible to make a clock that changes its pace according to the motion of the sun because a clock running by mechanical force will always run at the same pace. Therefore, the time known by such clocks is different from the time of a sundial because the value of the Sawan day is known from the sundial, which changes every day. If a clock that tells the sidereal time is used, it is not convenient in practical behavior because the sidereal time of 24 hours is about 4 minutes shorter than the 24 hours of the solar day. Therefore, if the solstice of the sun today is exactly 12 o'clock in the sidereal clock, then the solstice of the sun tomorrow will be at 12:04 in the sidereal clock. In this way, the solstice of the sun falls four minutes behind each day, and in 15 days, the solstice of the sun will be at 1 o'clock in the sidereal clock, in 1 month, the solstice of the sun will be at 2 o'clock in the sidereal clock, and in two months, it will be at 4 o'clock in the sidereal clock, etc. Thus, it is evident that the rising and setting of the sun may occur at any time of the day according to the sidereal clock, which may not be useful for practical behavior because time is generally determined by the rising and setting and solstice of the sun.

To eliminate this dilemma, astrologers have decided that for the work of astrology, such clocks should be used that indicate the sidereal time, but the clocks should also have worldly behavior so that they indicate the hours, minutes, seconds, or clock of the mean Sawan day. Doing this, the time of these clocks will necessarily differ from the sundials that indicate the true Sawan day, but this difference does not exceed 1: minute. The value of the mean Sawan day is the mean (average) of the true Sawan days of several years. The mean value of the four days written above 1606 AD is 24 hours 3 minutes 57.1 seconds, which is very close to the mean value of a Sawan day. If the mean value of the values of several years of true Sawan days is calculated, then a mean Sawan day is similar to the sidereal time of 24 hours 3 minutes 56.555 seconds. The examples below will clarify how the mean Sawan day value is known by observation. Determining the value of the mean Sawan day

On the fourth day of July of 1836, at the time when the center of the true Sun was in the meridian

Source page 362

On the circle at that time its true right ascension was 6 hours 54 minutes 703 seconds. Similarly, on the day of July 4th of 1860 AD or in the time of Yamottaro-Llanghankal, the true right ascension of the Sun was 6 hours 53 minutes 54.61 seconds. Determine the value of the mean Savan day from this.

First it is necessary to know how much time passed in the sidereal time from July 4th of 1860 AD at 6 hours 53 minutes 54.61 seconds (sidereal time).

It is clear that in one year, that is, in the time from one sidereal Aries solstice to the next sidereal Aries solstice, the Vernal Equinox passes one time less than the Sun. This is because due to the motion of the Earth, the Sun moves one degree towards the east every day, causing it to pass one less time than the Vernal Equinox by approximately 4 minutes each day. Thus, in one year, the Sun falls behind by 1 day, meaning the Sun's passage of the Aries solstice is one less than the Vernal Equinox's passage of the Aries solstice.

From July 4th of 1836 AD to July 4th of 1860 AD, there are 54 years in which there are 13 more years (leap years) such as 1840, 1844, 1848, and the remaining 41 years are ordinary years. Therefore, this period is equal to 41 X 365 + 13 X 36 = that is, equal to 19723 Savan days. It has been proven above that in one year, the passage of the Vernal Equinox is one time more than the passage of the Sun, so in 54 years, the passage of the Vernal Equinox will be 54 times more. Thus, in the above period, there were 19723+54=1977 sidereal days. Therefore, from the time of the Sun's passage of the Aries solstice of July 4th of 1836 AD to the time of the Sun's passage of the Aries solstice of July 4th of 1860 AD, there were 19777 days 6 hours 53 minutes 54.61 seconds - 6 hours 54 minutes 7.03 seconds, that is, 19776 days 23 hours 56 minutes 47.58 seconds in sidereal time.

Therefore, this sidereal period was equal to sixteen thousand seven hundred twenty-three clear Sawan days. Now if the above sidereal period is divided by sixteen thousand seven hundred twenty-three, the value of one mean Sawan day in the sidereal period is 24 hours 3 minutes 56.555 seconds. Therefore

The part of the meridian that the polar circle reaches at the point where it meets the tropics is called the meridian part of the center of the sun. This fraction is revealed in degrees, arts, arcseconds, and also in hours, minutes, and seconds. One degree is equal to 4 minutes or 10 minutes of arc.

1 medium Sawan day = 24 hours 3 minutes 560555 seconds (Nakshatra)

The difference between mean and true Sawan days is explained by astrologers by imagining a sun that is considered to move at the same speed on the ecliptic and comes behind the sidereal time of 24 hours 3 minutes 54.555 seconds every day on the meridian. The moment this imagined sun crosses the meridian is the mean meridian, and it is exactly 12 o'clock in the clocks indicating the mean period. It is shown that the mean value of the true Sawan days throughout the year is the same as the mean Sawan day, so it is apparent that the time taken by the aforementioned imagined sun to complete one revolution on the ecliptic is the same time taken by the true sun to complete one revolution on the ecliptic. Therefore, the mean daily motion of the true sun on the ecliptic is the motion of this imagined sun on the ecliptic. It is proven that in the same time, the portion of the imagined sun on the ecliptic increases as much as the portion of the true sun increases.

It is revealed from the table of 320 pages that as long as the portion of the true Sun is less than 60 degrees, its declination is less than the portion of the mean. However, the declination of the hypothetical Sun is always equal to the mean portion of the true Sun. Therefore, it is proven that as long as the declination of the hypothetical Sun or the mean portion of the Sun is less than 60 degrees, the polar transit of the hypothetical Sun is to the east of the polar transit of the true Sun. Therefore, the polar transit of the true Sun comes before the hypothetical Sun on the meridian circle and the true meridian comes before the mean meridian. Therefore, at the time when the sundial indicates 12 o'clock according to the true Sun, the clocks indicating the mean time will also show 12 o'clock. That is, the sundial will be faster than the mean clock. The faster it is, the more the time of the mean clock will be found by subtracting from the sundial time.

Similarly, as long as the mean portion of the true Sun is more than 60 degrees and less than 180 degrees, that is, when the Sun's sine will be between the sine of Cancer and the sine of Virgo.

It becomes clear from this table that if the declination of the imagined Sun is taken as the solstice and the declination of the true Sun is taken as the solstice, then at what time the true Sun's pole-transit is ahead or behind the imagined Sun's pole-transit.

Source page 364

Until then, the polar transit of the true Sun remains to the east of the hypothetical Sun. Because the latitude of the true Sun will be greater than the latitude of the hypothetical Sun, which is equal to the mean portion of the true Sun (see Table 320). In this situation, the true Sun will pass behind the hypothetical Sun, meaning the sundial will remain behind the mean hour (slow or sluggish). Therefore, by adding the difference of the latitudes of both in the time of the sundial, the time of the mechanical clock (mean clock) will be found. Similarly, when the true Sun is in three zodiac signs, the sundial will be ahead of the mean hour, and by subtracting the difference of the latitudes of the true Sun and the hypothetical Sun from the time of the sundial, the time of the mean clock will be found, and when the true Sun is in three zodiac signs, the difference of the latitudes of both in the time of the sundial will be added to find the mean time.

But the true Sun does not move with the same speed on the true Sun circle always. Sometimes its speed becomes fast and sometimes slow. Therefore, for this reason also the true Sun will not come to the true Sun meridian at the time when the mean Sun comes, as stated above. The true Sun and the mean Sun stay together only at the apogee and nadir of the true Sun circle (see pages 80-82). When the Sun moves ahead of the apogee, the daily motion of the true Sun is less than the daily motion of the mean Sun, so the true Sun falls behind the mean Sun, that is, the true Sun remains ahead of the mean Sun towards the east. Therefore, the true noon comes before the mean noon. For this reason also the time of the sun-dial remains ahead of the mean time. This condition remains until the Sun reaches the nadir. From here on, the motion of the true Sun is greater than the mean motion, so the true Sun remains ahead of the mean Sun towards the east. Therefore, the true noon is behind the mean noon, that is, the sundial remains slow compared to the mean time.

Due to these two reasons, that is, the movement on the true Sun circle and the difference in daily motion, there is some difference between the true time and the mean time. The time taken to subtract or add from the true time to find the mean time is called the 'Equation of Time'. It is also written as:-

Mean Time = True Time + Equation of Time*

* Venkatesh Vapu Ketkar has named it Udayantara in his astronomy (Jyotg. Ga. page 75)

Source page 365

When the time equation is positive, it is added and when it is negative, it is subtracted.

Refraction of Light

Air, water, glass, amber are substances in which light enters and travels to the other side. Therefore, they are called transparent. When light passes from one homogeneous transparent substance to another homogeneous transparent

Source page 383

When it goes into matter, its direction is not the same as it was in transparent matter before. This phenomenon is called the deflection of the ray or simply deflection. Some writers have named it refraction of the ray, but for the sake of convenience of many things, it seems better to call it deflection. From this, a big difference in the reality and apparent positions of an object is seen. Sometimes objects take on a divided form. But this place is not appropriate for discussing all these events. Only what is related to astrology will be stated here. Giving a small example for experience will be sufficient:-

Fill a glass with water and keep it in the sun and see how much of the glass is illuminated by the sun. Pour the water and keep the glass in the same place. This time, some less part of the glass will be illuminated. In figure 65, there is a glass 'ga'. If water is filled and it is kept in the sun, it is seen that from 'ga' to 'bha' is illuminated, that is, it is seen that the sun reaches even to the edge of the glass. But when the water is poured and the glass is kept in the same place, it is seen that now only the part 'ga' to 'kha' of the glass remains illuminated, the sun does not reach the edge. This shows that if the ray is in the direction 'gā kha' in the air, then it becomes in the direction 'gā bha' as soon as it dissolves in the water.

Refraction related to astrology—when the rays of light coming from celestial bodies that come to the earth enter the atmosphere, they undergo refraction. This refraction is called astronomical refraction. The density of the atmosphere is not the same from top to bottom. As the distance from the earth increases, the atmosphere becomes thinner, so the total atmosphere is not homogeneous. When a ray coming from a celestial body enters the atmosphere, it first goes into a very thin layer, and as it approaches the earth, due to entering layers of less dense to more dense, it bends slightly towards the vertical and reaches the earth. Therefore, the path of it in the atmosphere is curved. The direction of the ray when it reaches the earth is in which the celestial body is seen.

A ray from a star enters the atmosphere at a point in the direction of k. From this point, its path is not straight. The ray has to enter the different levels of the atmosphere from k to the observer's position d, which become progressively denser. Therefore, the ray also becomes curved and finally reaches d. At the point d of this curve, there is the tangent d to d. The observer realizes that the star is in the direction d. If a line parallel to k is drawn from d to t, the star appears in the direction t at that time when there is no atmosphere that bends the ray. Therefore, the effect of the atmosphere is that

The direction is absolutely pure, but the star is so far that the angle of the star is equal to zero.

Due to the motion of celestial bodies, their rising and setting appear a little earlier and later respectively, so the day length increases.

The rising of celestial bodies is understood at the time when their center comes to the eastern horizon. At that time, their true position is 60°. However, it has been proven that the true position is greater than the apparent position due to motion. It has also been stated that when the apparent position is 60°, the motion is approximately 35’. Therefore, at the time of rising, the true position of the celestial body is approximately 60035’. This means that when the center of the celestial body appears to be on the horizon, it is approximately 35’ below the horizon. Therefore, it is evident that when the center of the sun is 35’ below the horizon, then it appears to have risen, and when its center does not reach 35’ below the horizon, it appears to be setting. Because of this, the apparent day length is about 5 minutes or 12, 13 minutes more than the true day length. To know the exact magnitude of this increase, we should calculate the instantaneous motion of the sun at the time of rising.

Considering the variation, the maximum day length nowadays is 34 hours 10 minutes. This is only 5 minutes more than 34 hours 5 minutes. This inaccuracy cannot be considered more than for the arc of rising and setting time.

The difference in the shape of the Sun due to variation—as the Sun rises and sets, the shape of the Sun appears larger and somewhat oval. The reason for this is that the increase in variation near the horizon is very intense. The image of the Sun is about 32 degrees. Therefore, at the time when the lowest point of the Sun's image remains in the horizon, its true position is 60°, and the true position of the highest point of the image is about 32 degrees less. Due to this difference, the lower point remains higher and the upper point remains less than it. This causes the apparent vertical to appear as if the image is 5 degrees less, making the Sun appear oval.

Further investigation of the motion will increase greatly. If one wants to know when the upper image of the sun appears on the horizon, then the amount that comes from adding 35’ + the semi-diameter of the sun or 35’ + 16’ elevation in place of ta(n) in the equation (2) on page 376 should be added to the time calculated mathematically.

Sūrya Siddhānta has named the part of the arc and the name of the hour length. In other treatises, the part of the arc is only called arc or true arc length, and the name of the hour length is called nati.

Now in brief, it will be explained what our Acharyas have written about the arc:-

Bhaskaraacharya has written* that when the daily motion of a planet is divided by 15, the absolute arc length (horizon arc length) of that planet is obtained. The reason for this is explained:-

The circle of the sky that is touched by a horizontal (plane) touching any place on the earth is called the horizon circle of that place. This horizon circle divides the sphere of the sky into two parts. This horizon circle is called the sensible horizon circle. If a plane of sky is extended parallel to this sensible horizon circle towards another plane of sky passing through the center of the Earth, the circle that this plane cuts in the sky is called the true horizon circle of that place. In Figure 78, the position of the observer and the center of the Earth on the earth surface are shown. The line drawn from D touching the earth surface intersects the orbit of the Moon at point C and the orbit of the Sun at point S. Therefore, C, S are on the sensible horizon of the place. If a plane of sky is extended parallel to this, passing through another plane of sky which cuts the orbits of the Moon and the Sun at points C and S respectively, then this plane is called the true horizon of the place of D. It is apparent that when the Moon and the Sun or any other planet is on the true horizon of the place of D, at that time it is in the plane B C S which is below the sensible horizon of D, so it will not be seen by the observer. In such a situation, the magnitude with which the planet remains below the sensible horizon is C or S (which is equal to B D, i.e., the semi-diameter of the Earth).

Source page 431

Therefore, there is nothing wrong in saying that when a planet is on the true horizon of a place, it is below the true horizon of that place by the same amount as the semi-diameter of the Earth, that is, its latitude is the same as the semi-diameter of the Earth. If you understand 'cha' as 'cha' and 'sa' as 'sa', there will be no much difference because 'cha' or 'sa' is much smaller than the whole orbit. Therefore, it can be said that when a planet is on the true horizon, it is below the horizon of the observer by the same amount as the semi-diameter of the Earth in its orbit.

This has been stated before (see pages 16-17) that our teachers assumed that the planetary motion of each planet is the same. According to the verses 81-82 of the upcoming Geography chapter, the daily motion of each planet is 11858.72 yojanas. The semi-diameter of the Earth is 800 yojanas according to Sūrya Siddhānta and 760.5 yojanas according to Siddhānta Shiromani (see Chapter on Mean Motions page- 53). What was written in the previous text is exactly one-tenth of the planet's daily motion. According to the earlier text as well, the daily motion of the planet is the semi-diameter of the Earth

Source page 432

It is often equal to fifteen times. Therefore, it can be said that at the time when the planet is on the actual horizon, at that time it is below the true horizon by the fifteenth part of its daily motion. That is, the true declination of the planet is equal to the fifteenth part of its daily motion. One day is equal to 60 *ghadi* (hours), so the fifteenth part of the motion in 60 *ghadi* is equal to the motion of four *ghadi*. This means that as much the planet moves in four *ghadi*, so much is its true declination (in the arts). In units of time, the true declination of the planet is equal to four *ghadi*.

If the daily qualitative motion of the planet, and its daily planometrical motion, and the utmost declination, and the distance of the planet's orbit from the Earth and the semi-diameter of the Earth can be expressed in this way, then the above statements can also be revealed as follows:-

The speed of light—there are many ways to measure the speed of light. The discussion here will be about the first method:

The speed of light was determined by a astrologer named Roman in the year 1732 Vikram Samvat. Before this, no one had imagined that light also requires some time to travel from one place to another. It is also astonishing how Roman found this out. You all must have seen lunar and solar eclipses many times. During a lunar eclipse, the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon falls into the Earth's shadow. When the entire Moon falls into the shadow, a total eclipse occurs, and when only a part falls into the shadow, a partial eclipse occurs. Just as the Moon revolves around the Earth and sometimes appears half, sometimes quarter, sometimes three-fourths, similarly, four or five moons revolve around Jupiter. Jupiter's moons are so small that they cannot be seen without a telescope. These moons move very quickly into Jupiter's shadow as they revolve, so they are not visible for a while. Therefore, it can be said that when Jupiter's moons fall into its shadow, they are eclipsed. Even during these eclipses, they are known in the same way as during solar and lunar eclipses by calculating many years before. Sailors use these eclipses to tell time. Just by thinking about this, Roman found out the speed of light.

Imagine that in figure 87, there is the sun, and p, pa, pi are three places of the Earth on its orbit, and g, ga, gi are three places of Jupiter on Jupiter's orbit. It takes the Earth 6॥ months to reach from p to pa. In 13 months, the Earth, while being from p to pa, reaches pi and comes between the sun and Jupiter. 20".63 is called the constant of the coefficient of aberration of the motion of the Earth. Its more accurate value is 20".47. If the angle of the aberration is the same as 60°, then it is clear that the maximum value of the coefficient of aberration of the Earth's motion will be 20".47.

It is clear that the motion of the Earth is present in the coefficient of aberration as a multiple. However, the motion of the Earth is not always the same; at the time the Earth is at its lowest, its motion is very fast, and at the time it is at its highest, its motion is very slow. Therefore, in the first case, the constant of the coefficient of aberration is 20".80 and in the second case is 20".13.

The effects of the portion of the Sun, stars, and distant planets due to the correction of terrestrial motion, the shadow, the solstice, and the declination are left unexplained due to fear of expansion. Here, it is discussed in a simple manner:-

Just as a star appears to revolve in a small orbit around its true position due to the annual declination, similarly, due to the correction of terrestrial motion, it also appears to revolve in a small orbit around its true position. This orbit is also parallel to the plane of the ecliptic. The size of its orbit also changes in the same way that the orbit of the star changes due to declination. At the time when its size is elliptical, its major axis is equal to 20”.47 and its minor axis is equal to 20”.47 X ja when ja is the shadow or deflection of the star.

It is clear that the correction of terrestrial motion of the star is in the same direction as the motion of the Earth, but the Sun is 60° ahead in the direction of the Earth's motion because the Earth's motion is in the direction of the tangent of the geodetic, which makes an angle of 60° with the semi-diameter of the geodetic, and the Sun is at the center of the geodetic. Therefore, it is proven that the correction of terrestrial motion of the star is towards the point of the ecliptic which is 60° behind the Sun, i.e., whose portion is 60° less than the portion of the Sun.

The star that is on the ecliptic pole, i.e., Kadamba, revolves around its true position in a circle throughout the year, the angular value of whose semi-diameter is 20‘46.

The star that is on the ecliptic oscillates forward and backward by 20”.46 from its true position on the ecliptic like a pendulum. Therefore, the total difference throughout the year is equal to 40”.6.

If a star remains in another place from which its shadow is like that of the sun, it appears to revolve on an ellipse throughout the year whose center is the true position of the star, whose semi-major axis is 20046/2 and whose semi-minor axis is 20046 sine and whose plane is parallel to the plane of the ecliptic.

The effect of the motion of the planets on the geodetic signs happens in two ways, one due to the motion of the Earth; the other due to the motion of the planet. If the motion of the planet were the same as the motion of the Earth and in the same direction, then there would be no geodetic signs. In other conditions, the calculation of what the geodetic signs will be can be done easily separately.

The motion of the Moon is much less than the speed of light, therefore its cause can be considered as equal to zero in terms of terrestrial motion. Due to the motion of the Earth also, the motion of the Moon is not like terrestrial motion because the Moon also revolves around the Sun throughout the year along with the Earth. Therefore, the effect of terrestrial motion in the Moon is equal to zero.

Daily geodetic measurement—because of the daily motion of the Earth, the equator moves approximately 25,000 miles in a day because the circumference of the Earth at the equator is approximately 25,000 miles. The circumference of other places is shorter than this. Therefore, when there is a motion of 25,000 miles in a day, a motion of 3/10 miles per second is proven. But the annual motion of the Earth is 183/2 miles per second. Therefore, the one-twelfth part of the geodetic measurement due to the annual motion will be on the equator due to the daily motion. It will be even less at other places, so it is not unreasonable to understand it as such.

[ 1 verse—Value of the mean distance between the Sun and the Moon. 2-3 verses—Method of knowing the true diameters of each and the true diameter of the Sun in the Moon's orbit (in conjunctions and phases). 4-5 verses—Method of knowing the value of the diameter of the Earth's shadow in the Moon's orbit. 6 verses—Where the node of the Moon can be so that an eclipse may occur. 7 verses—In which date an eclipse may occur. 8 verses—Method of clarifying the Sun and Moon at the end of Amavasya and Purnima. 9 verses—Why an eclipse occurs. 10 verses—Method of knowing the magnitude of the occulted part. 11 verses—Method of determining whether a total eclipse or partial eclipse or no eclipse will occur. 12-15 verses—Method of knowing how long the eclipse and total eclipse will last. 16 verses—Method of knowing the beginning and end time of the eclipse. 17 verses—Method of knowing the beginning and end time of the total eclipse. 18-21 verses—Method of knowing how much part will be occulted at what time. 22-23 verses—Method of knowing the auspicious time knowing the magnitude of the eclipse. 24-25 verses—Need for knowing the declination to draw the picture of the eclipse. 26 verses—Method of knowing the angular value of the image at the auspicious time.

To know how an eclipse occurs between the sun and the moon, some properties of light are first necessary. Therefore, these will be considered briefly first. It is everyone's experience that in the light of a lamp at night, the shadow cast on the wall of an object is somewhere light and somewhere deep. The deep shadow is in the middle and the light shadow surrounds the deep shadow. If the object is near the wall, the deep shadow is large and the light shadow is small. As the object moves further away from the wall, the extension of the shadow increases, but the deep shadow decreases and the light shadow increases. If the object is smaller than the lamp, there will also be a situation where the deep shadow does not fall at all, only the light shadow will be seen on the wall.

Source page 467

Yes, if the object is larger than the lamp, a deep shadow will always fall on the wall.

The part of the wall where the deep shadow falls, no part of the lamp's light reaches that part, but in the light shadow, some part of the lamp's light must reach. If an insect is in the deep shadow on the wall, it will not see the lamp at all, but in the light shadow, it will surely see some part of the lamp. This can be tested as follows:-

Keep a lamp or candle lit. Place a pencil, bullet, or any object smaller than the lamp a short distance away, standing or hanging. Hold a thin paper in your hand in such a way that both deep and light shadows of the pencil fall on it. Make a hole with a needle in the deep shadow and see if the lamp can see or not. The lamp will not see. Make a hole by piercing in the light shadow and see. Some part of the lamp will be seen.

From geometry, it can be known where the deep shadow will fall and where the light shadow will fall. It is also possible to determine the extent of these. To know how eclipses happen in the Sun and Moon, the mathematics of the deep and light shadows has to be done, so it is necessary to think about this well. Further, the deep shadow will be called shadow and the light shadow will be called umbra.

Suppose R is a luminous body and C is an opaque body. Both bodies are spherical. The rays of light from R spread in all directions, but the rays that fall on body C cannot proceed further than it. If lines are drawn that touch both these bodies, they will move forward, intersecting each other at point T. It will be of the shape of a cone. This will be the boundary of the shadow formed by body C. Shadows will not fall above, below, to the sides. (See Figure 60).

The lines that touch both these bodies and meet at point T form the boundary of the umbra.

If a sheet (screen) is kept in shadow in such a way that it is at a right angle to the line joining the centers of the r and c bodies, then the diameter of the circle of shadow that will be formed on this sheet will be ch cha, and the diameter of the circle of the umbra will be u u, which includes the diameter of the shadow (see figure 61). If a hole is made at a point p in the segment u ch and the light-emitting body is seen through this hole, then the upper part of the body which is above the point p will be seen. This point p a

But if a hole is made in the shadow section, no part of the luminous body will be seen. The summary is that if the observer remains somewhere above the line of sight but below the line of the shadow, he will definitely see the upper part of the body but not the lower part. Similarly, if the observer remains below the line of sight and above the line of the shadow, he will definitely see the lower part of the luminous body but not the upper part.

If brought to the point, there will be no shadow here. The luminous body will not be seen, but its brightness will be seen all around. If it is moved further away from the point, another view will be seen. In the sections of the shadow of K, Kh, and Gg, the same thing will be seen as before, but in the space between the lines that form the boundary of the shadow in Kh and Gg, the entire edge of the luminous body will be seen, but there will be darkness in between (see figure 62). The figure shows that the lines drawn from any point between K and Gg that touch the body will reach both above and below the body. Since the body is round, it will be seen like a bead due to the darkness in between.

All these views can be seen by experiment. A round lamp, a ball, and wooden pegs are sufficient for these three things. The round lamp should be understood in place of the body and the ball in place of the peg. This experiment can be easily done in any place during a dark night.

All the things about a solar eclipse can be understood from this experiment. R should be considered the Sun and C the Moon. The place of Pat should be considered the Earth. Just as this body remains in both shadow and penumbra when it is near the body but in the lines forming the boundary of only penumbra or shadow when it is far, similarly the Earth remains in both the shadow and penumbra when it is near the Moon and only in the shadow when it is far. Since the Earth is much larger than the Moon, the entire Earth cannot fall in shadow or penumbra. The inhabitants of the part of the Earth that falls in shadow do not see the Sun at all. Therefore, a total eclipse of the sun or total eclipse occurs. The inhabitants of the part of the Earth that falls in penumbra

Just as the Earth comes into the shadow or umbra of the moon, a total eclipse or annular eclipse of the sun is seen, similarly when the moon comes into the shadow of the Earth, the light becomes without light. This is called lunar eclipse. If the entire moon comes into the shadow, a total eclipse of the moon occurs, and if an incomplete part comes into the shadow, a partial eclipse of the moon occurs. In this situation, the moon will appear to be in eclipse of the sun, but it may not have the good fortune to see an annular eclipse because the size of the Earth is larger than the moon, so the moon can never come out of the shadow.

From the picture it is also clear that it is necessary to enter the umbra before reaching the umbra. It should be remembered that a lunar eclipse is seen only when the moon enters the Earth's shadow. If the moon only goes into the umbra, no eclipse will be seen, yes some impurity will also occur.

Translation—(8) The time difference from the time when the sun and moon were made apparent to the time of the end of the lunar month or new moon, by knowing the true motions of the sun and moon for that time, by subtracting or adding from their true portions of the sun and moon, the ones that result are to be considered the apparent sun and apparent moon at the end of the lunar month. If the above time is behind the end of the lunar month, then subtraction should be done, and if it is before, addition should be done. But to know the true position of the node, its opposite action should be done, that is, if the above time is behind the end of the lunar month, the motion of the node for that time should be increased and if it is before, it should be decreased because the motion of the node is opposite.

(20) Taking the length of the moon at that time as the hypotenuse and adding its square to the square of the sidereal time to find the square root of the sum, and then subtracting the result from the arc, the remainder is the instantaneous grain.

Multiply the sine of the netaṃśa of the circumposition of the chhaya graha by the sine of the latitude of the desired place, and divide the product by the radius of the ahoratravritta of the planet, and make the quotient an arc. This is called the axis of the planet. If the planet is in the pāla, that is, before the yatrotarvitta, then the axis is towards the north, and if the planet is in the kapāla, that is, behind the yatrotarvitta, then the axis is towards the south. (25) Adding 60 degrees to the sine portion of the planet, the resulting portion is obtained by taking the inclination (according to chapter on true positions verse 28) by multiplying it by the sine of the ultimate revolution (of the ahoratravritta) and dividing by the radius. This quotient is called the inclination. This will be to the north or south. If the directions of the axis and the inclination are the same, add them, and if they are different, subtract them. The result obtained by doing this is called the sphutvalan. Dividing its sine by 70 gives the angular value of the arc.

Scientific Commentary—To know from which point the eclipse, moksha, etc., of the chhaya graha begins or ends, the inclination is required.

The angle at which the meridian is north or south from the east or west point of the chhaya graha is called sphutavalan. The east and west points of the planet's image are known in this way—they draw a great circle passing through the north-south points of the horizon from the center of the planet to the meridian, which is called the circle of position of that planet. This circle of position forms a right angle with the prime vertical circle. The vertical circle drawn from the center of the planet's image parallel to the prime vertical circle is also at a right angle to the circle of position. Among the points where this vertical circle intersects the edges of the planet's image, the one towards the east is called the east point of the planet and the one towards the west is called the west point of the planet. All these things are clarified by figure 101.

Calculation of the night-time—

To know the time of the moon, one must first know the time of the sun. In the meridian time, the sun remains on the meridian circle, and in the midnight time as well, it remains on the meridian circle below the horizon, therefore the center of the Earth's shadow remains on the meridian circle in the midnight time because the center of the Earth's shadow remains at exactly 180 degrees from the sun. Therefore, the time of the center of the Earth's shadow in the midnight time is zero. If it is known how much before or after midnight the time of touch is, then it is easily known how far east or west the time of the center of the Earth's shadow is in the time of touch. During a lunar eclipse, the moon is very close to the Earth's shadow, and it is known that the moon is at what distance from the Earth's shadow, therefore the time of the moon can be easily known.

Chapter on Solar Eclipse Authority (Brief Description)

Verse 1—When are the perpendicular and declination of the sun zero. Verse 2-8—Rules for knowing the perpendicular. Verse 6—Determining the time of Amavasya by giving the correction of the perpendicular and by inaction. Verse 18-11—Rules for knowing the declination. Verse 12—The declination-season is known by the sum or difference of the declination and the moon's season. Verse 13—From the declination-season, the position, etc., should be known. Verse 14-17—Knowing the perpendicular of the touch and the time of moksha, the calculation of touch and time of moksha should be done by inaction.

When is there absence of perpendicular and declination—

मध्यलग्नसमे भानौ हरिजस्य न संभवः ।
अक्षोदङ् मध्यभक्रान्तिसाम्ये नावनतेरपि ॥१॥

Translation—(1) When the sun is on the tribhone ascendant, there is absence of the portion of the perpendicular. When the north of a place is equal to the latitude and the north declination, that is, when the sun is on the x-cross, there is absence of declination, i.e., season-perpendicular.

Scientific Commentary—The translation of the chapter on mean motions in this verse is the tribhone ascendant, although it is stated on page 326 that the mean ascendant is different from the vitrim ascendant or tribhone ascendant. However, here the Acharya has written tribhone as mean because it is between the rising and setting signs, although the same word is ambiguous in two meanings. If the meaning of mean ascendant taken is the one considered in verse 48 of the Chapter on the Three Problems, then the feeling is impure, so here the meaning of mean-ascendant is tribhone ascendant. If the sun or any planet is on the tribhone ascendant, the portion of the perpendicular is zero. Its proof is explained in detail in the Chapter on the Three Problems (see p. 410). It has also been stated regarding the season-perpendicular.

(3) The portion of the time after the new moon is obtained by knowing the ascensions of the auspicious places (of the zodiac) and multiplying its sine by the sine of the ultimate revolution, and then dividing the product by the sine of the latitude or the latitude-longitude of the auspicious place, the resulting quantity is called the rising or rising sine. (4) In the time after the new moon, according to what was said before from the ascensions of the zodiac, if the mean ascendant or tenth ascendant is known, add its declination to the latitude of the auspicious place if their directions are the same. If the directions are different, find the difference between the declination and the latitude. (5) Whatever is obtained by adding or subtracting is the ntasha of the mean ascendant. The sine of this is called the mean sine. Multiply the mean sine by the rising sine and divide the product by the radius and square the result. (6) Subtract the year of the mean sine from the square and find the square root of the remainder. Whatever is known to find the square root is called the arc. Subtract the square of the arc from the square of the radius and find the square root of the result, whatever is obtained is the gnomon or the arc.

In this shorter method, the nataṃśa of the mean sign is taken as the nataṃśa of the three-quarters sign because there is very little difference between these two. But this inevitably brings grossness.

Translation—(6) If the portion of the sun from the three-quarters sign is more, then the sun is east of the three-quarters sign, so the difference between the portions of the sun and the moon altitudes should be subtracted from the end of the new moon. But if the portion of the sun from the three-quarters sign is less, then the difference between the portions of the sun and the moon altitudes should be added at the end of the new moon. The time that comes when the difference of the portions of the altitudes is processed in this way with the end of the new moon is the time of the portion altitude- Sanskrit-end of the new moon. In this time, the difference between the altitudes of the sun and the moon is calculated again by the aforementioned method and the above altitudes are added, subtracted. The time that comes from this is then calculated as an altitude and it is also processed. Such an action should be done until the time becomes stable, that is, when the end of the new moon comes again after processing the altitudes repeatedly, then this work should be stopped. By doing this, the middle time of the eclipse is known.

Source page 534

Scientific Commentary—the calculation becomes purer from non-action as previously stated (see page 266). At the time when the moon, while moving towards the east, becomes equal to the portion of the sun, at that time the end of the new moon occurs. This is called the mathematical proven new moon end. When the sun is to the east of the three-fold ascendant, the moon, due to declination, hangs to the east and becomes in front of the sun before the new moon. Therefore, as much as the relative declination of both, the end of the true new moon occurs earlier. For this reason, in the first half of the shloka, it is said to subtract the declination from the mathematically proven time. Conversely, when the sun is to the west of the three-fold ascendant, the moon does not appear in front of the sun even in the mathematically proven new moon time because, due to declination, it hangs a little lower towards the west. Therefore, as much declination occurs at this time, the true new moon time is behind. That is why adding this declination results in the true new moon.

(10) Multiply the difference in the mean daily motions of the Moon and the Sun by the radius fifteen and divide the product by the radius. (12) The declination is in the north or south direction according to the direction of the mean sine. That is, if the direction of the mean sine is south of the cross, then the direction of the declination will also be south, and if the direction of the mean sine is north of the cross, then the direction of the declination will be north. If the directions of the Moon's arc and the declination are the same, they should be added, and if they are different, they should be subtracted. Doing so, the resulting quantity is the declination of the Moon, the arc, or the deviation.

The essence of the ten and eleven shlokas of Vigyanbhashya is this.

Translation—(14) According to verse 6, subtract the position that comes in the time of Amavasya due to inaction and add the time of eclipse according to the 13th verse. Then, knowing the portions of the time of eclipse and the time of release, find the difference from the portion of inclination of the middle time of eclipse.

Source page 537

(15) If the eclipse is in the anterior skull, that is, if the portion of the sun during the eclipse time is more than the portion of the three-fold ascendant, then the declination of the touch time will be more than the declination of the mean time and the declination of the liberation time will be less than the declination of the mean time. But if the eclipse is in the posterior skull, that is, if the portion of the sun during the eclipse time is less than the portion of the three-fold ascendant, then the magnitude of the declination will be in reverse order, that is, the declination of the touch time will be less than the declination of the mean time and the declination of the liberation time will be more than the declination of the mean time.

(16) In both situations, whether the touch and moksha are in the anterior skull or in the posterior skull, according to the 14th verse, the true position should be known by adding the difference of the latitudes obtained by the touch-position and the moksha-position to the mean position. However, if there is a condition contrary to the rule stated in the 15th verse, that is, if the touch-position latitude in the anterior skull is less than the mean latitude and the moksha-position latitude is greater than the mean latitude, or if the touch-position latitude in the posterior skull is greater than the mean latitude and the moksha-position latitude is less than the mean latitude, then the difference obtained according to the 14th verse should be subtracted from the touch or moksha position latitude to obtain the true position latitude.

(17) When the tangents, mean, and motion are all in the same skull, then the difference of the above latitudes should be taken and the above action should be performed. If the tangent is in one skull and the mean in another skull, or the mean is in one skull and the motion in another skull, then the latitudes of the tangent and the mean, or the latitudes of the mean and the motion, should be joined with their respective positions. Similarly, the true position and the apparent position should also be known.

Scientific Commentary—it is clear that according to the 6th verse, the inclinations of the Sun and the Moon that occur in the time of Amavasya-antakaal or the middle of the eclipse are different from the inclinations of the time of touch and the time of liberation because the parts of the Sun, Earth, and Moon's continuous motion at the time of touch and liberation are different, and it is shown in the Chapter on the Three Problems that the inclination depends on the nataansh, that is, if the nataansh is more, the inclination is also more, and if the nataansh is less, the inclination is also less (page 383). Therefore, in the 14th verse, the need to know the inclinations of the time of touch and the time of liberation is indicated, and the difference in inclinations from the middle time is shown. If both touch and liberation are in the same protection, that is, the eclipse is the touch and liberation before the rising of the trilobhan lagna, then

Source page 538

It is clear that at the time of touch, the portion of the Sun or Moon will be greater than the portion of the Sun or Moon in the mean time and less in the time of salvation because the ecliptic is the highest point of the declination above the horizon, and the Sun and Moon rise respectively, meaning their portion decreases, so the portion of the time of touch is greater than the portion of the mean time, and the portion of the time of salvation is less than the portion of the mean time. But if both touch and salvation are in the western hemisphere, then at the time of touch, the portion of the Sun will be less than the mean time portion, and the portion in the time of salvation will be greater than the mean time portion because the Sun or Moon descend in the western hemisphere, so their portion increases.

Adding the difference between the time of touch and the mean time of the latitudes to the mean position of the anterior hemisphere gives the true position of touch because the position calculated first is according to the latitude of the mean time, but the latitude in the time of touch is some more, so due to this, the Moon hangs a little lower, i.e., towards the east, so the touch is seen a little earlier, meaning the value of the position increases. But in the time of salvation (being in the anterior hemisphere), the latitude remains less compared to the mean time, so adding the difference between these two also gives the true position of salvation because when the latitude in the time of salvation is less, the Moon does not hang as much towards the east as in the mean time, so it remains for a longer time in front of the Sun and the position of salvation also increases.

Due to the obliquity in the western skull, the moon hangs towards the west, which causes a some delay in it coming in front of the sun because the motion of the moon is always towards the east and east, and due to the obliquity, it seems as if it is also going towards the west. For this reason, the time of eclipse is some behind the time of the mathematical amāvasyānta time. However, the lunar portion of the touch time is less than the mean time because the eclipse occurs some time after the touch time, and in this time, due to the daily motion of the earth or the flow of air due to the ancient view, the sun and moon all appear below. Therefore, the touch time obliquity in the western skull is less than the mean obliquity due to the lesser portion of the lunar portion, which has the effect that the eclipse does not take as much delay in touching as it does in the mean time, that is, due to the lesser obliquity at the time of touch.

Source page 539

The true position of the apparent touch increases. In the same way, because the portion of the moon at the time of salvation is more than the mean portion, the salvation-time declination is more than the mean declination. This has the effect that the moon remains in front of the sun for a longer time because at the time of salvation the moon appears above the sun, but due to the greater declination, it does not go up but remains hanging down, which causes some delay even in the time of salvation, that is, the true salvation position also increases.

Thus it is proven that whether the touch and moksha are both in the anterior skull or both in the posterior skull, in every case the time of eclipse increases, that is, the time of touch is some earlier and the time of moksha is some later. Therefore, by adding the difference in the perpendiculars of the time of touch and the mean time and the time of mean and moksha to the mean, the true position is found. By subtracting the time of the touch-time true position from the mean time of the eclipse and by adding the time of the moksha-time true position to the mean time of the eclipse, the true time of moksha is obtained.

Up to this, the first half of the 16th verse has been explained. The latter part does not make sense because the condition given in it is against nature. In the anterior skull, the tangential inclination will always be greater than the mean inclination because the tangential part is always greater than the mean part, and by the same logic, the rectilinear inclination will always be less than the mean inclination. Similarly, in the posterior skull, the tangential inclination will always be greater than the mean inclination. Yes, there is another matter if there is a total solar eclipse or lunar eclipse. But in such a situation, calculations will have to be done in a special manner, and it will be necessary to know only for a place when the eclipse occurs in the total eclipse. In the first case, one will have to consider how much of the sun is eclipsed at the time of sunrise and how long this eclipsed part will take to pass out. For this action, the verses of the lunar eclipse chapter 18, 16, and 20 will have to be used. In the second case, that is, in a lunar eclipse, one will have to consider how much of the sun is eclipsed at the time of sunset and how many eclipses have touched it before. For this action as well, the same verses will have to be used.

What has been said so far is for the state where touch and liberation are in one art. If touch is in one skull and the mean in another skull or the mean in one skull and liberation in another skull then the signs of touch and mean time

Source page 540

ಃ

Or by joining the latitudes of the middle and the time of salvation, what is obtained should be added to the mean position because in such a situation the eclipse period will increase greatly. Suppose the eclipse occurs in the anterior skull and the middle in the posterior skull. It is clear that in such a situation the middle period of the eclipse will be in the posterior latitude in a short time, that is, because the moon will move in front of the sun in a short time due to the moon moving away. But at the time of touch, the latitude of the moon will be towards the east, so the touch will happen a little earlier. From the first reason, the middle period of the eclipse will shift a little back, and from the second reason, the time of touch will be a little earlier, so the time from the touch to the middle period will increase due to both reasons. In such a situation, to find the true position of the time of touch, the sum of the latitudes of the touch and the middle period should be added to the mean position, but for the true position of the time of salvation, the difference of the two latitudes should be added to the mean position because both the middle period and the time of salvation will be in the posterior skull, only the time of touch will be in the anterior skull. But if the touch and the middle are in the anterior skull and the salvation is in the posterior skull, then the difference of the latitudes should be added to the mean position for the true position of the time of touch and the sum of the latitudes should be added to the mean position to know the true position of the time of salvation.

That which is explained here to know the time of touch and liberation should also be known in that same manner the times of combination and motion.

Chapter on Mean Motions (Brief Description)

[Verse 1—Purpose of the treatise. Verses 2-12—The method of drawing the treatise of the touch, liberation, and the eclipses of the mean time. Verse 13—How much part is covered when an eclipse is seen. Verses 14-16—The method of drawing the path of the observer. Verses 17-19—The method of drawing the treatise of an eclipse at a specific time. Verses 20-21—The method of drawing the treatise of the beginning time of a total eclipse. Verse 22—The method of drawing the treatise of the end time of a total eclipse. Verse 23—In what kind of lunar eclipse the moon is black, brown, etc. Verse 24—Whom should the method of drawing the treatise be followed.]

The name of this chapter is sometimes Chedyakaadhikar also. Both have the same meaning. Since Parilekha is simpler than Chedyaka, Parilekha is written here.

Purpose —

न छेद्यकमृते यस्मात्क्षेपा ग्रहणयोः स्फुटाः ।
ज्ञायन्ते यत्प्रवक्ष्यामि छेद्यरुज्ञानमुत्तभम् ॥१॥

(1) Without a diagram, inscription, or picture, there is no exact knowledge of the difference between the eclipses of the Sun and the Moon regarding which direction the eclipse begins, which direction it ends, and how much it will be. Therefore, I say that the best knowledge is that of making a diagram.

(2) On a well-measured flat land, fix a point and draw a circle with a diameter of 46 angulas with this point as the center. This is called the involute circle. (3) From the same center, draw another circle whose diameter is equal to the sum of the diameters of the shadow and the apparent figures. This circle is called the composite circle. Similarly, from the same center, draw a third circle whose diameter is equal to the diameter of the figure of that planet on which the eclipse occurs. (4) From this point, draw the North-South line and the East-West line according to the manner described in the first (Chapter on the Three Problems verses 3, 4). In a lunar eclipse, the touch occurs from the east direction and the exit from the west direction, but in a solar eclipse, it is the opposite, that is, the touch occurs from the west and the exit from the east in a solar eclipse. (5) In a lunar eclipse, draw a line from the center to the involute circle at a distance equal to the sine of the touch time from the east point and in the same direction as the involute. Similarly, draw another line from the center to the involute circle at a distance equal to the sine of the exit time of the moon, but in the opposite direction to the direction of the involute, from the western point. In a solar eclipse, the order of the directions of the above lines is the opposite, which

Source page 572

It is explained in the lunar eclipse. These lines are called the lunar lines, and the points where these lines intersect the lunar circle are called the lunar points. (6) From the points that are made from the touch and demise times on the lunar circle (according to the 5th verse), the lines that go to the center from them, draw lines to the points where the compound circle intersects, and draw lines from the center to the compound circle on the difference between the lunar touch time and demise time of the moon. These lines are called the deviation points of the points where they intersect the compound circle. (7) The lines that go from these deviation points to the center and the points where they intersect the reflected image are called the touch points and demise points in sequence.

(8) In the diagram of solar eclipse, make the displacement point in the same direction as the direction of the Moon's shadow, but in the diagram of lunar eclipse, the direction of the displacement point is opposite to the direction of the Moon's shadow. Accordingly, make the displacement point for the mean eclipse period as well.

(6) In the diagram of the middle period of lunar eclipse, if the directions of the declination and deviation are the same, the nodal point should be made in the east of the north-south line. But if the directions of the declination and deviation are different, the nodal point should be made in the west of the north-south line. If the direction of deviation is south, the nodal point should be made east or west of the north point. But if the direction of deviation is north, the nodal point should be made east or west of the south point. In the diagram of the middle period of solar eclipse, the opposite should be done, that is, if the directions of both the nodal and deviation are the same, the nodal point should be made towards the west of the north-south line and if the directions of both are different, the nodal point should be made towards the east of the north-south line. But if the direction of deviation is south, the nodal point should be from the south point and if north, from the north point towards the east or west.

(10) Draw a line from the nodal point to the center of the eclipse. On this line, make a point at the difference of deviation from the center in the direction of the nodal point; this is called the point of deviation of the middle period.

(11) Taking the point of deviation as the center, draw a circle with a radius equal to the semi-diameter of the client or the shadow. This circle is the part of the eclipse that is covered by the shadow of the moon (in lunar eclipse) and the shadow of the sun (in solar eclipse).

(12) The astrologer should draw a diagram on a flat surface or the celestial sphere (on a wooden board). The order of directions that exists in the anterior skull should be in the reverse order in the posterior skull, that is, where the directions of east, south, west, and north will be in the anterior skull, the directions of west, north, east, and south will be in the posterior skull respectively.

Scientific Commentary—in these verses, the method of knowing the distance and the direction in which the center of the observer is located at the touch, mean, and culmination of the reception, assuming the received image is fixed, is explained with the help of trigonometry. In a lunar eclipse, the moon is the received and the Earth's shadow is the observer. In a solar eclipse, the sun is the received and the moon is the observer. Now, the explanation of each method in the order of the verses is given:—

Verse 2—It is stated in verses 24-25 and pages 475-480 that the subtension is and how the knowledge of the ecliptic is obtained from it. It is also stated there that when the sine of the subtension is divided by 70, its sine value comes in angulas. Thus, the value of the radius is approximately 46 angulas because the radius is 3438 arts, which when divided by 70 gives a remainder of 46·1, which should be understood as 46 in integers. Therefore, in this verse, the method of drawing the circle with the semi-diameter of 46 angulas is explained. The line indicating the subtension can be easily drawn from this circle. Bhaskaracharya and other Acharyas have not stated the rule for drawing the semi-diameter circle. They have only written that on the circle of conjunction, the angles for east, west, north, and south should be made according to the direction for the magnitude of the subtension.

Verse 3—In this verse, the discussion is about the drawing of the circle of the image of the planet in which an eclipse occurs, that is, the circle of the apparent image. However, it is not made clear what its magnitude should be. If one considers one angula of 70 degrees, then the circle of the conjunction and the apparent image will be very small because the diameter of the apparent image circle is less than 16 degrees or one-fourth of an angula, and the diameter of the conjunction circle is about 1 angula. Therefore, considering one angula of 70 degrees will not be convenient for these circles. In such a situation, the angula discussed in the 26th verse of the chapter on lunar eclipse is necessary.

Source page 574

But the value of the inch given in it is stated to change according to the advanced time (see page 481). But I understand that if the magnitude of the inch is always considered as 3 arts, there may be no special loss because as stated in page 482, due to the motion, a greater difference in the rise or set time of the sun or moon's images is seen in the time of rising or setting. At other times, this difference is so small that there is no need to consider it. Therefore, I find it easy to assume an inch of 3 arts here, no need to make any modifications in it.

Verse 4—In the first half of this, it is stated that the lines of North-South and East-West should be drawn from the point taken as the center, to draw the circle of the shadow, the circle of the mean motion, and the circle of the apparent image according to the three problems verses 2-4 and figure 44. In the latter half, it is stated that in a lunar eclipse, it occurs in the anterior part of the moon's image and in the posterior part of the moon; but in a solar eclipse, it occurs in the posterior part of the sun's image and in the anterior part of the sun's image. The reason for this is clear. The moon moves towards the east in the sky while revolving around the Earth, so at the time it begins to enter the shadow of the Earth, its eastern part enters the shadow first. Similarly, the posterior part of the lunar image is separated from the shadow at the time of the moon; but in a solar eclipse, the lunar image moves from the posterior to the anterior of the sun's image and covers the sun's image, so at the time of contact, the posterior part of the sun's image begins to be covered and at the time of eclipse, the anterior part of the sun's image is separated from the lunar image.

Verse 5—In the time of lunar eclipse, the direction of the radiation of the moon should be marked on the circle of the shadow in the direction of the radiation, same direction as the eastern point. But in the time of the eclipse, the direction of the radiation should be marked from the western point in the opposite direction. These marks are called the nodal-point. The reason for reversing the direction in the time of the eclipse becomes clear from Figure 101 of page 476. There it is shown that at the time when the ecliptic from the planet's arc, i.e., the eastern point, is towards the north, at the same time the ecliptic from the western point is towards the south. Therefore, the time when the direction of radiation is said to be north, at that time it is towards the eastern point, not the western point. But the direction of the radiation, which is proven by the 24-25 verses of the lunar eclipse, is understood from the eastern point, so that rule

Source page 575

According to which the direction of the motion at the time of salvation comes is according to the east point, but in a lunar eclipse, the motion is towards the west point, so to make the angle of the quadrature or the direction of the ecliptic, the direction of the quadrature is reversed.

What is written above should be done in the opposite direction in a solar eclipse. That is, in the time of touch, the direction of the quadrature should be made from the west point in the opposite direction, but in the time of salvation, the quadrature should be made in the direction of the east point. The reason is clear. In a solar eclipse, the shadow of the sun is towards the west and the salvation is towards the east. But the direction of the quadrature is reversed towards the west as stated above. Therefore, the direction of the quadrature at the time of touch has to be reversed in a solar eclipse, but no change is needed in the direction of the salvation time.

Verse 6-8—The line drawn from the nodal point to the center of the image that is inscribed in the circle, whether it is the circle of the shadow or the circle of the compound, only allows one to know the direction of the ecliptic. In a solar eclipse, the image is the Sun, and the Sun always remains on the ecliptic, so the line going from the nodal point to the center can be understood as the ecliptic. But in a lunar eclipse, the image is the Moon, and the Moon is uttara or dakṣiṇa at a distance equal to its distance from the ecliptic, so the line going from the center of the lunar image to the nodal point cannot be the ecliptic. This line is parallel to it. Whether it is a solar eclipse or a lunar eclipse, in both situations, the center of the occluder does not lie on the line joining the nodal point to the center because in a solar eclipse, the occluder is the Moon, which does not move in the Moon's orbit, so to find the center of the occluder in the time of contact or occultation, from the point where the nodal line intersects the compound circle, a line is drawn to the center of the compound circle in the difference of the lunar deflection. The point where this line intersects the compound circle is called the deflection point. At the time of contact or occultation, the center of the occluder is at this point. Therefore, if a circle is drawn with a radius equal to half the diameter of the occluder, taking this point as the center, where it touches the image, there will be the contact or occultation of the eclipse. The location of contact or occultation can also be known from the line drawn from the deflection point to the center because the point where the occluder and the image touch is the same point where the line from the deflection point to the center

Source page 576

The line drawn also cuts the accepted image (see page 467 figure 100). In this figure, if C is taken as the center of the accepted image, the line drawn parallel to the declination circle D from C to the point V can be called the line going to the nodal point. The difference in this line from the earth shadow D is like the shadow of C. If C is taken as the center, the circle drawn with the radius of D will be the circle of conjunction. Where the line from C intersects the circle of conjunction, the difference of C from D will also be like the shadow of the moon. Thus, the rule stated in the seventh verse is proven.

This is not stated in the sixth verse in which the direction of the deviation line should be drawn from the declination line. This is stated in the eighth verse. In a solar eclipse, the deviation line should be drawn in the same direction as the direction of the moon's shadow, that is, if the direction of the lunar shadow is north, then the deviation line should also be north of the declination line, and if the lunar shadow is south, then the deviation line should be drawn south of the declination line. The reason for this is clear from figure 100 page 467. If we assume that 'ch' in this figure is the center of the sun's image and the ecliptic is the path of the moon, then if the lunar shadow is south, the moon touches the sun's image at a point to the south of the sun's image. That is, when the lunar shadow is south, the moon touches the sun's image to the south. Similarly, it can be proven that if the lunar shadow is north, then it will touch the sun's image to the north.

But in lunar eclipse it is opposite to this. This is also clear from this figure, if we assume 'cha' as the center of the umbral shadow. In the figure, the lunar arc is shown to the south. In such a situation, the umbral shadow touches the lunar image at a point which is to the north of the lunar image. Similarly, if the lunar arc is to the north, it can be proven that the umbral shadow will touch the lunar image to the south. Therefore, this rule is established that in a lunar eclipse, the direction of the point of contact should be opposite to the direction of the lunar arc, that is, in a lunar eclipse, the line of deviation and the line of declination should be drawn in the direction opposite to the direction of the lunar arc.

1. If 'ch' is taken as the center of the solar image and its circle is taken as the solar image, then all matters related to solar eclipse can be known from this figure.

The direction of the deflection of the nodal point in the time of salvation should also be determined according to this rule. If the direction of the lunar shadow is south, then the salvation of the moon in a lunar eclipse is in the latter part of the lunar image, as shown in the above figure where the moon is shown in the position of eclipse. But in a solar eclipse, the salvation of the sun is in the latter part of the solar image to the south. Similarly, if the direction of the lunar shadow is north, then the salvation of the moon is in the latter part of the lunar image to the south and the salvation of the sun is in the latter part of the solar image to the north.

The direction of deflection can also be determined by this rule even in the time of mean eclipse. From the same figure, it is revealed that when the lunar shadow is south, then in the middle period of a lunar eclipse, the center of the umbral shadow is to the north of the lunar image, but in the middle period of a solar eclipse, the moon is to the south of the center of the sun image. Similarly, when the lunar shadow is north, then in the middle period of a lunar eclipse, the center of the umbral shadow is to the south of the image and in the middle period of a solar eclipse, the moon is to the north of the center of the sun image.

Verse 6—In the time of the mean eclipse, if the direction of the lunar shadow and the direction of the epicycle are the same, then the nodal point should be made to the east of the north-south line. But if there is a difference in their directions, i.e., if the epicycle is north and the lunar shadow is south, or if the epicycle is south and the lunar shadow is north, then the nodal point should be made to the west of the north-south line. But it should be remembered that if the lunar shadow is south, then the nodal point should be made to the east or west of the north point, and if the lunar shadow is north, then the nodal point should be made to the east or west of the south point.

But for drawing the arc of the middle period of a solar eclipse, what is said in relation to the lunar eclipse should be opposite to it. That is, if the direction of the lunar shadow and the umbra are the same, then the umbra point should be towards the west from the north-south line, and if there is a difference in their directions, then the umbra point should be towards the east from the north-south line. Also, it should be noted that if the lunar shadow is south, then the umbra point should be made to the east or west from the south point, and if the lunar shadow is north, then the umbra point should be made to the east or west from the north point. This knowledge can be easily obtained from figure 102. The shadow on the earth in relation to the lunar eclipse can be taken as the sun's image in relation to the solar eclipse, so this picture can serve for both the lunar eclipse and the solar eclipse.

In the latter part of this verse it is stated that the order of directions in the circumscription of the anterior skull should be opposite to that in the posterior skull. But this is not understood because if the touch of the eclipse is in the anterior skull and moksha in the posterior skull, as usually happens, then the circumscription of the time of eclipse or conjunction should be different from the circumscription of the time of inclination or moksha. But such a thing is neither convenient in practice nor very necessary. Apart from these, the methods for knowing the directions of conjunction and inclination mentioned in the following verses are only possible if the same circumscription is taken. Other Acharyas have not written anything in this regard. Only in the verse 1 26 of the chapter on eclipse response of Brahma Sphuta theory is written that if a circumscription is made on the celestial sphere, the directions marked on it will be opposite to the directions of the terrestrial circumscription. The reason for this is that the order of directions in the terrestrial circumscription is that which is stated in the verses 1-4 of the Chapter on the Three Problems. But there is also the facility in the circumscription of the celestial sphere that we can turn it towards the image of the grasped, and easily know the direction of the touch or moksha point. In such a situation, on the celestial sphere, east will be to the left hand, west to the right hand, north to the north, and south to the south. But in the terrestrial circumscription, east is to the right hand, west to the left hand, north to the north, and south to the south.

The commentators of Sūrya Siddhānta have written that one should make a difference in the order of directions by the difference of east or west skull. But I do not yet know the reason for this, so I do it against the method as explained in Brahma Sphut Siddhanta. I hope some learned will express their opinion on this and kindly explain its reason.

Scientific Commentary—Commentators have revealed a big difference of opinion in interpreting this. Acharya Ranganath ji, and his followers Madhav Purohit ji and Pandit Indra-Narayan Dwivedi ji interpret this that even if the 12th part of the moon is eclipsed, it is not seen due to clearness. But this meaning does not seem right to me. The word clearness cannot be taken as sharpness. From the word clearness, it is understood that the light of the moon is clean or clear, therefore even if the twelfth part is eclipsed, it can be seen clearly with clearness. The meaning as I have written above is the same as Shri Vignanananda Swami has done on page 203 of his Bengali translation.

In this regard, Bhaskaraacharya1, Brahmagupta etc. have written that if the eclipse of the moon is less than the 16th part, it cannot be seen and if the eclipse of the sun is less than the 12th part, it cannot be seen. From this, the meaning of the aforementioned verse of Sūrya Siddhānta is the same as what I have done. Brahmagupta ji has used the word clearness in this meaning as revealed by his quotations.
