What is the color of the image of the observer--

अर्धादूनं च धूम्रं स्यात्कृष्णमर्धाधिकं भवेत् ।
विमुञ्चतः कृष्णधूम्रं कपिल सकलग्रहे ॥२३॥

(23) When less than half of the lunar image is covered, the covered part has a smoky color. When more than half is covered, the covered part appears black. When a large part of the lunar image is covered and only a little remains, the color of the covered part is black with a reddish tinge. But

Source page 585

The color of the total eclipse is reddish-brown. (In a solar eclipse, the color of the part of the sun being eclipsed is always black.)

Scientific Commentary—As long as the moonlight remains bright, the eclipsed part appears smoky or black in comparison. But when only a small part of the moon remains, its light becomes without heat. Therefore, the color of the eclipsed part also appears somewhat red. The reason for this redness is that the subtle light of the sun, refracting through the atmosphere, falls on the lunar image, so some redness appears on the black eclipsed part. At the time when the entire lunar image falls into shadow, the lunar image does not appear black but brownish with redness. The reason for this is also the refracted light of the sun, which falls on the moon by passing through the Earth's atmosphere. If there were no atmosphere, the color of the eclipsed part of the moon would always be black, as the color of the eclipsed sun.

Due to the rotation of the atmosphere, sometimes another astonishing phenomenon is also seen. When an eclipse occurs during the rising or setting time, the eclipsed moon is seen in the presence of the shining sun, where one side of the moon is eclipsed and the other side of the sun keeps the Earth illuminated by its brightness. Such phenomena were seen in the years 1666, 1668, and 1750 AD.

Calculation of the direction of the touch point according to the new method—

Western astrologers do not calculate the direction of the point of contact from the direction of the pole circle, but calculate the direction of the touch or the point of motion from the direction of the polar circle. Therefore, they do not need to know the declination. The following method is also explained in brief:

ch = center of the Earth's shadow, dh = North Celestial Pole, ch = center of the Moon at the time of touch, ca = center of the Moon at the time of Moksha, sa = point of touch, m = point of Moksha, ch u dh = pole of the center of the Moon at the time of touch, u = point of the lunar image at the time of touch, u = point of Moksha...

Source page 593

l or l = perpendicular distance of the polar circle of the Moon from the center of the Moon

∠ Uchas = direction of the point before the moon's northern point to the point of contact ∠ Ucham = direction of the point after the moon's northern point
chadh = difference in declination of the center of the lunar image = 60^° - moon's true time
chadha = difference of latitudes of the center of the shadow = 60^° - declination of the shadow
Chad = difference in declination of the center of the lunar image = 60^° - moon's nodal revolution

This is clear that in the time of contact or no return, the Moon remains very close to the Earth's shadow and the distance between these two is similar to the arc of a degree, the magnitude of which is approximately one degree, so in comparison, the difference in latitude of the Moon or the Earth's shadow is much larger than that of the Moon or the Earth's shadow. Therefore, the lines cha la, cha ca or cha lā, cha cā, the arc, and the straight lines and spherical triangles cha la or cā cha lā can be taken as simple triangles (Plane triangle) without any loss. From this reasoning, the difference in latitude can be considered equal to the difference in latitude because a perpendicular is drawn on the difference in latitude. Therefore, if the declination of the Moon and the declination of the Earth's shadow are the same,

chadh — chhad = chadh — chhad

If both the motion of the moon and the terrestrial shadow have a northern declination,

chadh - chhad = ( 60° - k ) - ( 60° - ka ) = ka - k

And if both have a southern declination,

chadh - chhad = ( 60° + k ) - ( 60° + ka ) = k - ka = = - ka - (- k)

That is, to know the magnitude of ch, in both cases, the declination of the terrestrial shadow should be subtracted from the declination of the moon. It should be remembered that northern declination is written as positive and southern declination as negative.

Therefore, jyauchas = jyalachcha = chalaka - kachchamanayakkhandbhuchayakikranti - chandramakikranti-manayakkhand

Source page 594

In the same way in the time of moksha;

Kojyaucham = Kojyauchach = Chala / Chach = Ka - K / Manayakhand

It is necessary to remember here that when the moon is north of the umbra, the angle Uchasya or Uchacham will be greater than 60°, so its cotangent will be negative. But when the moon is south of the umbra, the angle Uchasya or Uchacham will be less than 60°, and its cotangent will be positive. The moon is north of the umbra when the north declination of the moon is greater than the north declination of the umbra, or the south declination of the moon is less than the south declination of the umbra. In the opposite case, the moon is south of the umbra.

It is stated in pages 457-58 that an eclipse of the Sun or Moon is possible only when the Sun or Moon is near a node of the Sun, Moon, Rahu, or Ketu. Therefore, it is proven that the cycle of an eclipse depends on the motions of the nodes of the Sun and Moon. If the Moon's node were stationary, the Sun would reach near both nodes in a year twice in the same month, keeping the month and date of the eclipse constant. However, the Moon's node moves towards the west by 3^ h10'' 64 daily, while the Sun's mean daily motion is 56^ h8'' 33 towards the east. Therefore, the Sun moves 62^ h18'' 67 or 62^ h16'' away from the Sun-Moon node each day. When the Sun moves this far each day, it reaches the same node in 360^ ^ extdegree / 62^ h16'' = 1266000 / 3736 = 346.62 days. It takes half this time, 173.31 days, for it to reach the other node. If the cycles of Amavasya or Purnima also completed in such a short time, eclipses would be seen after every 346.62 or 173.31 days. However, the mean value of the lunar month is 26.53056 days, which is similar to 324.83647 days in 11 months and 354.36705 days in 12 months. Thus, it is proven that the cycle of an eclipse cannot occur in 346.62 days.

But there are 223 X 26053056 days or 6585032 days in 223 lunar months and 346062 days in 16 revolutions of 346062 days, so the cycle of eclipses, i.e., eclipse-cycle, is of 6585032 days. After these days, the same type of eclipses begin again. Therefore, this period can be called the eclipse-cycle. This cycle is not discussed in our ancient astrology. In Western astrology, it is called Saros and it was determined by the inhabitants of Khaldia about six hundred and five years before the beginning of the Vikram Samvat.

This eclipse cycle gave the people of Khaldia great facility in finding eclipses because without long calculations, they could easily know when eclipses will occur in the table of eclipses of 6585.32 days. But it should be remembered that this cycle (age) is calculated according to the mean motions of the Sun, Moon, and Rahu, so it has a little imprecision. Second,

Source page 597

This era is not for the entire 6585 days, but rather seven to eight hours more. Its result is that in the same place and at the same time, the same eclipse will be seen sometimes and sometimes not. For example, when the lunar eclipse was seen at sunset in Prayag, after 6585 days, seven or eight hours after sunset, it will again be seen at 2 o'clock at night. But the third time this eclipse will occur when the sunrise has already happened in Prayag. Therefore, it will not be seen in Prayag, but in the place west of Prayag where the night will remain at the time of the eclipse.

There are 365.25876 days in a solar year. Therefore, in 18 years, 6574.6577 days have passed, which is only 10.66 days less than the eclipse cycle. Therefore, it is apparent that if the beginning of the eclipse cycle happened on the day of Aries transit, then the beginning of the second cycle will be 10.66 days after the Aries transit, and the beginning of the third cycle will be on the 21.32 days from the Aries transit.

How many eclipses can occur on one node—there are 26.53 days in one lunar month, so 14.765 days have passed on one side. It is stated above that in 1 day, the Sun is 62°16' away from Rahu. Therefore, on one side, 14.765 x 102°16' = 15°20' 6' away. If the day of the full moon is on the node, then a total lunar eclipse will surely occur on this day. At this time, the Sun will be on the second node, so it will be 15°20' ahead and behind the two new moons on both the preceding and succeeding days, which is less than the maximum limit of a solar eclipse of 18°5. Therefore, a partial solar eclipse may occur on these two new moons (see pages 463-64). Thus, a maximum of three eclipses can occur in one lunar month while the Sun is 15°20' ahead and behind one node. However, these three eclipses are seen from the same place very little.

The solar eclipse on the day of Amavasya 13 days after the eclipse cannot be seen from the same place. My opinion on this is as follows:-

The wonder of the 13-day period is because at that time the values of the dates were known according to the mean calculation of Vedanga astrology, according to which there are 14 days 45 hours 26 minutes in one side. In this situation, the 13-day period is considered impossible, which is not surprising nowadays because according to the true calculation, the 13-day period has occurred many times and will continue to occur. In that ancient time, the 13-day period was known from the observation of eclipses. This is possible in this way:-

According to the true value, there are at least 13 days 50 hours in one side. Suppose that the full moon was one hour after the sunrise of the 11th date and the moon afflicted by this day set. In such a situation, it is evident that the beginning of the side will be considered on the 12th date. If the side is 13 days 57 hours, then the end of the new moon will be at 58 hours from the sunrise on the 24th date. If there is also an eclipse in the sun, the eclipsed sun will rise on the 25th date and the eclipse will be relieved shortly thereafter. From this, it is naturally apparent that the new moon ends on the night of the 24th date. In this way, the first day will be calculated on the 12th date and the new moon on the 24th date, and the side of 13 days will be seen. Such an event must have happened in the time of Mahā-Bhārata.

In this way, according to three eclipses on both nodes, there are 6 eclipses. However, the sun will reach the first node in 346 days, so a solar eclipse may occur after 346 days. In this way, if 3 eclipses occur in the first month starting from a solar eclipse at the beginning of the year and three more eclipses occur in the middle of the year, then one more solar eclipse may occur at the end of the year. In such a situation, seven eclipses can occur within the same solar year. However, in a year of 12 lunar months or in the solar year starting from the Aries solstice, if there are no intercalary months, there will be only 6 eclipses because when the beginning of the year is considered from the first day of the waxing moon in Chaitra, the first lunar eclipse will be on the 15th day of the waxing moon in Chaitra. The solar eclipse before this will fall on the new moon of Chaitra, which will be counted in the previous year. In this way, although seven eclipses can occur in a year of 365 days, in a solar year starting from the Aries solstice or a lunar year starting from the waxing moon in Chaitra, at most only 6 eclipses will be seen. Of these 6 eclipses, 4 will be of the sun and 2 of the moon. If a maximum of 7 eclipses are considered in a year, there will be 5 solar eclipses and 2 lunar eclipses.

It has already been proven that if there is a solar or lunar eclipse at a node or three parts ahead or behind it, then there cannot be lunar eclipses of the full months coming before or after it. Therefore, there will be only one solar eclipse at this node. There may be only one solar eclipse at the second node as well. Therefore, at least 2 eclipses of the sun must occur within the year and these will be solar eclipses.

When the difference between the daily motions is divided, the resulting distance is the time before or after which the conjunction has already occurred or will occur.

Scientific Commentary—The two rules explained from the latter part of the 3rd verse to the end of the 6th verse are very similar to the rules of "time and distance" in arithmetic. An example of this is—a passenger train started from Prayag towards Patna at 6 o'clock in the morning at a speed of 25 miles per hour, and the mail train started in the same direction at 8 o'clock at a speed of 40 miles per hour. Then tell us where and when both will meet?

The same method is used to calculate the conjunction of the planets. In such questions, it is first necessary to know at what time the mail train started, what the difference was between the passenger train and that time, then it is necessary to know how long it will take for the mail train to cover this difference by moving 15 miles more per hour. Here, 15 miles is the difference in the hourly speeds of both trains because both trains are moving in the same direction.

If the passenger train starts from Prayag towards Patna and the mail train starts from Patna towards Prayag at 6 o'clock, then by adding the speeds of both and dividing this sum by the distance between Prayag and Patna, the time at which both trains will meet will be known. Here, the speeds are added because both trains are moving towards each other, so their speed of meeting is equal to the sum of their speeds.

Similarly, the conjunction time and conjunction position of the planets are calculated. Suppose that in an auspicious time, the fraction of planet a in planet b is k = b and the fraction of planet x in planet y is k = a. Also suppose that in the same auspicious time, the daily motions of a and x are respectively g and ga.

Difference of both planets k x = bh - bh

Difference of the daily motions of both planets = g - ga

The proof of the second verse—if g is greater than a, then h will be positive, from which s will also be positive, in this case the conjunction will happen after so many days. But if g is less than a, then because h is negative, s will also be negative, which means that the conjunction of both planets has already happened so many days ago. Here, the motions of both planets are considered positive. For simplicity, it should be remembered here that the geocentric motion is considered positive and the retrograde motion is considered negative.

If both g and a are negative, that is, if both planets are retrograde, then the every (-g) -(-a) = a-g will be the exact opposite of the previous one, that is, if g is less than a, the time will be positive and there will be a conjunction, but if g is greater than a, the time will be negative and the conjunction has already happened. Thus, the proof of the second verse is proven.

Proof of the first half of the third verse—if k is geocentric and x is retrograde, then g will be positive and a will be negative, so the every of the equation will be the same as g-(-a), which will actually be g+a, i.e., positive, so the conjunction will happen after the same time.

But if x is geocentric and k is retrograde, then g will be negative and a will be positive, in this case the every of the equation g-a=a-g+(a)=a-g-a=(g+a) which is negative, so the conjunction has already happened at that time.

Here it is also proven that to know the time of conjunction, the difference of the portions of both planets should be divided by the difference of the motions of both planets if both planets are geocentric or both planets are retrograde; but if one of them is geocentric and the other is retrograde, then the division should be done by the sum of their motions.

Bhaskaracharya says that at the time when the position of the planet's ecliptic is in the horizon, the planet is above or below the horizon due to its shadow. When the planet is above the horizon, it rises before the position of its ecliptic, and when it is below, it rises behind. How much earlier or later it rises is known by the apparent motion. This apparent motion has two parts. One part depends on the motion of the nodes, and the other depends on the motion of the axis. The part that depends on the motion of the nodes is called the nodal apparent motion, and the part that depends on the motion of the axis is called the axial apparent motion.

Translation -(15) In the flat land on which the gnomon is planted and the shadow is measured, in the opposite direction to the direction where the planet is, the planet should be shown in the mirror placed in front of the shadow of the time of conjunction. In such a mirror, the planet is seen joined with the tip of the gnomon. (16) Plant two gnomons of five hands high in the directions where the planets of the time of conjunction are. Want. (17) Tie a rope that indicates the shadow hypotenuse from the foremost point of the planetary conjunction shadow to the peak of the gnomon. The viewer should place their eye on this same formula of the shadow hypotenuse. (18) By doing this, the planet will appear attached to the peak of the gnomon in the sky.

Sūrya Siddhānta—these three and a half shlokas are of great importance. From these it is proven that our Acharyas performed the subtle calculations of astrology because the direct position of the planets is the same as what is seen through the sight, because until the calculation of the planets is absolutely pure, we cannot see them in this way as stated in these shlokas. One more thing is also known from this that our Acharyas also knew the law of reflection of light.

To calculate the shadow of the planets, according to the method described in Chapter on the Three Problems, the sidereal time of the planets should be known according to the method stated in page 331 for their portions, declination, and variation. Upon knowing the sidereal time, the planetary positions should be known according to equations (b) and (c) on page 262. From the sidereal positions, the azimuth or altitude is necessary according to equation (b) on page 273. To know the shadow from the sidereal positions, the tangent of the sidereal position should be multiplied by the magnitude of the gnomon. If the magnitude of the gnomon is 12 angulas for the 15th verse, there is no objection, but for the 16th verse, the result of the gnomon should be 4 hands. By doing so, the observer can easily determine the positions of the planets while standing.

The essence of the 15th verse can be shown by the diagram as follows:-

When the eye of the observer is at any point on the line, they will see the planet G and the top K of the gnomon together in the mirror.

If the gnomon is four hands, then the line from the apex of the gnomon from k to d, which is the formula, will have the eye of a spectator at some place, then even the planet g will be seen joined with the apex of the gnomon from k. This is the essence of the first half of the 16th, 17th, and 18th shlokas.

It is necessary to understand here that nowadays this arc can only be precisely obtained when the planet's portion goes purely according to the sight. For this work, it is extremely necessary to make amendments in our Siddhanta texts according to new arcs.

Translation—(18) Latter part--If there is only a touch between the images of both planets in the conjunction, such conjunction is called Yuti. But if the image of one planet penetrates the image of the other, meaning it covers some, such conjunction is called Bheda. (16) If the images of both planets are some distance apart but their rays appear to meet, such conjunction is called Anshuvimard. If the difference between the images of both planets is less than one degree, such conjunction is called Apasvya Yuddha. In this war, if the image of one is small, it is expressed as Apasvya, otherwise Avyakta. (20) If the difference between both images is more than one degree, such conjunction is called Samagam. If both planets are Bali, meaning large, then it is Vyakta Samagam. Otherwise, it is Avyakta Samagam.

(23) Whether Venus is to the north or to the south, it is often victorious. Similarly, the conjunction of the five luminaries with the Moon should be achieved.

Scientific Commentary—from the table of the smallest and greatest apparent sizes of five star planets it is revealed that the smallest apparent size of Venus is greater than the smallest apparent sizes of Mars and Mercury, therefore at the time of their conjunction, Venus is more victorious due to its greater luminosity and bulk. At the time when the apparent size of Mars is supreme, it is 180 degrees ahead of the Sun. In such a situation, the conjunction of Venus with it cannot happen; the conjunction of Venus and Mars can only happen when Mars is also near the Sun. In such a situation, the apparent size of Mars will always be smaller than the apparent size of Venus. Therefore, Venus is always more luminous and victorious than Mars and Mercury. Yes, when Venus is in conjunction with Jupiter or Saturn, then Venus is smaller than them for some time before setting in the east and rising in the west. Therefore, it can be said that it is defeated by Saturn or Jupiter, but such a state occurs very rarely. That is why it is said in this verse that Venus is usually victorious.

Eighth Chapter

Chapter on Mean Motions

(Brief Description)

Verse 1—How are the fixed stars known from the enjoyment of the constellations. Verse 2-6- The value of the enjoyment and projections of the constellations. Verse 10, 11 and 12 first half—The enjoyment, fixed stars, and projections of the stars named Agastya, Mrigvyadha, Agni and Brahma-hridaya. Verse 12 second half—The method of testing the fixed stars and projections. Verse 13—When can Rohini-Shakta difference occur. Verse 14-15—The method of knowing the time and place of the conjunction of a star with a planet. Verse 16-16—Which star is the yogtara among the constellations. Verse 20-21—The fixed stars and projections of the stars prajāpati, Apamvatsa and Aap.

In this right it is stated that which constellations fall in the path of the sun, the moon, and the planets, where their positions are, and how the time of the conjunction of the planets with their main stars or yogtāras is known. Some such stars have also been discussed which are extremely talented and hold a special place in the literature of ancient times, but with which the planets do not conjoin. But why is the discussion of such stars or star clusters not mentioned here? I will also discuss such stars or star clusters in the appendix which are not given in this right but have come in ancient literature or have special importance such as Saptarshi, Kashyap Mandala, etc. Whatever has been known about these stars by new observations nowadays will also be given briefly there.

It is neither a share nor is its magnitude in parts or aspects. The self-enjoyment of the star means the distance of the star from the beginning point of its constellation. This distance is in a unit that cannot be called a part nor an aspect. Therefore, it is stated that if this self-enjoyment is multiplied by ten, its magnitude is known in aspects. It seems that a unit different from the prevalent units has been used for brevity. What results from multiplying by ten is the angular distance of the star from the beginning point of its constellation in aspects. By adding this distance to the enjoyments of the preceding constellations, the pole of the star is known in aspects from the beginning point of Ashvini, that is, from the beginning point of the zodiac. It is stated earlier that the difference between any planet and the ecliptic is called Bhogansh, and the difference between the ecliptic and the meridian of that planet is called Vikshep. However, here instead of Bhogansh, Dhruvansh or Dhruv is mentioned. This is made clear by figure 110. If the meridian and the polar meridian are drawn while going from the star, they meet at two different points on the ecliptic. The difference from the beginning of Ashvini to the point where the meridian meets the meridian is called the enjoyment or Kadambabhimukh Bhog of the star. As stated in the earlier chapters, and from this point, the difference of the star is called Vikshep or Shar. It would be more appropriate to call this Kadambabhimukh Vikshep, but in this chapter, Bhog and Vikshep are used in another sense. Bhog does not mean Kadambabhimukh Bhog, but rather Dhruvabhimukh Bhog, and the Vikshep discussed further does not mean Kadambabhimukh Vikshep, but rather Dhruvabhimukh Vikshep. This is further clarified by the description given below the figure. Confusion arises in expressing two different meanings with the same technical term, so it should be taken into good consideration.

In the Chapter on Planetary Motions, it is stated that two mental operations, āyana dṛkkarma and ākṣadṛkkarma, are required in the pleasures and displacements of the planets. The result obtained by performing the mental operation of āyana dṛkkarma in the pleasure of the planets is the polar-facing pleasure or pole of the planet. Therefore, when the polar-facing pleasure of the planets is written in this chapter, the need for āyanadṛkkarma with the constellations will not be necessary, only the need for ākṣadṛkkarma will be necessary, as stated in the 14th verse of this same chapter. Source page 633

Scientific Commentary—by multiplying the self-elongation of each star by 10 according to the first verse, the self-elongation art of the star will be obtained. By adding this to the courses of the past constellations, the pole of that star will be known. For example, the self-elongation of the Ashvini star is 48, multiplying it by 10 gives its self-elongation as 480 degrees. The Ashvini star is in the first constellation named Ashvini, so the past constellation is zero, hence the pole of the Ashvini star is 480 degrees or 8 arc minutes. Similarly, the self-elongation of the Rohini star is 570 degrees in arc minutes. The first three constellations of Rohini are Ashvini, Bharani, Krittika, so their elongation is 3 X 800 arc minutes because one constellation is equal to 800 arc minutes (see Chapter on True Positions verse 64). Therefore, the pole of the Rohini star = 570 + 3 + 800 arc minutes = 570 X 2400 arc minutes = 2670 arc minutes = 46 degrees 30 arc minutes.

Similarly, the declination of each star can be known. This is a characteristic of the elongations of the Uttaraashadha, Abhijita, Shravana, and Dhanishtha stars, so their declinations are stated as below:-

The star of Uttaraashadha is at half of the Purvashadha constellation, that is, at 400 arc minutes of the Purvashadha constellation. There are 16 constellations from the first Ashvini to the root of Purvashadha, whose elongations are equal to 16 X 800 arc minutes = 15200 arc minutes. Therefore, the declination of Uttaraashadha is 400 + 15200 arc minutes = 15600 arc minutes = 260 degrees.

The Abhijita star is stated at the end of Purvashadha, so its declination is 260 degrees + 400 arc minutes, that is, 266 degrees 40 arc minutes.

The pole of the Shravana star is at the end of the Uttaraashadha constellation. One constellation = 13 degrees 20 arc minutes. The end of the Purvashadha constellation is at 266 degrees 40 arc minutes, so the pole of the Shravana star at the end of Uttaraashadha is 280 degrees.

The Pole Star is at the end of the third quadrant of the Navagraha constellation. The three quadrants of the constellation are 600 degrees. Or they are equal to 10 degrees. Therefore, the pole of Dhinishtha is 280+10=260 degrees.

The deflection is given in degrees, so there is no need to write more on this.

It is necessary to state here that the poles of the stars given above are not the same in all Siddhanta texts. There can be many reasons for this—(1) the arcs

Source page 634

Difference (2) in determining the position of the initial point of Ashvini (3) in determining the stars and (4) the motion of the nodal point. The first reason is clear because there is a natural difference in the results of the observation due to the crudeness of the instruments. The second reason is also of special importance. It is understood from this that there was a difference of opinion among the old teachers in determining the initial point of Ashvini, as is the case today. However, this difference causes great difficulty in determining the conjunctions and occultations today, which prevents the stability of all-India dates and festivals. If unity is achieved in the astrology of all the provinces on this matter, a great work will be done, and those who dedicate their body, mind, and wealth to this industry will be the recipients of great merit. Work has been done in Maharashtra and Gujarat provinces on this matter for a long time, but no determination has been made yet.

In this way, due to the motion of the nodal point, a difference occurs in the poles and deviations of the stars, although they remain stable in their courses and arcs.

In the 10-12 shlokas, the pole and deviations of the stars are explained, and an effort will be made in several tables to show what the opinions of ancient and modern commentators are regarding the relationship of the stellar polaritudes.

The poles and deviations of the Brahma Gupta Siddhanta are similar to those of the Dhruva and Vikshep in the Siddhanta Shiromani of Bhaskaraacharya. The poles and deviations of Lalitantra, Damodariyabhata Tulya, and Sundari-Siddanta are taken from the Indian astrology of Swargiya Shankar Balakrishna Dikshit. Dikshit ji, assuming the pole of the star Chitra to be 180 degrees, and the poles and deviations of the stars given in the Nautical Almanac of 1887 AD, which he had fixed from the latitudes and declinations, will also be given in this table. Dikshit ji has given two poles and two deviations for the star Revati. The reason for this is that according to their opinions, the sum of Revati may be Yata Pisium or Mu Pisium. Therefore, the first pole or deviation is of Jata Pisium and the second is of Mu Pisium.

When does the separation of the planet Rohini-Shakta occur—

(13) The planet situated at the 17th degree of the Taurus zodiac whose southward deviation is more than 2 degrees penetrates the shadow of the Rohini constellation.

Source page 644

Scientific Commentary—There are 5 stars in the Rohini constellation whose shapes are like a cart or the letter V of the English alphabet. The southern deviation of the northernmost star among these five is approximately 2 degrees 35 arc. This star is called Apellan star nowadays. And the southern deviation of the star conjunct Rohini is 5 arc 32 arc. The planet whose southern deviation or deviation falls between these two limits falls within the shadow of Rohini. This is called the penetration of the shadow of Rohini. It is apparent that the deviation of the planet depends on its node. The Moon completes one revolution in 18 years. In this one revolution, the Moon only passes through 5,6 years of shadow. If the southern deviation of the Moon is more than 2 degrees 35 arc and less than 5 arc 32 arc and at that time it is in the Rohini constellation, then it will certainly be within the shadow of Rohini, therefore the Moon will have the Rohini-shadow-penetration. Now it is to see that at the time the Moon is in the Rohini constellation, its southern deviation is less than 2 degrees 35 arc.

In page 75 of the Chapter on Mean Motions it is stated that the ultimate displacement of the Moon is 5 degrees 8 nakshas 42 vikalas. This means that when the Moon is 60 degrees ahead of Rahu, its south is 5 degrees 8 nakshas and 42 vikalas, and when it is 60 degrees ahead of Ketu, its south is the same. But when it is on Rahu or Ketu, its south is zero. Therefore, based on the verses of the Chapter on True Positions 28 and figure 25, it can be easily known that the south of the Moon is more than 2 degrees 35 nakshas. In this figure, if we assume the Moon's orbit, the ecliptic, the position of Rahu, the position of the Moon, the Moon's south, and the Moon's ultimate displacement, then the relation between the Moon and the ecliptic can be easily known. Here, if we assume that the Moon and the ecliptic are 2 degrees 35 nakshas, then

sine (Vasa) = sine (Sapa) / sine (Savpa) = sine2035' / sine506' = .0451 / .0868 = .5022
,. Vasa = 30 degrees 6 arcminutes

That is, when the moon is one amount ahead of its node, then its shadow is more than 2 degrees 35 arcminutes. But Rohini is to the south of the ecliptic and its polar-facing portion according to Sūrya Siddhānta is 46 degrees 30 arcminutes and according to Shankar Balakrishna Dikshit is 47 degrees 37 arcminutes and the Kadamba-facing portion

Source page 645

From the calculation of Sūrya Siddhānta, there are 48 degrees 6 kala and Shankar Balakrishna Dikshit has 45 degrees 57 kala from the calculation. Therefore, if the portion of the star of Rohini facing Kadamba is assumed to be 46 degrees, then at the time when the portion of the moon is the same, the Rohini-Shakta-Bheda may occur if its south shadow is more than 2 degrees 35 kala. In such a situation, the moon should be at least 1 rashi ahead of Ketu, that is, the Rohini-Shakta-Bheda can only occur when the portion of Ketu is at least 16 degrees.

From the above calculation it is proved that when the Moon is 1 sign ahead of Ketu, its southern deviation is 2°35' art. After this, its southern deviation increases to 5°8' art. At that time it is 3 signs ahead of Ketu. Then its southern deviation begins to decrease and when it is 5 signs ahead of Ketu or 1 sign behind Rahu, its southern deviation is not less than 2°35' art. Within this limit, the Moon passes the shadow of Rohini. However, it is proved above that when Ketu's portion is 16 art, that is when Ketu is at the 16th degree of Aries, if the Moon's southern deviation is 2°35' art, then there will be a Rohini-shkat-bhed. After this, even when Ketu moves backward due to its retrograde motion, the Moon will still pass the shadow of Rohini because at that time its southern deviation in Rohini constellation will be more than 2°35' art. Thus, until Ketu moves 4 signs behind the 16th degree of Aries, the Moon's southern deviation in Rohini constellation will remain less than 2°35' art. This means that when Ketu comes to the 16th degree of Aries, the beginning of the Moon's Rohini-shkat bhed will occur, and until it does not come to the 16th degree of Sagittarius, the Moon's Rohini-shkat-bhed in Rohini constellation will be there. However, it remains 6 signs ahead of Rahu-Ketu. Therefore, it can also be said that until it remains in the range from the 16th degree of Gemini to the 16th degree of Libra, the Moon's Rohini-shkat-bhed occurs.

Similarly, the Rohini shadow-difference of other planets can also be calculated. However, it is revealed by the table given in Chapter on Mean Motions on page 75 that no planet, except for Venus and Mercury, has a true shadow-difference of more than 2 degrees 35 arcminutes, so only the Rohini shadow-difference of Mercury and Venus is possible. Saturn's true shadow-difference is 2 degrees 26 arcminutes 36 arcseconds, so Saturn's Rohini-shadow-difference is also considered impossible.

Which time should one see the sky picture? If one needs to use the sky picture from any other date of the month, then it should be kept in mind that the view seen at 10 o'clock on the 1st date of the month will be seen 4 minutes before 10 o'clock on the 2nd date, 4x2=8 minutes before 10 o'clock on the 3rd date, 4x7=28 minutes before the 8th date (i.e., one week later), and 15x4=60 minutes or 1 hour before on the 16th date, meaning it will be seen at 6 o'clock. The reason for this is that the Earth moves forward by 1 degree in the orbit of the Sun during the day and night, causing the Sun to appear one degree towards the east of the stars. Therefore, the Sun takes 4 minutes longer to come into the meridian circle each day, or the Sun's declination increases by approximately 4 minutes per day. However, the celestial time for which the sky picture is made is fixed, so the time at which the sky is seen on any day is seen 4 minutes before at the same time on the next day (see pages 463-466). The direct rule is that the view shown in the sky picture appears in the sky at the same time as the celestial time of the sky picture is earlier or later than the Sun's declination at noon. For example, on the 1st date of Vaishakh, the noon declination of the Sun is approximately 1 hour 26 minutes, and the celestial time of the sky picture of Jyeshtha is 10 hours 30 minutes, which is 12 hours 1 minute behind the noon declination. Therefore, the sky picture of Jyeshtha will be seen at 12:01 at night on the 1st date of Vaishakh. But the reason why 11:56 is mentioned in the 6th column is that 12 hours 1 minute is in the celestial time and 11 hours 56 minutes is in the Sun-dial time for Savan. Because it has been stated that the Savan day is approximately 4 minutes larger than the celestial day (see pages 337-36), the 6 hours of celestial time are the same as 5 hours 56 minutes of the Savan time.

According to this rule, if you wish to see all the stars in the sky on the first day of the month of Magha in the same night, you can see them easily. On this date, the stars set before five and a half o'clock of the sun in the directions of the lines connecting Bombay and Jagannath Puri, that is, in all of North India. Therefore, the stars in the sky become clearly visible at the time of 6 o'clock in the evening. On this date, the obliquity of the meridian sun is 16 hours and 42 minutes, so from noon

Source page 664

The sky picture of Makara (Margarita) can be seen at 6 o'clock in the evening. This means that you can easily recognize the 13 constellations from Shravana to Punarvasu or the 12 constellations from Dhanishtha to Punarvasu by listening. If you look at the sky at 12 o'clock at night, 6 hours behind, then the Nakshatra time will be approximately 7 hours 42 minutes, which can be useful for the sky picture of Phalgun month because the sky picture of Phalgun month is the one when the Nakshatra time is 7 hours 30 minutes. From this picture, you can easily recognize the stars from Ashvini to Hasta. Similarly, if you look at the sky at approximately 6 o'clock in the morning or 10, 12 minutes before on the same night, the sky picture of Jyeshtha can be useful because the Nakshatra time at 6 o'clock in the morning will be approximately 13 hours 40 minutes, and the sky picture 12, 13 minutes before will be from the time of the Nakshatra time of 13 hours 30 minutes. From this sky picture, you can see the stars from Punarvasu to Moola or Purvashadh. Similarly, it can also be calculated what sky pictures of which month can be useful on which other night.

Simple description of the diagram—the round line drawn in the diagram is the horizon of 25 degrees latitude, so it is usually found with the horizon of Prayag or Kashi. A sign of wealth is shown in the center in this manner. From this, the point in the sky is revealed which is just above the head at 25 degrees latitude. This is called khswastik or khmadhya. North, South, East, West and the directions between them are visible near the round line. The straight line seen from North to South is the meridian circle. The sun remains on this line at noon. The crooked line seen from East to West is the equator. On the days of spring equinox and autumn equinox, the sun appears on this and rises exactly in the east and sets exactly in the west. There is another line that cuts the equator, which is called the ecliptic. The sun is seen moving on this every day. In reality, this is the path of our Earth on which the sun travels and completes one revolution throughout the year. This path is of great importance. The moon and planets revolve around it in the sky.

Source page 665

See the following. The ecliptic is divided into 27 equal parts which are called constellations. The names of the constellations are also given in the sky picture of Margashirsha, but in other pictures, only the serial number of the constellations is given. For example, where '1' is written on the ecliptic, the 1st constellation Ashvini ends, where '5' is written, the 5th constellation Mrigashirsha ends, etc. Where a mark is made within a small circle on the ecliptic, according to Sūrya Siddhānta, the end of the constellation Revati and the beginning of the constellation Ashvini are understood. The lines of the ecliptic, the equator, and the meridian are not visible in the sky. Astrologers have imagined them for convenience.

Even when there is a dark night in the clear sky, countless stars are visible, but in these pictures only those are shown which can be seen even in a moonlight night. Some such stars have also been taken to show the shape, which do not appear because of the greater light of the moon three or four days before-after the full moon. The Akash-Ganga, in which numerous tiny stars appear joined to each other, is not shown in these pictures. In the dark night, this Akash-Ganga surrounds the sky from north to south, nourishing the Scorpio and Sagittarius constellations, and separating the famous Agrahayana and Lubdhaka maṃḍala, which bathe the Akash-Ganga, with the Capricorn, Mizar, Kashyap, Rajahamsa, and Shravana constellations from north to south.

When looking some time before the picture was made, they will not see the stars near the eastern horizon because they have not risen, and they will see the stars near the western horizon a little higher, and the stars near the meridian circle will seem to have moved a little towards the east. But if the sky is seen some time behind the above time, the stars near the eastern horizon will seem to have risen a little higher, and some new stars will also have risen near the horizon; some stars will remain set in the western horizon, and the stars near the meridian circle will have inclined towards the west.

There will be some other stars seen in the north where the latitude is 25. But in the places where it is south, some other stars will be seen in the south and there will be some difference in the height and lowness of the stars, but this cannot cause any difficulty.

The method of viewing the picture—the direction from which one is to look at the sky, bring that same direction down and stand the picture up. The star at the very bottom is the one that will be seen near the horizon. The stars from below to the center in the picture

The same stars will be seen from the horizon to the zenith in the same order.

The sky of the jyeṣṭha month—

East—near the horizon, there are three stars of the śravaṇa constellation shifted slightly towards the north, the star between which is very bright and of the first class. which has many small stars shining. The stars of the original constellations also appear close to each other near the horizon. The first-class star is some distance above between the cross and the southern horizon, which is of great importance due to its position. It is usually on the ecliptic. One and a quarter thousand years ago, the autumn equinox was near this star, meaning when the sun reached here, it went to the southern hemisphere. Nowadays, the autumn equinox has shifted by about 22 degrees 50 minutes from this star to the west, and it is at the place where the letter 'Sh' is written near the 12th constellation. A big debate is going on in the Maharashtra province regarding this star. Those who say that the beginning of Ashwini constellation or Aries sign should be considered from the point which is 180 degrees away from the citrā star are called the Chaitra pakṣa. The supporters of this side are Acharya Venkatesh Bapu Ji Ketkar and other gentlemen. There is another side against them, which Lokmanya Tilak also supported. Their opinion is that the beginning of Ashwini is the point which is about 184 degrees away from the citrā star. This point is in the Revati constellation (see the picture of the Bhadrapada month). That is why this side is called the Revati pakṣa.

Sky Picture of Margashir Month

In this month the sky remains very clear. The dust of the months of Vaishakh and Jyeshtha and the clouds of Shravan and Bhadrapada are not seen anywhere, nor does the fog of Magha and Phagun reach the vision. Therefore, there is both knowledge and mental delight from the sky-picture of this month. In the sky of this month, many new stars and star groups are seen in the east direction, which have also been discussed in many places in ancient literature.

It has been discussed in the Greek and Persian literature in very figurative language. In the middle of this constellation, three bright stars often appear close to each other in the same line, which are called Ilvak. Four stars show their extraordinary appearance on the four corners of Orion. The star at the bottom, the northern one, is somewhat red.

Chapter on the Right Ascension

(Brief Description)

[1 verse—The idea that planets and stars become invisible due to coming near the sun. 2-3 verses—The direction of the rising and setting of planets. 4-5 verses—The method of knowing the occultation of planets. 6-6 verses—The ultimate occultation of planets. 10-11 verses—The method of knowing how many days are remaining or have passed for a rising or setting at a certain time. 12-15 verses—Which star has what ultimate occultation. 16-17 verses—The method of knowing the day of visibility or disappearance of a star. 18 verses—The names of those stars that are never invisible]

In this chapter, it is explained when the rising and setting of planets and stars occur and how they are known. Here, the meaning of rising and setting is different from the ordinary meanings of rising and setting. Generally, when the sun, moon, etc., come above the eastern horizon, they are considered to have risen, and when they go below the western horizon, they are considered to have set. This is due to the daily motion of the Earth, which the old Acharyas called Pravah-gati. Besides this, when planets, the moon, or stars come very close to the sun, so that they come above the eastern horizon almost before sunrise and below the western horizon almost after sunset, they are also considered to have set. In such a situation, they cannot be seen due to the intense light of the sun. The time from which they become invisible because they come near the sun is considered as setting, and the time when they are so far from the sun that they begin to be seen a little before sunrise or a little after sunset is considered as rising. Similar discussions of rising and setting are mentioned in this right. Western astrologers call this heliacal rising and setting.

Purpose of the chapter—

अथोदयास्तमययोः परिज्ञानं प्रकीर्त्यते ।
दिवकरकराक्रान्त मूर्तीनामल्पतेजसाम् ॥१॥

Source page 678

Translation—(1) The method for knowing the rising and setting of bodies that have little light due to being affected by or obscured by the light of the sun is explained.

Scientific Commentary—Its explanation has been given above. Direction of rising and setting -

सूर्यादभ्यधिकाः पश्चादस्तं जीवकुजार्कजाः ।
ऊनाः प्रागुदयं यान्ति शुक्रज्ञौ वक्रिणौ तथा ॥२॥
ऊनाः विवस्वतः प्राच्यामस्तं चन्द्रज्ञमार्गवाः ।
व्रजन्त्यभ्यधिकाः पश्चादुदयं शीघ्रयायिनः ॥३॥

Translation—(2) When the portions of Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn are some more than the portion of the Sun, they set in the west, and when they are some less than their portion, they rise in the east. Similarly, the rising and setting of retrograde Venus and Mercury also occurs, that is, when the portions of retrograde Venus and Mercury are more than the portion of the Sun, they set in the west, and when they are less, they rise in the east. (3) The Moon, (emergent) the portions of Mercury and Venus are less than the portion of the Sun, then they set in the east, and when they move some ahead of the Sun due to rapid motion, they rise in the west.

Scientific Commentary—In these two verses, it is briefly stated how the positions of the portions of the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, etc., or true positions, can be ascertained in a thick manner as to which planet will rise or set in which direction. For this work, the planets have been divided into two parts. In one part are Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn whose motion is slower than the motion of the Sun, and in the other part are Mercury, Venus, and the Moon whose motion is faster than the motion of the Sun. There is some difference in the motions of Mercury and Venus in these as well.

Because the Sun moves more than the Guru, Mangal, and Shani, the Sun appears to be further and further than the Guru, Mangal, and Shani. When the Sun gets so close to them that they become invisible, the portion of the Sun is greater than their portion because the measurement of the portion is from west to east. Before becoming invisible, these three planets are seen near the western horizon behind the sunset and there, due to the intensity of twilight, they become invisible, so it is said that these three planets set in the west. In some days when the Sun is ahead of them

Source page 679

It increases and their portion becomes less than the portion of the sun, then they begin to appear a little before sunrise in the east. Therefore it is said that they rise in the east.

When the portions of retrograde Mercury and Venus are more than the portion of the sun, they appear in the western horizon after sunset and become invisible there. In a few days, due to their retrograde motion, they move very quickly to the other side of the sun and their portions become less than the portion of the sun. In such a situation, they begin to appear in the eastern horizon before sunrise. Therefore it is said that retrograde Mercury and Venus also set in the west and rise in the east.

But the motion of the Moon and the direct Mercury and Venus is more than the motion of the sun, so when they move towards the sun and reach close to it so much that they become invisible, their portions become less than the portion of the sun and they become invisible in the eastern horizon before sunrise. Therefore it is said that they set in the east. When they move ahead of the sun, their portions become more than the portion of the sun and begin to appear in the western horizon after sunset. Therefore it is said that the Moon and direct Mercury and Venus rise in the west.

Method of knowing the dark portion-

सूर्यास्तकालिकौ पश्चात्प्राच्यामुदयकालिकौ ।
दिवाकरग्रहौ कुर्यात् दृक्कर्माथ ग्रहस्य तु ॥४॥
तयोलंग्नान्तरप्राणाः कालांशाः षष्टिभाजिताः ।
प्रतीच्यां षड्भयुतयोस्तद्वल्लग्नान्तरासवः ॥५॥

(4) If one wants to know the time of rising or setting of a planet in the west, then clarify the Sun and the planet of the sunset time of the day estimated by estimation, and if one wants to know the time of rising or setting of a planet in the east, then clarify the Sun and the planet of the sunrise time of that day and perform the visual impression of the planet. Find the difference in the angles of the Sun and the planet of the rising signs of the Sanskrit planets and the Sun and divide it by 60, then the portion of time related to the rising or setting of the planet in the east is known. If one wants to know the portion of time related to the rising or setting of the planet in the west, then by adding 6 to the portions of the Sun and the planet in the shadow, find the portion of time by dividing the difference in the angles of the rising signs by 60.

Source page 680

Scientific Commentary—The time before the rising of the sun when any planet comes into the eastern horizon, that time is called the interval of that planet. The calculation of the ascendant time is done in asus for subtlety, and the rise of one aspect of the Vishnu-circle is one asu. Therefore, the rise of 60 kals is 60 asus, but 60 aspects are like a fraction. Therefore, the difference between the rising times of the sun and the planets, which usually occurs in asus and which is called lagnantara-prana or lagnantaras in the 5th verse, when divided by 60, should be understood in fractions, this is called the kālāṃśa of the planet.

It is stated in page 561 that to know at what time the planet is in the ascendant in the horizon, the axial and meridian coordinates should be calculated in the true portion because according to the true positions, only the portion of the planet that comes from the planet's orbit is known. However, the planet's orbit is different from the ecliptic, so at the time when the planet's ecliptic point comes to the horizon, the planet's image does not rise on the horizon but some ahead or behind according to its shadow (see figures 107, 108), the knowledge of which is obtained from the meridian coordinates. That is why in the fourth verse, it is said to perform the meridian coordinates first. When the exact position of the planet on the horizon is known after performing the meridian coordinates, then it can be known how much before sunrise the planet is in the ascendant in the eastern horizon.

But when the rising or setting of the planet is in the west, the time of the sun and the planet at sunset is clarified because then it is necessary to know how much time the planet sets behind the sunset. For this work, the *drikkarm sanskara* is also required in the planet, as is done at the time of the rising ascendant. Now, the difference between the *drikkarm sanskara* of the planet or in the words of Bhaskaracharya, *driggraha* and the *asatalagna* of the sun should be known, that is, to see how many degrees after the time the sun sets the image of the desired planet appears on the western horizon. Dividing these degrees by 60 gives the knowledge of the time or fraction of the setting time. But it is stated in the latter part of the 5th verse that the difference between the ascendants of the setting sun and the *driggraha* is obtained by adding 6 signs or 180 degrees to both and taking the difference of their ascendants. The reason for this is that at the time when the sun is setting, the point of the meridian of the ecliptic in the eastern horizon is

Source page 681

It is that which remains 180 degrees ahead of the sun. Similarly, when the planet is setting, that point remains in the eastern horizon which is 180 degrees ahead of the planet. Therefore, if it is known what the difference is in the ascensions of the positions of the eastern horizon in the settings of the sun and the planet, then the knowledge of the azaansh or kalansh can be obtained.

The ultimate azaansh of the planets—

एकादशामरेड्यस्य तिथिसङ्ख्याऽर्कजस्य तु ।
कालांशा भूमिपुत्रस्य दश सप्ताधिकास्तथा ॥६॥
पश्चादस्तमयोऽष्टाभिः उदयः प्राङ्महत्तया ।
प्रागस्तमुदयः पश्चादल्पत्वाद्दशभिः भृगोः ॥७॥
एवं बुधो द्वादशभिः चतुर्दशभिरंशकैः ।
वक्री शीघ्रगतिश्चार्कात्करोत्यस्तमयोदयौ ॥८॥
एभ्योऽधिकैः कालभागैर्दृश्या न्यूनैरदर्शनाः ।
भवन्ति लोके खचरा भानुभाग्रस्तमूर्तयः ॥६॥

Translation—(6) The ultimate azaansh of Jupiter is 11; that of Saturn is 15 and that of Mars is 17. (7) Because the image of Venus appears to be larger, the ultimate azaansh of it setting in the west and rising in the east is 8, but because the image is smaller, the azaansh of it setting in the east and rising in the west is 10. (8) Similarly, when Mercury, which has retrograde and quick motion, is at 12 azaansh from the sun, it sets in the west and rises in the east. But the azaansh of it setting in the east and rising in the west is 14. (9) Because it is affected by the light of the sun or is suppressed, if the azaansh of any planet at a certain time is more than its ultimate azaansh, then that planet is seen, and if it is less, it is not seen.

Scientific Commentary - In these verses, the limit of the azaans of the planets is indicated beyond which the planets are seen and below which they are not seen. Therefore, this limit can be called the ultimate azaansh. The ultimate azaansh of each planet is different. The reason for this is that the planet whose image is larger can be seen easily even when it is near the sun, and the planet whose image is smaller can be seen with some difficulty. Among the distant planets, Jupiter's image is the largest, so its ultimate azaansh is 11

Source page 682

It is considered that if Jupiter rises or sets 11 degrees or 110 pal 44 minutes before sunrise or 110 pal 44 minutes after sunset, then it can be seen even in the twilight of the morning or evening. Therefore, when the dark portion of Jupiter decreases until it becomes 11, then it becomes invisible in the western horizon. After this, when its dark portion decreases until it becomes zero, the knower knows that it rises or sets with the sun. From this time, its dark portion begins to increase, and until it becomes 11 degrees, it remains invisible because it cannot be seen in the intense light of the sun. This is also called Guru-Aditya or 'Guru-Badik' in common speech. This period is usually 1 month. During this period, Hindus do not perform any auspicious work like marriage, tonsure, etc.

The image of Saturn is smaller than the image of the Sun and larger than the image of the Sun, therefore the ultimate position of Saturn is considered to be 15 and that of the Sun is 17. However, the rising and setting of these are not considered in auspicious matters.

The supreme aspects of Venus are considered to be 8 and 10. The reason for this is that when Venus is retrograde and sets in the west and rises in the east, its distance from the Earth remains very small because it is between the Sun and the Earth (see Chapter on True Positions pages 101-103). Because of the closeness, its image appears very large, so it can be seen for a long time in the twilight. Its limit is considered to be 8 aspects 32 minutes or 80 shadows, meaning that if Venus sets in less than 32 minutes after sunset, it is not seen, and it is said that Venus has set in the west. After this, when Venus begins to rise 32 minutes before sunrise, it starts to be seen again, and it is said that Venus has risen in the east. This period is not more than a week because when Venus is retrograde, the distance between Venus and the Sun decreases or increases by the sum of their motions daily, so Venus quickly goes behind the Sun.

But when Venus sets in the east and rises in the west, its absolute position is 10 because at this time it remains on the other side of the Sun, very far from the Earth (see, figure 21, 22). Because it is far, the image of Venus appears smaller, so it does not remain visible for as long during twilight as it does when retrograde.

Source page 683

When it happens, it is seen. When it sets in the east, it remains in the same direction, that is, its motion is in the direction in which the sun appears to move. Therefore, the difference between these two is the same as the difference in their motions per day. Therefore, this period of the setting of Venus is about two months.

Until Venus is set, no auspicious work like marriage, tonsure, etc., is done among Hindus.

Like Venus, when Mercury is retrograde, it appears larger due to being near the Earth and its ultimate degree is 12. But when it is in the other side of the sun, very far from the Earth, it appears smaller and its ultimate degree is 14.

The thought of Mercury setting is not done in marriage, tonsure, etc.

Up to here it has been stated how the rising and setting of the planets are calculated according to the Sūrya Siddhānta and what their ultimate positions are. Now here two questions arise, one is whether this method of knowing the positions is pure, and the other is whether these ultimate positions are correct. Answering this is easy because it can be checked by the direct observation of these planets. Because the definition of their rising and setting is such that they should be considered set until they cannot be seen without any instrument because they are near the sun, otherwise they should be considered risen. Applying this test proves that in the rising or setting times derived from the Sūrya Siddhānta or any other Indian astrological principle, there is sometimes a difference of ten or fifteen days. It is apparent that the exact calculation of the positions is only possible when the true portions and shadows of the planets are exact. However, the portions and shadows taken based on Indian principles are not correct as stated in many places in the previous chapters. For example (Pūrṇimānta) Chaitra Krishna 11 Bhauamvara Samvat 1683 according to the days, the midnight of 26 March 1627.

Childhood and Old Age

It is clear that the atmosphere is not always clear. In the days of summer, there is so much dust that the sun cannot be seen even a little distance above the horizon, therefore it is very difficult to see Venus or Jupiter in such a condition. The second thing is that due to the decline and intensity of the observer's vision, there can be a difference of two or three days in the visibility of the planets. Due to all these reasons, the days of the rising or setting of the planets may be two or three or four days before or after they become invisible. It seems for this reason that the old sages considered the childhood and old age of Jupiter and Venus, but there is no consensus in this either, as written in Muhurta Chintamani:-

पुरःपश्चाद्धगोर्बाल्यं त्रिदशाहं च वार्धकम्
पक्षं पंच दिनं ते द्वेगुरोः पक्षमुदाहृते ॥२७॥
ते दशाहं द्वयोःप्रोक्तं कैश्चित्सप्तदिनं परैः ।
त्यहं त्वात्ययिकेऽप्यन्यैरर्धाहं च त्यहं विधोः ॥२८॥१

Even in the childhood and old age of Jupiter and Venus, many auspicious acts are prohibited just as in their setting.2

Should the consideration of rising or setting be from kalaansh or unnataansh?

Another point is worth considering in this regard. From what has been said so far about the rising and setting of planets, it has become clear that they are said to have set only when they come so close to the sun that they cannot be seen due to the twilight of morning or evening. However, the intensity and limit of twilight are not the same in all seasons and places. Anyone can experience that the limit of twilight increases in the winter days and decreases in the summer days. The reason for this is that twilight is related to the portion of the sun below the horizon, which depends on the sun's declination and the latitude of the ecliptic (see page 261 sutra 1). It has been proven by experience that as long as the sun is not more than 180 degrees below the horizon, some part of its light still returns to the Earth through the atmosphere. From the time of the sun's setting until the time when it does not go more than 18 degrees below the horizon, when dim light is seen, that is called twilight.

Source page 693

Similarly, from the time when the rising of the sun is eighteen degrees below the horizon, the commencement of the morning twilight begins. It is apparent that when the sun remains eighteen degrees below the horizon, it is 60+18=108 degrees below the cross. Therefore, it can be said that the twilight begins when the eastern part of the sun is 108 degrees, and the morning twilight remains until the time when its western part is 60 degrees. Similarly, as long as the western part of the sun remains between 60 and 108 degrees, the evening twilight remains.

In Sutra (1) of page 261, it is stated what is the relationship between nataansh and natkal and how it depends on latitude and declination. In this sutra, if the values of 108 for nataansh, and the latitude and the solar declination of the iststhan are raised, then if the solar rising or setting natkal is subtracted from the natkal that will arise, the magnitude of the saṃdhiprakāśa ( saṃdhiprakāśa) of that day will be known. To know the natkal of rising or setting, the magnitude of nataansh of 60 degrees 35 art must be taken because the direct nataansh of the sun or any planet rising or setting is 60, but due to the rotation of the atmosphere, the actual nataansh increases by 35 art (see pages 378-380). Therefore, the nataansh of the solar rising or setting in reality is 60035’.

Thus it is proven that the meridian light is not the same in all seasons and all places, therefore for knowing the appearance and disappearance of planets, the ultimate portion of the same planet for all places and all seasons will have to be considered different, where the meridian light will remain for a long time, the same ultimate portion will not work, which can work for a short meridian light. Considering all these things, it seems reasonable that the consideration of the disappearance and appearance of planets should be done from their altitude rather than the declination, as written by Acharya Ketkar ji on page 333:-

All planets appear in the vicinity of the Sun by some measure. The opinion of the preceding four treatises does not agree that this wonder is due to the conjunction of the Sun and the planets. Because the twilight glow of the evening reflects the portion of the Sun's setting, and also the time intervals. In the country of 350 degrees of latitude, the light of the conjunction of the Sun and the twilight occurs 3 hours 40 minutes before the sunrise. On the day of the supreme inclination, it is 4 hours.

(10) The difference between the instantaneous time and the ultimate time of the planet, written in the arts, and dividing it by the difference in the daily timings of the sun and the planet (if the planet is direct) and by the sum (if the planet is retrograde), is the number of days. (11) Multiplying the ascendants of the sign in which the sun or planet is, by the true daily motion, and dividing the product by 1800, what is obtained is the planet's time motion. The days of rising or setting are known from the difference or sum of the time motions of the sun and the planet.

Scientific Commentary—if one wants to know on any day that the rise of a planet

Source page 697

If there are how many days until setting or how many days have passed after rising or setting, then the zodiacal portion of the planet of that day should be known according to 4-5 shlokas so that it is known that the planet rises how many before sunrise or sets how many after sunset.

If the kālāṃśa is more than the paramakālāṃśa and the portion of the sun is more than the portion of the planet—and this planet is Mercury or Venus in the direct motion—then it should be understood that there are still some days remaining until its setting. But if this planet is Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn, or retrograde Mercury or Venus, then it should be understood that some days have passed since its rising. But if the kālāṃśa is more and the portion of the sun is less than the portion of the planet, and the planet is Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn, or retrograde Mercury or Venus, then it should be understood that there are still some days remaining until their setting. Conversely, if the kālāṃśa is less than the paramakālāṃśa and the portion of the sun is more than the portion of the planet—then it should be understood that some days have passed since the setting of the direct Mercury or Venus, and some days remain until the rising of Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and retrograde Mercury or Venus. But if the portion of the sun is also less than the portion of the planet, then it should be understood that some days remain until the rising of the direct Mercury and Venus, and some days have passed since the setting of Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and retrograde Mercury or Venus. In all these cases, to know the number of these days, the difference between the kālāṃśa and the paramakālāṃśa should be calculated and observed how many days this difference will reduce to zero or how much it has increased. To do this, this difference should be divided by the difference in the daily motions of the sun and the auspicious planet if the planet is in direct motion, but if it is retrograde, their daily motions should be added as stated in the grahayutyadhikāra. However, the daily motion of the sun or planet is generally circumpolar, and the kālāṃśa is viṣuvad-circular, which is why in the 11th verse it is stated that to convert the circumpolar daily motions to the viṣuvad-circular, one should multiply the daily motions of the sun or planet in the zodiac sign in which it is, and divide by 1800 because the time of rising of the sign is the same as the time of rising of the zodiac signs; therefore, the time of rising of the planet should also be understood in the same proportion as its daily motion. Since the daily motion is small, it is generally written in degrees, which is why a sign is also written in 1800 degrees. This results in the daily motion of the planet becoming viṣuvad-circular, which is why

The time of the house rightarrow time in the house = time of the sun × time of the house (1)/(1800) years of the number of days of the house × time of the house = time of the sun + time of the house (7) (R) (3)

If the planet is retrograde, the sign of the positive should be kept in the final equation, otherwise the difference of both should be calculated. Here the sign of difference is more appropriate than the sign of negative because the time of motion of a planet is more or less than the time of motion of the sun.

The rule given for knowing the time period of a planet is somewhat crude. The reason for this is that the motion of the planet does not occur on the ecliptic but on its orbital circle, which is somewhat different from the ecliptic, but this causes no particular loss. If the obliquity and declination of the planet are known, then the difference in the obliquity per day is the time period. Knowing the obliquity, the zodiacal position of the planet can also be known conveniently and accurately because then the need for the quadrant is not necessary. Therefore, in my opinion, more knowledge of the obliquity is required for calculating the rising, setting, and conjunction of planets or stars than the zodiacal positions, which can only be obtained with the help of modern astronomical principles and instruments. For this, a observatory is necessary, where our astrologers can observe the planets and stars and determine their positions and nodal points exactly.

Nowadays, the division of stars according to brightness is done in a very subtle manner. In a dark night, without the aid of any instrument, a sharp-eyed man can see no more than 6000 stars in the entire sky. These 6000 stars are divided into 6 categories (magnitudes). The division of these categories is done in such a way that a star of the first category is 100 times brighter than a star of a particular star in the sixth category. It follows from this that a star of any category is 2.5116 times brighter than the star of the category below it, that is, a star of the first category is 2.5116 times brighter than a star of the second category, the star of the second category is 2.5116 times brighter than the star of the third category, but the star of the first category is...

Tenth Chapter Chapter on Mean Motions

(Brief Description)

[Verse 1—The method of knowing the rising and setting of the Moon is the same as before and the phase is 12. Verse 2-4—The method of knowing the daily setting of the Moon in the waxing phase. Verse 5—The method of knowing the daily rising of the Moon in the waning phase. Verse 6-8—The method of knowing the linear difference between the Sun and the Moon at sunset. Verse 9—The method of knowing the image of the waxing part of the Moon. Verse 10-14—The method of drawing the outline of the waxing part of the Moon. Verse 15—The rule for drawing the outline of the lunar image in the waning phase.]

The method of knowing the rising and setting time of the Moon is explained in this chapter. In the preceding chapters, only the type of rising and setting is described in which the planet becomes invisible due to coming very close to the Sun. However, in this chapter, in addition to this type of rising and setting, there is also a method of knowing the daily rising and setting time of the Moon. Then the method of knowing is explained that what part of the lunar image is illuminated on which day and how its shape can be drawn. At the beginning of the waxing phase or at the end of the waning phase, the shape of the illuminated or waxing part of the Moon is like a snake and it remains raised towards the north or south, that is why the name of this chapter is Śr̥ṅgonnatyadhikāra

It is necessary to remind that the true position of the Moon is very different from the position known by the method of calculation of the Sūrya Siddhānta, as well as is well shown in pages 186-196 of the Spashtādhikāra. Besides this, the true declination of the Moon is also not correct according to the method of the Sūrya Siddhānta. For all these reasons, the calculations for this chapter should be taken from the principles of trigonometry, otherwise the time of the Moon's rising obtained by the principles of the Sūrya Siddhānta will be fifteen, sixteen minutes ahead or behind the actual time. Therefore, it is necessary to have a good observatory for revising Indian astrology in which the Moon, planets

Source page 707

and the roots of the constellations should be re-fixed by taking the most minute arc of them. In such work, the navigator should not depend on the almanac in any way. The time of the rising and setting of the Moon—

Rising time of the Moon and its phase—

Method of rising: it is the duty of the fore-knowledge, even in winter.

The five visible directions are seen from the two directions. 1.1.

Translation—(1) The time of the rising and setting of the Moon should be known according to the method explained in verses 4, 5 of the Upadasha regarding the rising and setting of the Moon. When its phase is 12 degrees behind the Sun, it is visible in the west, and when it is earlier, it becomes invisible in the east.

Scientific Commentary—no special writing is required on this because just as the rising time of other planets is known, so is that of the Moon. The rising and setting of the Moon occurs only once in the lunar month. The motion of the Moon is very fast, so the setting of the Moon occurs in the west on the full moon of the Chaturdashi of the Krishna Paksha, and the rising occurs in the evening time after the Pratipada of the Shukla Paksha.

From which it is proven that Chandrashekhar Singh Samant considered one and a half verses of the inserted verses of the Surya-Siddhanta to be very necessary. In reality, this is also necessary as will be shown now. Therefore, in my understanding, this

Source page 709

It is not appropriate to simply state that it is displaced and not to give its meaning because even if it is displaced, it is not improper, because according to this, not calculating may result in a difference of 1 hour or 24 minutes in the time of the moon's setting. Acharya Ranganathji had made his commentary in 1525 Shakas 1, so this dispute is several hundred years old whether it is displaced or not. I want to tell what the meaning of these shlokas is. The first half of shloka 2 alludes to the rule mentioned in the fourth and fifth shlokas of udayāstādhikāra, which is correct. The latter part states that if the sun and the moon are in the same zodiac sign, then the difference between their apparent-circumscribed-enjoyments should be taken as the angular portion to know how much time after sunset the moon will set. The reason for this seems to be that when the moon remains so little distance from the sun that they are in the same zodiac sign, the difference in their conjunctions is not very different from the difference in their enjoyments, so this gross rule is stated for ease.

After this, in verse 3, the method of knowing the setting time of the moon with subtlety from approximation is explained. The reason for this is that according to the first half of the preceding verses, the time of the moon's setting is not exact because the moon's motion is very fast. Therefore, the portion of the moon's setting in the setting of the sun increases by some amount, causing it to set a little later. The farther the moon is from the sun, the longer the delay in the moon setting. On the days of the thirteenth or fourteenth of the waxing moon, this delay becomes approximately 20 minutes because on these days, the moon sets more than 10 or 11 hours after sunset, and in such time, its motion is approximately 5 or 6 degrees, which can cause a delay of 20 to 24 minutes in its setting. To know this, it is said that by adding 6 signs to the Sun and the Moon, the resulting Lagnaantarasu can be made smaller by dividing the Asuas by 6 and the minutes by 60 to make a clock, and multiplying this by the daily motions of the Sun and the Moon and then dividing the product by 60, it will be known how much motion occurred in the Lagnaantarasus of the Sun and the Moon. Because when the Sun and the Moon in 60 minutes

Source page 710

If the motion is the same as the daily motion, then in the lunar intervals it will be in the same ratio. Upon knowing this motion, by adding it to the portions of the setting sun and the moon in the sunset time and adding 6 to the sum, the intervals of their signs are then found. In this way, when the difference becomes constant after performing the unobserved action 2 or 3 times, the moon sets at the same time after sunset.

One thing to consider here. When the portions of the setting sun and the moon are clarified once, and it is known for the first time that the moon will set after such a time from sunset, then the difference in the direct setting time of the moon will only be due to the motion of the moon, so for the unobserved action, only the motion of the moon should be added to the portion of the setting moon, not the motion of the sun as well. However, the rule asks to add the motions of both the sun and the moon. Adding the motion of the sun also results in a time that will not be the sidereal time but the Sawan time. But the first difference comes in the sidereal time, so the sum of sidereal time and Sawan time cannot be. Therefore, it is appropriate to perform the unobserved action only for the motion of the moon, but the difference from taking the motion of the sun can be at most 2 minutes because the 12 hours of sidereal time is only 2 minutes more than the 12 hours of Sawan time. Therefore, it does not seem wise to understand the rule as a mistake for such a error.

Method of knowing the linear difference between the Sun and the Moon at sunset

अर्केन्द्वोः क्रान्तिविश्लेषः दिक्साम्ये युतिरन्यथा ।
तज्ज्येन्दुरर्काद्यत्नासौ विज्ञेया दक्षिणोत्तरा ॥६॥
