कोटिश्शङ्कुस्तयोर्वंगयुतेमूल श्रवो भवेत् ॥८॥

Translation—(6) If the directions of the Sun and the Moon are the same, then find the difference of their sines, and if they are different, then find the sum. The direction in which the Sun is, that direction should also understand this difference or sum; that is, if the Moon is south of the Sun, then understand the direction of the difference or sum as south, and if it is north, then understand it as north. (7) Multiply this sum or difference by the instantaneous shadow hypotenuse of the Moon. If the direction is north, then subtract this product from the product of 12 and the sine of latitude, and if it is south, then add it. (8) Divide this remainder or sum by the sine of colatitude and consider the result as the length of the desired direction. The result obtained by taking the square root of the sum of the squares of the length and the latitude is the hypotenuse. This hypotenuse is the formulaic or linear difference between the Sun and the Moon.

The method to know the bright half of the lunar image—

सूर्योणशीतगोलिप्ताः शुक्लं नवशतोद्धृताः ।

Translation - The part of the moon obtained by subtracting the part of the sun from the part of the moon, which is obtained by making the art of the art by dividing by 600, is the bright half of the moon in fingers. Multiplying this by the instantaneous finger image of the moon and dividing by 12, the value of the bright part comes in fingers.

Scientific Commentary - The mean image of the full moon is considered to be 12 fingers. At the time the moon is full, it appears the whole bright part, and at the time of new moon, there is a lack of the bright part of the moon. As the moon moves further from the sun, its bright part also increases, and finally in the full moon period, its whole image appears bright. In such a situation, the difference between the moon and the sun is 180 degrees or 180 X 60 = 10800 art, so the magnitude of the bright part of the moon is such that when the moon moves 10800 art ahead of the sun, its bright part is equal to 12 fingers, so when the moon is 'a' art ahead of the sun in a certain period, its bright part = a X 12 / 10800 = a / 600 fingers

But this is based on the mean image. The true image is different from this, which should be calculated according to the lunar eclipse chapter (pages 481-82). When the value of the true image comes in fingers, then the ratio should be calculated that when the mean image is 12 fingers, then the desired bright part is a a 600 fingers, so when the true image is c then

Bright part = true image × 600 div 12 = true image × 600 × 112

Source page 717

This rule is gross because the increase in the waxing phase of the lunar phase does not increase in the ratio of the increase, as will be revealed. The cusps or horns of the waxing phase of the moon are called shringas. The line joining both shringas is the diameter of that circle of the lunar phase which separates its illuminated part from the unilluminated part. Therefore, it is at a right angle to the line joining the centers of the moon and the sun. It is also the diameter of the circle which separates the front part of the moon as seen by the observer from the rear part. Therefore, it is also at a right angle to the line joining the observer and the centers of the moon. When the line joining both shringas is at a right angle to the lines joining the observer and the centers of the moon and the sun, then it will also be at a right angle to the plane that passes through the observer, the center of the moon, and the center of the sun, that is, it cuts the diameter joining the shringas in half, which is the great circle joining the centers of the sun and the moon. The angle that this great circle makes with the horizon plane is very variable, so the moon's shringa varies in different ways in different months, that is, sometimes it is parallel to the horizon plane and sometimes in the direction of the perpendicular.

The bright half of the Moon's visible hemisphere is between two circles, one of which is the lunar image in front of the observer and the other is the lunar image in front of the Sun. The circle of the lunar image in front of the observer is towards the edge towards the Sun, but the circle of the lunar image in front of the Sun is inwards, and the observer sees it in an oblique direction, so it appears in the shape of an ellipse because the projection of a circle in an oblique line is an ellipse. Any person can easily check this with a circular rod and a lamp. The rod should be held between the wall and the lamp in such a way that the plane of the rod is parallel to the wall and the center of the lamp, the center of the rod, and the center of the shadow of the rod on the wall are at a right angle to the plane of the wall in the same line. In such a situation, the shadow of the rod will be round. If the rod is held in this place and tilted so that its plane is not parallel to the wall, or if the plane of the rod is kept parallel to the wall and the rod is moved down or up so that the line joining the centers of the three does not lie in the vertical direction of the wall, then the shadow of the rod on the wall

Chapter Eleven Right (Brief Description)

[Shlokas 1-2—Definition of validity and deviation of nodes. Shlokas 3-5— Nature and effect of both nodes. Shloka 6—When the revolutions of the Sun and Moon are determined. Shlokas 7-8—Knowing whether the nodal period has passed or is about to happen. Shlokas 6-11—When the revolutions of the Sun and Moon are equal. Shlokas 12-13—Knowing the true nodal period from the true revolution. Shlokas 14-15—When the beginning, mean, and end of the nodal period occur. Shlokas 16-18—What should be done in the nodal period. Shloka 16—When do the nodes occur twice, and when do they not occur. Shloka 20—Knowing the deviation of the Panchang. Shloka 21—Definition of Sandhi and Gandant periods. Shloka 22—Why the node and Gandant period are prohibited. Shloka 23—Conclusion.]

This right includes not only mathematical astrology but also predictive astrology. This is its special feature. The second feature is that the three chapters that follow are not named 'rights' but 'chapters'. The nodes discussed in this right are also called Mahapata.

Definition of validity and deviation—

Ekayanagatau syatām sūryācandramaso yadā. Tadyutau maṇḍashe krāntyoh tulyatve vaidhritābhidhḥ॥ Viparītāyagatau candrākau krāntiliptikāḥ. Samastadā vyatīpāto bhagṇādhiṁ teyoruyutauḥ॥

Translation—(1) When the Sun and Moon are in the same inclination and when the sum of their portions is equal to 12 signs, then the revolutions of both are equal, this node is called validity. (2) When the Sun and Moon are in different inclinations and when the sum of their portions is equal to 6 signs, then the revolutions of them are equal, this node is called deviation.

Source page 727

Scientific Commentary—When the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon are the same, then the nodes and apogees exist, that is, when the distances of the Sun and the Moon from the equator are the same, then the nodes and apogees occur. But even when the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon are the same, both can be North or both South; or one North and the other South. Now we have to see when this condition occurs. When the Sun is on the equator, its revolution is zero. This phenomenon occurs twice a year—on the vernal equinox and the autumnal equinox. From Aries to Cancer, the revolution of the Sun increases from zero to about 23 degrees 27 signs. It begins to decrease from Cancer and decreases to Libra, becoming zero again. From Libra, the revolution is South, and it increases to Capricorn, becoming 23 degrees 27 signs. From Capricorn to Aries, it decreases and becomes zero. When the Sun moves ahead from Capricorn, it appears to move towards the North on the horizon at the time of rising or setting, and this motion is seen up to Cancer. That is why the time from the Aries equinox to the Cancer equinox is called Uttarayana. But after the Cancer equinox, the Sun appears to move towards the South on the horizon, that is why the time from the Cancer equinox to the Capricorn equinox is called Dakshinayana. The Moon also, like the Sun, remains in Uttarayana for half a month and Dakshinayana for half a month in its revolution of almost one month, but because its orbit is somewhat different from the ecliptic and due to the self-retrograde motion of its orbit and the ecliptic at the points of intersection with Rahu and Ketu, it is somewhat difficult to fix the time of its Uttarayana and Dakshinayana. But in broad terms, there is no harm in saying that when the Moon comes near the Capricorn sign, then it is Uttarayana, and when it comes near the Cancer sign, then it is Dakshinayana because the angle between the lunar orbit and the ecliptic, that is the Moon's true position, is only about 506. This is made clear by the given figure 120.

Suppose the given ellipse is the ecliptic and its V and Sh points are in sequence of vernal and autumnal equinoxes where the equinoctial circle meets the ecliptic. For simplicity, the equinoctial circle is not shown. If it is assumed that the orbit of the Moon is the ecliptic, then it is clear that when the Sun and the Moon are at the same distance from the V and Sh points, then their inclinations will be the same. Now to see that

Source page 728

How many times can this event of one revolution of the moon occur? Suppose the position of the sun is somewhere between the vernal equinox and the autumnal point. When the moon is also at the same place, i.e., on the day of Amavasya, then both of their revolutions will be the same. When the moon is at C, Cha, and Chi, the revolutions will also be the same if Var = Ch = Shcha = Chiv. But when the moon is at the point Cha, it will be the full moon. According to Sūrya Siddhānta, for instantaneous revolution equality, the days of Amavasya and Purnima are not considered, so when the moon is at Ch and Chi, the sum of revolution equality will occur.

The first verse states that when the sum of the portions of the Sun and the Moon is 360 degrees, a node called Vaidhriti occurs. This condition can only happen when the Sun is at R, C, CA, or CI, and the Moon is in sequence at CI, CA, or R, because only then the sum of the portions of the Sun and the Moon can be 360 degrees during the vernal equinox. It is clear from the diagram that the position R and CI is between the Uttarayana point U, the vernal equinox V, and the Southayana point D, so both R and CI are in the Uttarayana. Similarly, C and CA are both in the Southayana. Therefore, it is stated in the first verse that a Vaidhriti node occurs when the Sun and Moon are in the same Ayan and the sum of their (sine) portions is 360 degrees. Conversely, when both are in different Ayans and the sum of the portions is 180 degrees, a Vyatipata occurs. In the diagram, if the Sun and Moon are at R, C, the sum of their portions will be 1800, and if they are at CA, CI, the sum of their portions will be 360 + 180 degrees or 180 degrees. However, since R and C or C and CI are in different Ayans, the sum of the Krantisamy is only when the Sun and Moon are in different Ayans.

To know whether the node-time has passed or is yet to come—

अथौजपदगस्येन्दोः क्रान्तिविक्षेपसंस्कृता ।
यदि स्स्यादधिका भानोः क्रान्तेः पातो गतस्तदा ॥७॥

Translation —(7) After knowing the true motion of the sun and the moon, one should see whether the moon is in an odd position or an even position with respect to the vernal equinox. If the moon is in an odd position and its deviation-motion, i.e., the true motion, is more than the true motion of the sun, then it should be understood that the node-time has passed,(8) and if it is less, then it should be understood that the node-time is yet to come. But if the moon is in an even position, then the opposite should be understood, i.e., if the true motion of the moon in an even position is more than the motion of the sun, then it should be understood that the node-time is yet to come, and if it is less, then it should be understood that the node-time has passed. If the motion of the moon or the shadow is less and subtraction is required, then what is said about the odd position in the above rule should be understood about the even position, and what is said about the even position should be understood about the odd position.

Scientific Commentary—the discussion of Ojas and Yugmapada or viṣama and samapada has been well discussed in Chapter on True Positions pages 126-27. Here, from the vernal equinox point to the sine of Cancer point or the sine of Sagittarius point for the first part, from the sine of Sagittarius point to the autumn equinox

Source page 731

The second part up to the point, the third part up to the point of Capricorn or Uttarayana from the autumn equinox, and the fourth part from the Uttarayana point to the spring equinox is. The first and third parts are called odd or Oja parts, and the second and fourth parts are called even or pair parts.

From Figure 120 it is clear that when the Moon remains in an odd position, i.e., in V or Shu, then for the transit or occultation, the Sun should be in the Shu or U position in sequence. It is also clear that the revolution of the Sun or Moon increases in odd positions and decreases in mean positions. Therefore, when the Moon is in an odd position and the Sun is in a mean position, the revolution of the Moon continues to increase and the revolution of the Sun continues to decrease. Therefore, the gross time of the nodal period extracted from the sixth verse, if the revolution of the Moon is more than the revolution of the Sun at that time, the revolution of the Moon will increase and the revolution of the Sun will decrease. Therefore, both revolutions have become equal before this time and the nodal period has passed. Conversely, if the revolution of the Moon is less than the revolution of the Sun, due to the revolution of the Moon continuing to increase, the time is coming when both revolutions will be equal and then the nodal period will occur. Similarly, when the Moon is in mean positions, the Sun will be in odd positions. In such a situation, the revolution of the Moon will decrease and the revolution of the Sun will continue to increase. Therefore, if the Moon's revolution is more, it will become equal to the decreasing revolution of the Sun and will come after the time extracted from the nodal period verse 6. But if the revolution of the Moon is less, then the nodal period should be considered as passed.

In the latter part of the eighth verse it is stated that if the true motion is obtained by subtracting the mean motion from the epicycle motion, then the rule stated above must be used because if the mean motion and the direction of the pole are different, it cannot be directly stated whether the lunar motion is increasing or decreasing. In such a situation, it will be necessary to know the motion one day ahead and one day behind.

If the nodal period has passed, subtract this difference or half of it from the Moon's portion. Multiply the difference or half that is added or subtracted by the motion of the Sun on that day and divide by the motion of the Moon on that day. The resulting period should be added or subtracted from the Sun's portion in the same way as it is added or subtracted from the Moon. Here is the method to know the portion of the sine of declination, radius, and the supreme sine of declination. The portion obtained by this method will be less than 60 degrees. There is no need to know more than this because we only need to see how far the sun and the moon are from the vernal or autumnal equinox. Although the true declination will be different, these portions will also be close to each other. The difference between these portions will be the amount by which the moon will be ahead or behind the nodal time. If the nodal time is coming, this difference should be added to the moon's portion because by that time the moon will move only that much further, and if the nodal time has passed, this difference should be subtracted from the moon's portion because at the time of the passed nodal time, the moon will remain only that much behind. But the sun will also leave some place in such a time. Therefore, it is necessary to also determine the sun's position of the nodal time. However, to know the true revolution of the Moon, it is necessary to know the Moon's shadow, which is dependent on the Moon's path of Rahu or Ketu, and in such a time, the lunar eclipse will also change its position due to retrograde motion, so similarly, the change of Rahu should also be known by the ratio. However, this change should be performed in the opposite manner in Rahu, that is, when adding the Moon and the Sun, one should subtract, and when subtracting, one should add because the motion of Rahu is opposite. When the true revolution is obtained by performing the operation of the Moon's shadow in the lunar revolution, then it will be seen that the Sun's revolution is still somewhat different. Repeat the procedure mentioned in 6-11 shlokas and repeat it until both revolutions are equal. This is called asakritkarma, which has been discussed in many places behind.

The explanation of the rule mentioned in 6-11 shlokas is sufficient. Translation—multiplying the difference between the instantaneous lunar portion and the half-night time lunar portion, determined by the above rule, by writing it in degrees of arc and multiplying by sixty and dividing the product by the half-night time lunar motion, the resulting gain is the nodal time that has passed or will pass that many hours before or after.

The nodal time should be this much further or behind.

If the calculation of the Sun and Moon is made very subtle by modern principles, then the resulting time of the node will be gross because the nodal calculation is very subtle and the daily motion of the Moon is so great that if the half-night motion is taken as nodal, as explained in this rule, subtlety cannot be achieved because if there is a great difference between the time of the node and the half-night, the lunar motions of both times will not be the same, therefore it would be better in my understanding to use the lunar motions two hours ahead and behind from that time according to this rule.

It is not wise to understand everything only from ancient theories and not to make amendments according to the country time, nor to consider the pure scientific method as inferior, nor is it in accordance with the method of ancient astrologers.

रवीन्द्वोः तुल्यता क्रान्त्योविषुवत्सन्निधौ यदा ।

Translation - When the revolutions of the Sun and Moon are the same near the equinoxes, i.e., near the vernal or autumnal equinox, the node occurs twice. In the opposite situation, i.e., near the points of Aries or Capricorn, there is no node.

Sūrya Siddhānta — Scientific Commentary — when the Sun and the Moon are near the vernal or autumnal equinox, the motion of their revolutions is very rapid. Therefore, when the Moon is south of the ecliptic and the Sun is north, their revolutions are equal. After this, when the Moon becomes cause north with quick motion, its revolution also becomes the same as the revolution of the Sun. In this way, revolution-equality can occur twice between the same two days. But when the Sun and the Moon both

If the answer is from the solstice, then it will be the time of amāvasyā and in such a condition, the lunar motion is not considered as before and second shlokas prove it. Therefore, it is known that only shloka 16 is given to state that the sine of declination can happen twice, two in the difference of one day.

But if the sun sine is near the points of Cancer or Capricorn, then its motion remains near the supreme motion. If at this time the motion of the moon is less due to the direction of the direction of Shar being different, then motion of conjunction cannot happen and neither the conjunction of validity nor the conjunction of deviation can occur.

The method of knowing the third type of deviation--

शशाङ्कर्कयुतेलिप्ता अभोगेन विभाजिताः ।
लब्धं सप्तदशान्तोऽन्यो व्यतीपातः तृतीयकः ॥२०॥

Translation—Add the portions of the sun and the moon to make the art and divide it by 800. If it is at the end of 17, that is, near 17, then there is the third deviation.

Scientific Commentary—In shloka 65 of Spṣṭāadhikar, the method of knowing the 27 yogas is given. In these, the 17th yoga is stated as deviation (see page 216). The method of knowing this is repeated here as well. That is, so that it may be known that the deviation called by the conjunction of motion in this right has an equivalent yoga called deviation. From this reasoning it can be said that the validity of the 27th yoga should also be understood as a great motion called validity.

One thing to note here. The calculations of latitudes and longitudes are done from the ecliptic portions of the Sun and Moon, but the calculations of the great circles are done from the sine portions. Therefore, this question arises here whether the sine portions or the ecliptic portions should be used in the rule given in the 20th verse. In the commentary of the Gūḍhārtha Prakāśikā Sanskrit Tika, it is stated that the precession angle, i.e., the sine portion, should be used for calculation, and this has been followed by Pandit Mādhava Purohit and Pandit Indranārāyaṇa Dwivedi. However, Swami Vidyanānanda has not discussed this in his Bengali ṭīkā. It seems to me that this latitude is the latitude of the latitudes and so forth, it is no different from it. Therefore, just as these latitudes are calculated, so too the latitude mentioned in this verse.

Source page 738

It should be calculated from the portions of the lunar months only and the precession angles of the light rays should not be taken. There is an obstacle in taking the sine portions. That is, the declination or right ascension that will arise from this will be different from the declination and right ascension of the prime vertical circles. Thus, one will have to imagine four periods of declination and right ascension in one month, which seems improper even in the style of argumentation to the author.

When does the conjunction of Sandhi and Gandanta occur—

सार्पेंद्रपौष्णधिष्ण्यानामन्त्याः पादा भसन्ध्यः ।
तदग्रभेष्बाधपदो गण्डान्तं नाम कीर्त्यते ॥२५॥

Translation—The fourth quadrant of the constellations Ashlesha, Jyestha, and Revati are the constellation conjunctions, and the first quadrant of the following constellations Magha, Moola, and Ashvini are called Gandanta.

Scientific Commentary—In Muhurta-Chintamani and other Muhurta texts, their discussion is special. For the progeny in the constellation conjunction or Gandanta, it is called Sadha-ranta that it has occurred in Moola. It is considered inauspicious. On the 27th day when that same Gandanta or Sandhi period comes again, a special type of worship is done for peace in Moola. The meaning of discussing Gandanta here is that the inauspicious effects of the great misfortunes are also those of Gandanta, as revealed in the next verse. These Sandhis are the last parts of the fourth, eighth, and twelfth signs, and Gandanta are the initial parts of the fifth, ninth, and first signs.

व्यतीपातत्रयं घोरं गण्डान्तं वितयं तथा ।
एवं ससन्धित्रितयं सर्वं कर्मसु वजंयेत् ॥२॥

Translation—All three declinations, all three Gandantas, and all the constellation conjunctions are very terrible, so they are forbidden in auspicious deeds, that is, when these occur, no auspicious action should be done.

Scientific Commentary—this verse does not discuss valid expenditure, but from the style of argument and earlier verses it is known that validity is also included. Commentators have done so too.

Scientific Commentary — The Jyotish (astronomy) story which Surya (Sun) began in possession of from Mayur has ended here. The questions asked by Mayur on this will be discussed in three chapters further. Therefore, what has been said till here is called the first half of Sūrya Siddhānta. The three chapters that follow are called the second half. Now we will conclude this first half by briefly telling how the great latitudes are calculated.

Determining the gross time of the great latitudes from the Panchangs—The calculation of the 27 yogoṃ of Viṣkambhādi must be in the Panchangs. The method to know these is explained in the 65th verse of the Chapter on True Positions, which is—add the portions of the Sun and the Moon to make the arts and divide it by 800. The number of yogoṃ that have passed since that obtained and the knowledge of the current conjunction is known from the remainder.

In this rule, the portions of the Sun and the Moon are measured from the initial point of the Ashwini constellation, and the portions are measured from the Vernal Equinox point for the calculation of the great latitudes. If the portions for both are measured from the Vernal Equinox, then knowing the time of the great latitudes would be much easier because at the time when half the time of the 14th conjunction passes, the sum of the portions of the Sun and the Moon is 180 degrees, and it is the midpoint of the nodal period called Vyatipata, and at the time when the Vaidyutī conjunction ends, the midpoint of the node called Vaidyuti occurs. But this is not the case. Therefore, a little calculation will be necessary. According to Sūrya Siddhānta, the initial point of Ashwini, where it is nowadays, is about 22 degrees 45 minutes west of the point corresponding to the vernal equinox as seen by the zenith. This difference is called the precession angle. If the portions of the Sun and the Moon are taken from here, the sum of both is 45 degrees 30 minutes more. The sum of the sines of the portions of the Sun and the Moon for Vyatipata is 180 degrees, so 180^° - 45^° 30' = 134^° 30' = 8070 minutes. This is the sum of the portions of the Sun and the Moon for Vyatipata from the initial point of the Ashwini constellation. Dividing this by 800 minutes leaves 10 lekhas and 70 minutes. It is proven by 10 that the Gandha conjunction remains in the Vyatipata period and the growth conjunction begins. This-

To determine the time of eclipse in a gross manner, one should calculate the subtle time of eclipse by knowing the true motion of the sun and moon at the time when the increase of conjunction begins.

To determine the nodal period named Vaidhriti, one should subtract 45 degrees 30 art from 360 degrees. Doing this leaves 314 degrees 30 art = 18870 art. Dividing this by 800 leaves 23 degrees and 470 art remaining, which shows that the 23rd conjunction in the nodal period named Vaidhriti remains auspicious and the half of the 24th conjunction of Shukla is also passed. Therefore, in a gross sense, Vaidhriti is at half the part of the Shukla conjunction. Therefore, to make finer calculations, the Sun, and the Moon and the true declination should be known at the same time. For this, the correction is made by knowing the true portions of the Sun, Moon and Rahu, the true declination of the Sun, the mean declination of the Moon and the shadow, to know the true declination of the Moon, the method of which is explained in Chapter on True Positions (spaRectaadhikar) pages 166-200. In this chapter, all matters of the origin, position, extension, etc., of geography are described, that is why it is named Geography Chapter. Along with that, proofs of the orbits of the planets, constellations, and the sky are also given.

(1) Thereafter, Mayasura, joining his hands and worshipping with great devotion, asked after bowing to the man born from the portion of the sun.
(2) O Lord, what is the magnitude of this Earth, what is its shape, and on what is it based, how many divisions it has, and how are the lands of the seven paradises situated in it.
(3) How do the Sun and the Asuras arrange themselves and revolve around the Earth while illuminating the worlds.
(4) Why are the days and nights of the Devas and Asuras opposite to each other, and how does this happen when one revolution of the Sun is completed?
(5) Why is the day and night of the Pitrs (ancestors) one month and that of humans sixty hours? Why are not the days and nights the same everywhere?
(6) Why are the masters of day, year, month, and hour not the same, how do the constellations revolve with the planets, and what is their basis?
(7) What are the heights and the mutual differences of the orbits of the planets and constellations above the Earth, what are their values, and in what order are they situated?
(8) Why are the rays of the Sun very intense in the summer season and not in the winter season? How far do these rays extend; what are the values of the solar, lunar, etc., and what is the purpose of these?
(9) O one who feels the past, please remove these doubts from me because you are omniscient; no other human can remove my doubts except you.
(10) Hearing these words of Mayasura spoken with devotion, Suryansh Purusha called it the second chapter, the other mysterious form of the previous one.
(11) With a focused mind, listen to this element called spirituality which I say, because I do not consider any object unattainable for the devotees.

Scientific Commentary—All the elements know the desire to know the answers to the questions asked by Mayasura. Suryaansh Purush has stated on this that the mystery to be explained in the answer is related to spiritual knowledge. Many people will say this, but Suryaansh Purush has discussed the origin of this world, which can certainly be said to be related to spirituality because it is beyond physical science.

Sūrya Siddhānta – in these six shlokas there is a very clear description of the position of four cities located on the Tropic of Cancer. These cities are in the fourth quadrant of the Earth's circumference from each other, that is, they are separated by 60 degrees and North Meru (North Pole) is also at the same distance from them to the north. The directions of these cities are considered from the Indian subcontinent. Lanka is at the Tropic of Cancer of the south of the Indian subcontinent, and its position should be considered as the longitude of Ujjain according to the 62nd shloka of the Chapter on Mean Motions (madhyamādhikāra) (page 65). The longitude of Ujjain from Greenwich is approximately 76 degrees. Therefore, if Lanka is considered at this longitude and the Tropic of Cancer, there is a sea here nowadays. The place 60 degrees east of this is at a longitude of 166 degrees east of Greenwich. Therefore, the place of Yamakoti city is also a sea nowadays. Since there are no land names on the Tropic of Cancer 60 degrees west of Lanka or 14 degrees west of Greenwich, the location of Romak city also cannot be determined. This Romak city would have been about 50 miles south of the Free Town of Western Africa nowadays. Similarly, Siddapuri would have been more than 1000 miles south of Mexico.

If the existence of these four spheres ever existed, then that time would be very ancient because nowadays the difference has become so much that there is no mark of that time in the present. It is also possible that the existence of these four spheres remained only in the poet's imagination and this has been described in figurative language that these four places on the equator are such that when noon is in Lanka, then sunrise is in Romaka, midnight in Siddhapuri, and sunset in Yamakoti.

It is clear that when the sun is on the cross on the equator, then at noon there is no shadow of any standing object. There are the north and south poles on the horizon of this line, so the height of the pole star here is zero. Therefore, the latitude is also zero. For this reason, the equator is called the meridian country. Its further and clearer description is in the next three verses.

Sūrya Siddhānta is stated to be emerging from the middle of the Earth on both sides, therefore it should be understood as the axis of the Earth whose northern end is the North Pole.

(44) Therefore, due to the presence of both pole stars on the horizon of these cities, the axis of these poles is not high, i.e., their latitude is zero, but the longitude is 60. Similarly, the latitude of Merus, i.e., the poles, is 60. (45) When the sun is in the deva-bhag, i.e., in the northern hemisphere, the gods get their first sight in the beginning of Aries, and when the sun is in the asur bhag, i.e., in the southern hemisphere, the asuras see them first in the beginning of Libra.

Scientific Commentary—Here it is stated that the North and South Poles have the Pole Star in the middle, which is on the horizon of the meridian. It can be estimated from this that when the Sūrya Siddhānta was said in ancient times, there were two Pole Stars. It can also be said that just as there is a star in the middle of the North Pole, a star was also understood to be in the middle of the South Pole. But it is certain that the star seen in the middle of the North Pole at this time was not at this place in ancient times because its position is also changing due to precession (see pages 240-42). Therefore, the Pole Stars described here are the positions of the celestial poles which are in the middle of the North and South Poles. They have no eternal relationship with any star. When a star comes near them due to precession, it also begins to be called the Pole Star in direct view. It has been stated in many places that the latitude on the equator is zero and

How the length 60° and latitude 60 and longitude zero occur at the northern and southern poles (see pages 58, 56, 256, 257 etc).

Verse 45 is of great importance. It is stated that when the sun is at the beginning of the Aries sign, the gods see it first, that is, when the sun rises for the inhabitants of the North Pole, and when it is at the beginning of the Libra sign, the demons see it first, that is, when it rises for the inhabitants of the South Pole. It appears that the beginning of the Aries sign should be understood as the place where the ecliptic and the tropics are in conjunction and where the sun becomes in the northern hemisphere. This place is called the Vernal Equinox point. Similarly, the beginning point of Libra is the Autumnal Equinox point where the sun becomes in the southern hemisphere. When the sun comes to the tropics at the beginning of Aries, sunrise occurs for the northern pole dwellers, and they see the sun equally for 6 months. This time is called the day of the gods. And the night of the demons because until the sun is seen by the northern pole dwellers, it remains invisible for the southern pole dwellers and there is night. When the sun reaches the beginning of Libra, sunset occurs at the northern pole and sunrise at the southern pole. For 6 months from this time, the sun is seen equally at the southern pole and there is the day of the month. These characteristics on the northern and southern poles and the equator occur because the poles are 60 degrees apart from the equator (see page 62).

Why are the rays of the sun slow and intense?

अत्यासन्नतया तेन ग्रीष्मे तीव्रकरा रवेः ।

Translation—When the Sun God is in the part, that is, in the northern hemisphere, due to being very close to the gods, its rays are very intense in the summer season and slow due to being far away in the winter season.

Scientific Commentary—this verse states that the rays of the sun are more intense in the summer season because the sun is near and less intense in the winter season because the sun is far, but this is not correct. Nowadays in reality, the sun is farther from the Earth in the summer season and nearer in the winter season as apparent from the size of its images (see page 85). The real reason is

Source page 757

Because the rays of the sun come in a vertical form in the summer season, their intensity is more, and in the winter season, because the rays come under the sun, they come crooked, so their intensity is reduced. This is seen every day. In the noon, the sun is high, so its rays are usually vertical and the heat also increases. But in the morning and evening, its rays remain very slanted, so there is not that much heat. This condition occurs on the entire earth in a period of one year. In the countries near the equator, the sun appears on the head all year, so its rays come vertically and are very intense.

It is clear that the plane k h is larger than the plane g h because it is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle k g h. Therefore, when the rays spread out over a larger space, their force is reduced, and the heat in the plane g h cannot be the same as in the plane k h. Translation—(47) On the day when the sun is on the equatorial circle, both gods and asuras see it on the horizon; their day and night are opposite to each other. (48) Rising at the beginning of the Aries sign, the sun moves towards the north in the three signs Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, completing the first half of the day of the North Meru-inhabitants, i.e., the gods. (46) Similarly, moving further from the beginning of the Cancer sign, it completes the second half of the day of the gods in the three signs Cancer, Leo, and Libra. Similarly, moving into Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius signs, it completes the first half of the day of the asuras, and moving into Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces signs, it completes the second half of the day of the asuras. (50) Therefore, the day and night of the gods and asuras are opposite to each other, and after one revolution (turn) of the sun, they have one day and night.

Scientific Commentary—The day when the sun comes to the vernal equinox point is called the equinoctial day. On this day the horizon from the north and south poles

Source page 760

Geography Chapter 735

Therefore, the inhabitants of the North Pole see the gods on the horizon and the inhabitants of the South Pole see the demons. However, because the sun's motion is towards the North, it appears to rise for the gods and set for the demons. That is, from this day the day of the gods and the night of the demons begins. This position of the sun, that is the Vernal Equinox point, is called the beginning of Aries. After this, the sun moves towards the North every day. When it reaches 60 degrees from the Vernal Equinox point, its northward movement stops. On this day, the gods see it at its highest point. This height is like the sun's ultimate revolution. Therefore, on this day is the noon of the gods and the midnight of the demons. From the Vernal Equinox point up to 60 degrees, there are three zodiacs: Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. When the sun passes from the beginning of Cancer to Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, and reaches the beginning of Libra, it comes onto the ecliptic. At this time, the gods see it setting. Therefore, from this time the night of the gods and the day of the demons begins. This position of the sun is called the Autumnal Equinox point, and this day is also called the Equinox day. After this, as long as the sun remains in the Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius zodiacs, there is the afternoon of the demons and the pre-night of the gods. When the sun reaches the Capricorn zodiac, it is the midnight of the gods and the noon of the demons. When the sun is in the Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces zodiacs, it is the afternoon of the demons. In this way, the time taken for one revolution of the sun is the same time for one night of the gods or one day of the demons. But the day of the gods is the night of the demons, and the night of the gods is the day of the demons.

From this description it is clear that the beginning of the zodiac signs such as Aries, Taurus, etc., is considered from the vernal equinox, not from the retrograde Aries which is currently 23 degrees ahead of the vernal equinox and which is always moving further ahead of the vernal equinox. This difference is called precession angle. More than 1400 years ago, when the vernal equinox and retrograde Aries were together, the position of Aries was the same as what is called retrograde Aries today, but this is not the case now. For this reason, two schools have emerged among astrologers today, the siderealists and the retrogradists. Those called siderealists consider the vernal equinox as the beginning of Aries. But the retrogradists consider retrograde Aries as the starting point of the zodiac signs.

After this, in the treatises like Siddhānta Shiromani, both are discussed.

In the countries of the North and South, the magnitude of day or night is 30 hours only for the vernal day when the precession of the sun is zero. And when the precession of the sun is south, the day is larger and the night is smaller in the southern countries, and the night is larger and the day is smaller in the northern countries. The consideration of the decrease or increase of day or night is done according to the precession of the sun and the latitude of the place, as stated in verses 60-61 of the Chapter on True Positions and their Scientific Commentary.

The mutual difference between the Pole Star and the constellation circle—

Translation-moving towards the poles, the declination of the Pole Star and the declination of the constellation circle increase, but moving towards the equator, it is the opposite, that is, the declination of the Pole Star and the declination of the constellation circle increase.

Scientific Commentary—the constellation circle is near the prime vertical circle, so the constellation circle appears directly above the equator and the pole star appears on the horizon. Moving towards the poles from here, the latitude of the poles increases, and the latitude of the prime vertical circle decreases or the declination increases. At the poles, the latitude of the pole star is 60 and the latitude of the prime vertical circle is zero or the declination is 60 because the prime vertical circle becomes the horizon at the poles. In contrast, moving towards the equator, the declination of the pole star and the latitude of the constellation circle increase.

Sūrya Siddhānta—Scientific Commentary—the Sun, Moon, planets, and stars all rise above the eastern horizon, move towards the west and set, and come to rise again above the eastern horizon in 24 hours. The reason for this is understood in ancient times that the entire celestial sphere is revolving by the flowing air bound in both celestial poles, and the orbits of the planets are also revolving from east to west in the same celestial sphere. Some scholars of Bharatavarsha still support this view and are ready to debate. However, it has now been proven by irrefutable evidence that the cause of the motion of the celestial sphere is not the flowing air but the motion of the Earth itself. With one motion, the Earth moves from west to east on its axis once every 24 hours; this daily motion is called the rotation of the Earth's axis. From this, all objects in the sky appear to move from east to west. From this, the origin of day and night occurs. With the second motion, the Earth completes one orbit of the Sun in a year, which causes the origin of the seasons, and in the sky, the Sun appears to move from west to east while orbiting the Earth in a year. This motion is called the annual motion of the Earth. Both these motions occur simultaneously in the Earth, as a ball thrown upwards dances on its axis and changes its position, or as a top played by boys dances and changes its position.

In our ancient religious texts, the Earth is considered motionless, therefore the motion of the Earth is not accepted by some scholars of Sanatana Dharma; however, in the debate, they present the same arguments that Acharya Varahamihira, Brahmagupta, etc., presented. Therefore, it must first be considered where these arguments are compatible with mathematics. After this, it will be proven by many proofs of mathematics and physical science that there are two motions in the Earth, daily and annual, and because of these, the constellations appear to move from east to west once a day, and the change of seasons, etc., occurs, and the motion of the planets appears to be of a certain type. The methods by which Acharya Varahamihira and Brahmagupta refuted the motion of the Earth are these ()^1. One argument of Acharya Varahamihira is that if the Earth revolves towards the east, then why do the birds that fly away from their nests reach back to the nest? The second argument he made is that if the Earth revolves towards the east, then the flag and so on always appear to fly towards the west, because this is a common experience that if a person runs with a handkerchief in hand, due to the speed, the handkerchief starts flying backward. And if it is said that the Earth moves very slowly, then the flag etc. do not appear to fly to the west, then how does the Earth complete a revolution in a day at such a slow speed?

The reason for the birds reaching their nests is that when the bird flies in the sky, the velocity of the geostationary motion remains in that nest, so the bird also moves with the same velocity, though it does not realize it. Also, it can generate its own motion, by which it can go wherever it wants away from the nest. (2) But this is even more intuitive and clear in Foucault's pendulum experiment. Mathematics proves that if a pendulum only oscillates due to the effect of gravity or swings, its plane of oscillation will remain the same, and the motion of the base of the pendulum will not be affected by the direction of this plane because there is no other force that can deflect it from this plane. It can be seen intuitively that if a heavy pendulum is hung by a thin string and swung like a clock pendulum, and if the base in which the pendulum is hung is rotated, its rotation does not cause any change in the plane of oscillation of the pendulum because the slight twisting of the string or cord to which the pendulum is attached is more natural than the change of the pendulum's plane of oscillation by a heavy pendulum when it is already swinging in one plane. Therefore, it is proven that if the Earth is stationary, the direction of the pendulum's oscillation will also remain stationary with respect to surrounding objects and the base, and if there is a motion in it, then there will be a change in the directions of the ground rather than the plane of the pendulum's oscillation, and the plane of the pendulum's oscillation will be seen as changing. Therefore, from this pendulum experiment, not only the motion of the Earth will not be known, but its direction will also be known.

Foucault performed this experiment in Paris in the year 1851 or 1608. He hung his pendulum from the dome of a large building named Panthéon. The wire was 200 feet long and the weight of the sphere was about 1 mina (80 pounds). At the time the pendulum swung, the needle that came out from below the sphere continued to make the mark of its swinging on the plane, and it was seen that the plane of the sand was rotating in the direction of the apse, that is, from right to left, from west to east.

Two things must be kept with great care in this experiment. The pendulum should remain swinging for as long as its string is long, otherwise it will stop quickly by rubbing against the air with its high speed. Secondly, it is good if its sphere is as heavy as possible because this reduces the effects of hanging defects and air friction greatly.

it is that when the air above the equator is warm and light, it rises, so to fill its place, the cold air near the poles flows towards the equator. However, the motion of the Earth on the equator is very rapid to the east, and as you go towards the poles, this motion slows down, so the motion of the air that flows from the equator also remains rapid to the east, so it reaches the countries towards the poles whose eastward motion is slow. Then it turns to the east. Similarly, the air that flows from the poles towards the equator turns to the west.

The direction of the ocean currents is also the same. The warm current near the Equator from the Gulf of Mexico flows north in the Atlantic Ocean, it then turns to the east and reaches countries like France, England, Norway, etc., on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean in the northeast direction, and the cold current from Greenland flows towards North America. The result of this is that the harbor of Harfangst in Norway, which is at 703 North latitude, remains free of ice for twelve months, whereas the western edge of North America remains covered with ice for more than 40 degrees of latitude due to cold and heat.

Similarly, the warm current flowing north from the Indian Ocean island group turns to the east and keeps the eastern part of Japan warm, and the cold current from the north flows in the exact opposite direction in the China Sea from the western edge of Japan.

This is briefly explained what changes happen in the directions of winds and currents due to the daily motion of the Earth. If you want to know more about this topic, you should use good books of geography.

Translation—Sur and Asura keep watching the sun that rises once and see it for half a year continuously, the inhabitants of the lunar world, the ancestors, watch it for one side, and the inhabitants of the Earth, humans, watch it for one day.

Scientific Commentary—The meaning of the first half of this verse is the same as stated in the 67th verse. There is some special meaning in the meaning of the first word of the latter part which needs to be explained. The Sanatana Dharma Hindus believe that the ancestors reside in the upper part of the lunar sphere. This part is not in front of the Earth. Western astrologers also say that the moon revolves around the Earth in such a way that its lower part remains in front of the Earth and the upper part always remains behind.

Source page 793

Thus, the Moon moves on its axis in the same number of days as it takes to orbit the Earth. Its proof is not difficult. By looking carefully at the lunar image, it is known that its black spots always appear in the same position relative to the edge of the image, which shows that the part of the lunar image facing the Earth always remains in the same condition, that is, the period of the Moon's axis rotation is the same as its orbital period. It can be said that the Moon does not have any axis rotation. But this is not correct. This will be made clear by an example. Place a lamp in the middle and look at it. Suppose the lamp is to your north. Now, while looking at the lamp, move around it in the clockwise direction. When you complete a quarter revolution, the lamp will be to your east. After completing half a revolution, the lamp will be to your south, after three-quarter revolution it will be to your west, and after a full revolution, coming back to the place from where the rotation began, the lamp will be to your north again. This proves that in such a revolution, your face always remains towards the lamp and your back always remains behind it. Also, your body also moves once because while rotating, your face is always towards north, east, south, and west.

When the upper part of the moon always remains opposite to the Earth, what is its relation to the sun? On the day of Amavasya, the moon is between the sun and the Earth, so its upper part remains directly in front of the sun. The Pitris reside in the upper part, so on the day of Amavasya, the sun is directly above the ancestors, meaning it is their noon on this day. That is why obituaries and offerings are done for the ancestors during the noon of Amavasya. On the day of Purnima, it is their midnight. After half of the Krishna Paksha passes, the sun appears to rise while seeing the ancestors, and for half of the Shukla Paksha, it appears to see them equally, meaning the ancestors' morning is on the eighth day of the Krishna Paksha and the evening is on the eighth day of the Shukla Paksha.

The fractions of the larger orbit are larger and the fractions of the smaller orbit are smaller. (76) Planets moving on the smaller orbit complete their revolution in a short time, and planets moving on the larger orbit complete their revolution in a long time. (77) The Moon's orbit is very small, so the Moon completes many revolutions, whereas Saturn, being in the larger orbit, completes only a few revolutions.

Scientific Commentary—Some explanation has already been given in Chapter on Mean Motions verses 26, 27, and its Scientific Commentary pages 14-17, so no further elaboration is needed here. The proof of how the fractions of the larger orbit are larger and the fractions of the smaller orbit are smaller can be easily found in the picture 1 of page 14. As much as 1/24 of the larger circle is as much as 1/36 of the smaller circle, meaning one part of the larger circle is greater than one part of the smaller circle. It is also clear that the time period for the revolution of the planets that move in the larger orbit is larger, and the time period for the revolution of the planets that move in the smaller orbit is smaller. However, there is no such simple relationship between the revolution period of the planet and its distance as understood by Indian astrologers and as further explained in this chapter. This relationship is according to Kepler's third law, which is determined by the subtle consideration of the motions and distances of the planets (see pages 84-61).

Translation—(80) Multiplying the sums of the solar orbits by 60 gives the value of the sums of the constellation orbits. The constellation circle revolves in the same amount above all the planets. (81) Multiplying the sums of the ecliptic by the number of revolutions of the lunar months gives the value of the celestial sphere. The sun's rays travel up to that point. (82) The value of the celestial sphere, when divided by the number of revolutions of the planet, the value of that planet's orbit will be found in the sums. Dividing the celestial sphere by the number of Sawan days of the kalpa gives the daily motion of all the planets in the sums. (83) Multiplying this planimetric planetary motion by the lunar orbit and dividing by the orbit of the planet, and then dividing the result by 15, the daily motion of that planet will be found in the arts.

Scientific Commentary—what is stated in these shlokas has been discussed in many places (see page 15-17; 451-53). In short, the essence of it is:—

(1) Constellation orbit = Solar orbit X 60

(2) Celestial orbit = Lunar revolutions X Celestial orbit (3) Number of revolutions of any planet in the kalpa = Orbit of that planet's celestial orbit (4) Sawan days of the kalpa = Daily planimetric motion of each planet (5) Planetary planimetric motion X Lunar orbit / Planetary orbit X 15 = Daily artistic motion of the planet

From the second and third equations it is clear that the extension of the celestial orbit is considered as much as each planet moves in conjunctions in a Kalpa. This proves that our Acharyas understood the planetary motion of each planet to be the same, which is inaccurate according to modern observations. The principle for knowing the daily art motion of a planet is the same which is well explained in pages 451-53.

The orbits of the constellations and the extension of the celestial orbit are hypothetical. There is no limit to the distance of the constellations or stars. Modern observations prove that some stars are so far from the Earth that it takes millions of years for their light to reach us.

Method of knowing the distance of a planet

कक्ष्या भुकर्णगुणिता महीमण्डलभाजिता ।
तत्कर्णा भूमिकणत्स्यु ग्रहोच्चे स्वे दलीकृताः ॥८४॥

Translation—When the orbit of a planet is multiplied by the geodiameter and divided by the earth's circumference, the diameter of that planet's orbit is obtained. By subtracting the geodiameter from the remainder and halving it, the height or distance of that planet from the earth is found.

Scientific Commentary—This is a rule for knowing the diameter from the circumference. The relationship between the geodiameter and the earth's circumference is the same relationship that exists in the diameters and circumferences of the orbits of each planet. The simple meaning of the first part of this verse is that dividing the planet's orbit by 301416 gives its orbital diameter.

What is stated in the latter part of the shloka is clear from figure 78 of page 408. In this figure, if the line BD is extended to D so that it reaches the lunar orbit and the solar orbit, then the distance from the point of the lunar orbit to D should be understood as the altitude of the Moon and the distance from the point of the solar orbit to D as the altitude of the Sun. Similarly, one should also understand the altitude of other planets.

Scientific Commentary—If the calculations of the orbits are done according to the verses 26-33 of the Chapter on Mean Motions and according to verse 82 of the Chapter on Mean Motions, then there is a slight difference in the digits of the units of the above numbers. The reason for this is that to write the whole number, the fractional part has either been omitted or taken as 1 because it is more than half. It seems that the orbits of the Moon and Rahu are given to show the similarity of the rule because they are not independent bodies in the sky; they are just two special points of the lunar orbit. The constellation orbit also does not seem to have special importance.

Nowadays, observations prove that the orbits of the planets are not round but elliptical, with the Sun at one focus, and all planets revolve around the Sun. The distance of any planet from the Earth is not always the same, as is clear from the table of latitudes in page 410 and the table of true positions given in page 568. The values of these true positions are given in units where 1000 units are considered the mean distance from the Earth to the Sun. Such 1000 units are equal to 6260000 miles (6 crore 26 lakh miles) because the mean distance from the Earth to the Sun is the same (see page 452). If this distance is to be known in miles, then the miles should be divided by 5 (see page 54).

Thirty Chapters of Astrology Upanishad (Brief Description)

Shloka 1-3—How should the instruction for the creation of Bhugol be given? Shloka 3-13—The method of making Bhugol. Shloka 13-15—Determining the positions of Lagna, Antya, etc. Shloka 16-17—How Bhugol can move by itself. Shloka 18-24—Discussion of other instruments that tell the time. Shloka 25—The greatness of astrology.

Preparation for making Bhugol—

अथ गुप्ते शुचौ देशे स्नातश्शुचिरलङ्कृतः ।
संपूज्य भास्करं भक्त्या ग्रहान्मान्यथ गुह्यकान् ॥१॥
पारंपर्योपदेशेन यथा ज्ञातं गुरोर्मुखात् ।
आचार्यः शिष्यबोधार्थं सर्वं प्रत्यक्षदर्शिवान् ॥२॥
भूभगोलकस्य रचनां कुर्यादाश्चर्यकारिणीम् ।

Translation—The teacher should create a composition that causes wonder for the Bhugol by worshipping the Sun, planets, constellations, and yakshas with devotion after bathing and wearing ornaments, in a secluded and pure place, and by the teachings received from tradition, and the knowledge heard from the teacher's mouth and seen directly by oneself, to fully explain to the disciple.

Scientific Commentary—Many commentators have taken the meaning of Acharya as Suryansh Purush and the meaning of disciple as Mayasur; but in my understanding, this is a simple instruction for all Acharyas. The word 'Kuryat' also reveals this. From these shlokas it appears that the Acharya should not be satisfied with oral instruction alone, but should also impart practical and action-oriented knowledge for which he should also possess practical knowledge and should be the one who directly shows the knowledge, not as if he were to comment on such esoteric texts as Surya Siddhanta, but not even recognize the main stars of the sky.

In the worship of the planets, the worship of the Sun also comes in, but here the word Sun appears separately with the planets, which indicates that the Sun in a special way

Source page 799

Worship should be done because the original Acharya of this principle is considered to be Suryadev. The Sun does not come in the modern definition of planets, but the Sun-Siddhantaka did not separate the name of the Sun from this idea because this opinion is not revealed anywhere else.

The Yaksha people are servants of the god of wealth Kubera, they guard his treasury and gardens. They are probably considered skilled in craftsmanship as well because the Pushpak Vimana belonged to Kubera. Therefore, they are also ordered to be worshipped to obtain divine help in the meaning of Yantra construction.

The word Bhugol is made from three words: Bhu, Bha, and Gol, so its meaning is a sphere in which the sky is the sphere with which the geography moves, in which planets and constellations etc are considered to revolve.

Translation—(3) A straight rod should be made by making a circle (geography) of the desired shape of wood (4) in it by making a hole so that it remains equal on both sides from the center of geography and acts as the Meru rod. Fix two base circles in this rod (at right angles to each other) whose midpoint is the ecliptic. (5) Divide these three circles into 360 degrees by an inch. In accordance with the diameter of the equator circle (6) of the Ahoratra circle, the differences in the inclinations of the final points of the Aries, Taurus, and Gemini signs marked on it by the degrees of the ecliptic and Sagittarius, these three signs' Ahoratra circles are fixed in the opposite manner as the Ahoratra circles of Cancer, Leo, and Virgo. Similarly, three Ahoratra circles (8) of the Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius and in the opposite manner of Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces signs are fixed in the South Celestial Sphere above both base circles. Similarly, the Ahoratra circles of the constellations, stars like Abhijit (9) Saptarshi, Agatsya, Brahmhridya located in the North and South Celestial Spheres are fixed. The equator circle is between all these Ahoratra circles. (10) Both the arc points and both the latitudes are at the conjunction points of the equator circle and both base circles. Start the zodiac cycle from the place of the latitude. (11) In this way, the divisions of signs like Aries, Taurus, etc., are done by the obliquity of the sines. The line of inclination which is fixed from one arc point to another arc point and from the second to the first (2) is called the ecliptic on which the sun always travels shining. The planets like the Moon, Mars, etc., appear at the end of their inclinations by their own latitudes (13) due to their own inclinations.

Sūrya Siddhānta - here it is not stated what the basis of the base orbit and the equatorial orbit should be made of. In other texts, thin rods of bamboo have been used because they are so flexible that they can be bent in a circle. Nowadays, this work can be easily done with iron or brass wire. The geoid formed by the method mentioned above becomes very incomprehensible due to many circles (circles), so nowadays, if the geoid is made according to figure 136, it will be easier to make and easier to understand.

The smallest circle in the middle of this picture indicates geography (Earth-sphere), which is why 'Bhū' is written in the middle. 'Dhadhā' is the line that passes through the center of the Earth-sphere and extends on both sides of it. The distance from Bhū to Dh and Dha is equal. Two meridians, 'Dhashdhāv' and 'Dhapdhāpū', are at right angles to each other from these places.

Source page 801

They are tied. On these two circles, a circle of 'P V P' is tied at the same distance from 'D' and 'DH', which is called the equatorial orbit. These three circles are divided into 360 equal parts, and marks are made on them, which are called degrees. After this, the order is to make the circumpolar circles of the twelve zodiac signs, such as Aries. But in my understanding, this is not necessary. After tying the three upper circles, it will be easier to tie the circumpolar circle directly. This should also be taken as equal to any of the upper circles. It should be tied at the junction of the equatorial circle and the meridian circle at the 'V' and 'SH' places first, and then tied at the second meridian circles at the 'K' and 'M' places. The difference between 'K' or 'M' should be the same as the ultimate revolution of the sun, which is nowadays approximately twenty-three and thirty-plus degrees (23° 30’). This revolution circle should also be divided into 360 equal parts. The 'V' place is called the vernal equinox or spring equinox, and the 'SH' place is called the autumnal equinox. The 'K' and 'M' places are called the sine of Cancer and the sine of Libra or the points of South and North transit respectively (see p. 230). With regard to these places, the 'DH' base orbit is called the equinoctial circle and the 'DPMDHPUK' base orbit is called the solstitial circle, because the first has both equinoctial points and the second has both solstitial points. In the picture, a circumpolar circle 'AI' is shown parallel to the equatorial circle at the 'A' place. This is found at the second place 'A' of the circumpolar circle. The point 'A' is at the same difference as the vernal equinox from 'V', but

Sūrya Siddhānta

In the opposite direction, the position of 'sha' in the autumn conjunction is either 'sha' from 'aa' or 'k' from 'a' and 'aa' are at the same distance. If 'a' sine is at the beginning of the Taurus sign, then 'aa' sine will be at the beginning of the Virgo sign, and if the first sine is at the beginning of Gemini, then the second sine will be at the beginning of Leo. Similarly, an apothem circle of any point of the ecliptic can be drawn. This is stated in shlokas 6-7. Besides this, an apothem circle can be understood near the position of 'dha'.

In the 12th shloka, the orbits of the classes of the planets like the Moon, Mars, etc., are also discussed, but no such orbit is shown in the picture. To draw such an orbit, the nodal point of the first planet should be fixed on the ecliptic. The orbit of that planet should be drawn such that its second conjunction is at 180 degrees on the ecliptic from that position. These two places are the nodal positions of the planet. Then this circle should also be drawn at the north and south positions equal to the ultimate deviation of that planet with a difference of 60 degrees from the ecliptic (the discussion of ultimate deviation is in Chapter on Mean Motions, pages 74-76).

Determination of rising sign, mean sign, setting, etc.

उदयं क्षितिजे लग्नमस्तं गच्छति तद्वशात् ॥१३॥
लङ्कोदयैस्तथा सिद्धं खमध्योपरि मध्यगम् ।
मध्यक्षितिजयोर्मध्ये या ज्या साऽन्त्याऽभिधीयते ॥१४॥
ज्ञेया चरदलज्या च विषुवत्क्षितिजान्तरम् ।
कृत्वोपरि स्वकं स्थानं मध्ये क्षितिजमण्डलम् ॥१५॥

Translation—(13) The point of the ecliptic that lies in the eastern horizon is the rising sign. According to this rising sign, the point of the ecliptic that lies in the western horizon is the setting sign. (14) The mean sign is on the meridian circle, which is calculated from the rising ascensions of Lanka. The sine that lies between the apothem circle and the meridian circle is called setting. (15) The horizon of the tropics, which is called the circumcircle, and the difference between the horizon of one's place and the horizon of its place is called latitude. When placing one's place at the top of geography, the horizon circle is in the middle of geography.

Scientific Commentary—the same word is used for several definitions in these verses, therefore their meaning is not easily understood. In the first half of the 12th verse, 'madhyam' has come for the mean ascendant. In the latter half, the word 'madhya'

Source page 803

The circle and the arc of the meridian have come for the place of the location. In the first half of the 15th verse, 'vishuvat' has been used for the horizon or the meridian for the celestial sphere, and the word horizon has been used for the circle of the horizon in its place. In the latter half, the word 'madhye' has come for the middle of the vertical meridian circle in its place. This type of usage is very misleading and is considered a defect for scientific texts.

All these definitions can be well understood on the 286-60 pages of the Chapter on the Three Problems and the figures 36, 42, 43 of the Chapter on True Positions and the figures 63 of the Chapter on the Three Problems. With the above description, knowledge of all these definitions can be easily obtained from the geodetic instrument.

The device by which the geodetic instrument always rotates—

वस्त्रच्छन्नं बहिश्चापि लोकालोकेन वेष्टितम् ।
अमृतस्रावयोगेन कालभ्रमणसाधनम् ॥१६॥
गुणबोजसमाकृष्ट गोलयंत्र प्रकल्पयेत् ।
गोप्यमेतत्प्रकाश्योक्त सर्वगम्यं भवेद्यतः ॥१७॥

Translation—(16) Make a sphere surrounded by the horizon, i.e., the horizon circle, cover it with cloth and arrange it by the flow of water so that it rotates by itself and indicates the time of the stars. (17) Or make this spherical instrument by the combination of mercury so that it rotates by itself. It should be kept secret. If it is stated clearly, then everyone in this world will know it.

Scientific Commentary—the language of these two shlokas is very obscure. There is not even a little understanding of how the armillary sphere proved the daily motion of the sky by revolving by itself. It is apparent that the meridian of the armillary sphere was fixed in such a way that it remained towards the pole. Then some device must have been made in it so that a collision from the flow of water occurred in it, so that it would revolve once in a nakṣatra day like a water wheel. Mercury was also used instead of water, but it is not known how. Finally, it is stated that this device should not be false at all. Perhaps this is why it is given only as a hint. From this people can deduce that the author himself did not know this action well. He only had the impression that such a machine could be made that moves by itself, that is why he kept all things round. It is also possible that in ancient times there was such advancement in craftsmanship that such self-moving instruments were made by the combination of mercury and water.

Scientific Commentary—many names of instruments for knowing time are mentioned in these verses, but the method of making them is not told anywhere. Since time can be known by observing the shadow of the sun using the first four instruments, they can work during the day and are called shadow instruments. The discussion of the gnomon among these is greatly discussed in the third chapter named Chapter on the Three Problems. It is stated in that chapter how the latitude, declination, local time, direction, etc. are known from a 12-finger gnomon. To know the time by this, a complex operation of multiplication and division has to be done; time does not come directly. The measurement of the shadow also cannot be taken very accurately, so the time obtained from this instrument can be four or five minutes more or less. Therefore, there is no need to use it nowadays.

Yasti instrument—it is not discussed anywhere else in this book, so it cannot be told how it was used. Bhaskaracharya ji has specially discussed it in the instrument chapter of Siddhanta Shiromani, which shows that even with this, complex calculations are needed to know the time. Therefore, even though good means are available nowadays, this instrument is not necessary.

Knowledge of time can be easily obtained from the dhanuṣa and cakra-yantra. These two instruments are actually the same. The cakra-yantra has a round circle whose edges are marked in equal parts. If there are 60 equal parts, each part indicates the time of a clock. If a straight spike of iron or brass is fixed from the center of this circle and the circle is fixed on the earth in two pillars in such a way that the head of the spike is in the direction of the pole of the sky, then the time of the sun (Hour Angle) can be easily known from this instrument. In the মান-mandiras of Delhi and Kashi, etc., circular instruments of stone have been made which are fixed on the earth in such a way that their planes are parallel to the equator and their center is about 6 inches in the direction of the poles extending on both sides of the spike. The edges on both sides of this circle-instrument are marked in equal parts. When the sun is in the northern hemisphere (from the vernal equinox to the autumnal equinox), the shadow of the spike falls on the northern plane of the instrument and tells the Hour Angle, and when the sun is in the southern hemisphere, the shadow of the spike falls on the southern plane and indicates the Hour Angle. As the sun rises, the shadow

Bhaskaracharya has described another type of wheel-instrument. It is also circular but is not fixed. There is a hole some distance from the edge in which a chain is attached. It can be hung with this chain. Its edges are marked in 360 degrees. When hung, its center remains directly below the hole. The line perpendicular to the line joining these two points, and which also remains at the center of the wheel, has a mark of zero on one edge and 180 on the other. When time is to be known, hang it and rotate it so that the shadow of the tip of the notch fixed at its center falls on the edge parts. If its edges are also divided in the rising points of the auspicious positions of the signs of the sine, then the knowledge of the ascendant can also be obtained from it. There is no special advantage from this instrument in front of modern instruments.

Arc or bow instrument—if half of the wheel-instrument is taken, then the time of the sun can be known in the same way.

Nowadays, the shadow of the sun at any time of the day can easily be known by a simple arc instrument made of cardboard, and the time can also be known from it. This author has discussed such an instrument in Science Part 43 number 1 page 138 in Figure 138. Besides these shadow instruments, work was also done with water-clocks and sand-clocks, etc. The water-clock was called the skull instrument because it was half-spherical like the skull and had a small hole in it. If it were floated in water, water would slowly fill the bowl through the hole and fill it so much that the bowl sinks. The shape of this bowl and the hole was such

that the sun sinks and rises 60 times in a day and night. The time it took to sink once was called a clock. For this reason, it got the name ghatiyantra, which later became famous as the clock. Rules were made in ancient times to make such instruments from which it was clear how large the skull or bowl should be and what the hole should be. This is specially described in the 23rd verse of the Vigyan Bhashya.

There is no detailed writing about the Mayur and Vanar instruments. These were probably instruments made in the shape of a peacock and a monkey, in which time was measured with the help of thread and sand. In these instruments, a device was done by means of mercury, oil, water, etc., so that they would move by themselves and indicate time, but there is no clear description of how they were made; it is only indicated that their use is very rare.

It is unknown whether such self-moving instruments were actually made or were only in imagination. Nowadays, all kinds of self-moving clocks can be used in work, but there is no need to explain their principle here.

Looking at the table will show that where 12 is written indicates the meridian time. In the next column, 1 is written below and 11 is written above. This means that the portion of the sun is as much as 11 o'clock as it is as 1 o'clock. However, the meridian portion does not differ much from these. In January and December, this difference is not more than two and a quarter degrees. In February and October, it becomes up to 2 degrees. In March and September, it becomes approximately 4. In April and August, it becomes more than 6 degrees. Therefore, this time from the sun's hour cannot be taken very accurately from 1 to 1 o'clock in the winter days.

Time from 1 to 2 o'clock or from 10 to 11 o'clock can be taken easily. Additionally, the knowledge of time in other times can be known with subtlety.

Time from the sun's hour is the pure local time. The time known from the star house clock is different from that. To know the time of the star house clock from the local time, two calculations in local time are required. One is called the time equation and the other is called the longitude calculation. The time equation is positive from January 16 to April 14, after which it remains negative until June 14. After June 14, it becomes positive again and remains so until August. From September to December, it is usually negative. When it is positive, it has to be added to the time of the sun's hour, and when it is negative, it has to be subtracted. Doing this calculation makes the pure local time equal to the mean local time.

Longitude calculation—After knowing the mean-local time, if the position is 1 degree before the longitude line by 82° degrees, then 4 minutes, if 2 degrees before, then eight minutes, and if 10 degrees before, then 40 minutes must be subtracted. But if the position is west of the longitude line by 82° degrees, then it has to be added accordingly. Doing this gives the time which is the time of the telegraph or railway clock.

Sunrise and sunset time—The sunrise time is also given in hours and minutes in the table. If the sunrise time is subtracted from 12 hours, the sunset time will come. This is the time when the center of the sun's image is on the horizon

Source page 813

According to mathematics, it should be. But in reality, due to the refraction of light, the image of the sun appears even while remaining below the horizon. Due to this motion, sunrise occurs approximately 2 minutes before the given time and sunset 2 minutes after.

The image of the sun is not like a point, therefore its upper edge often rises one minute before and sets one minute after. Therefore, by subtracting 3 minutes from the sunrise time, the time will come when the upper edge of the sun's image begins to be seen. Similarly, by adding 3 minutes in the sunset time, the time will come when the entire image of the sun disappears. But this time is the apparent time of space. To know the time of a railway clock, the time equation and the longitude calculation should also be done. Looking at the equation shows that the sunrise time is the same for two dates. For example, on January 10th and December 3rd, the sunrise time is 6 hours and 44 minutes in Allahabad or in all the places of 25 degrees latitude. However, in these dates, a difference in the railway clock time for the sunrise time is seen. The reason is clear. On December 3rd, 10 minutes must be subtracted from the time equation. And on January 10th, 7 minutes must be added. The other calculations are the same in both. For example, the sunrise time of these two dates as it comes from the railway clock is shown below—

3 December 10 January clear sunrise time 6 hours 44 minutes 6 hours 44 minutes ritual- correction —2॥ minutes —2॥ time equation ritual —10.” +7॥ country difference ritual (for Allahabad) + 2” + 2 train clock sunrise time 6 hours 33.min 6 hours 51 min

If one wants to know the time of rising of the upper edge of the sun's image, then one should subtract 1 minute.
