Knowing the time by measuring the portion of the Sun—

Example 1—On February 17, the portion of the Sun before noon is 50. What is the time? The portion at 10 o'clock is 47।।। And at 6 o'clock is 57।।। Therefore, the portion of the Sun between 6 and 10 o'clock will be 50. It is also apparent that the portion decreases by 10 degrees between 6 and 10 o'clock. Therefore, in this hour, the portion is decreasing at a rate of 10 degrees per hour, which means it decreases by 1 degree in 6 minutes. There are 7।।। degrees from 57।।। to 50. Therefore, the decrease of 7।।। degrees is in 6 X 7।।। minutes or 46।। mi0. Therefore, the true local time is 6 hours 46 minutes. On this day, the time-equation is + 14 minutes. Therefore, upon giving this calculation, the mean local time is 6 hours 46 minutes + 14 minutes = 10 hours 1 minute. If the place is Allahabad, then 2 minutes should be added. In this way, the railway time is 10 hours 3 minutes. If the place is Kashi, then 2 minutes should be subtracted from ten hours 1 minute, because Kashi is 2 minutes earlier. Therefore, at the time when the portion of the Sun is 50 in Kashi on this date, it would be 6 hours 56 minutes.

Example 2—On March 23, the nataṃśa of the Sun after noon in Patna city is 74 degrees. What time does the railway clock show at this time?

There is no 23 March in the table. It gives the nataṃśa and natakaal for the 21st and 26th of March. For 21 March, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock is 63. And the nataṃśa at 5 o'clock is 76. For 26 March, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock is 62. And the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock is 75. In 5 days, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock decreases by 1 degree and the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock decreases by a quarter degree. Therefore, in 2 days, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock will decrease by almost half a degree and the nataṃśa at 5 o'clock will decrease by almost a quarter degree. Therefore, for 23th, the nataṃśa at 4 o'clock will be 62. And the nataṃśa at 5 o'clock will be 76. The difference between these two is 13 degrees. This increase happens in 1 hour. Therefore, the speed of increase of the nataṃśa is approximately 4 minutes per degree. But the time of the 74 nataṃśa needs to be known.

To know the latitude of a place—know the meridian altitude (12 o'clock) of the desired day from a table. Then look in the same table what is the meridian altitude of March 21st. Know the difference between both. This is the precession of the sun on that day. Now look at the meridian altitude of your place from the meridian reflection. If the precession is north, adding it to this altitude and if it is south, subtracting it will give the latitude of that place.

Example—The meridian altitude of Raebareli on February 17th is 38.. In the table, the meridian altitude of February 17th is 37॥, and that of March 21st is 25; the difference between these two altitudes is 12. Therefore, the precession of the sun on this day is 120 South. Subtracting this precession from 38॥ gives 26॥, which is the latitude of Raebareli. This is 26. in reality. Therefore, there is an error of a quarter degree in this.

This chapter will be concluded by writing down the method for making a simple sundial. For such a sundial, a sheet of brass with a width of about 3 inches, a length of 15 to 20 inches, and a width of ten or twelve inches will suffice. From this sheet, a right-angled triangle should be cut such that the angle formed on the longer side is equal to the latitude of the place where the sundial is to be installed. A similar right-angled triangle will also be formed in the remaining sheet. Suppose there is a square piece of brass sheet, let's call it T. From this, a right-angled triangle is cut such that the angle of T is equal to the latitude of Prayag, 25^° 25'. The remaining piece is T, in which a line parallel to T is drawn, and the angle U of this line will also be equal to 25^° 25'. Now, from this piece, one should see what kind of circular segment can be cut from it. The center of such a circular segment should be determined, and two parallel lines should be drawn near it, whose distance between them is equal to the width of the sheet and which are perpendicular to the side of T. Then, drawing two equal arcs with the tips of each line as the center. The angle at the center of these arcs should not be less than 60 degrees and not more than 105 degrees because the day length in Prayag is not more than 14 hours. The edges of this circular segment should first be divided at intervals of fifteen-fifteen marks, and then these parts should be divided into three or four equal parts (only three parts are shown in the figure). The parts with fifteen-fifteen marks will indicate the hour, and if there are three parts in each hour, then from each one, twenty minutes can be known, and if there are four parts, then fifteen minutes can be known from each. Smaller parts are not shown in the figure, but in reality, three or four equal parts can also be made from every fourth part, from which five minutes can be known. Such sundials have been installed in the government high schools of Ballia and Raebareli. The sundial of Ballia was prepared under the supervision of a student of the ninth class by this author, but the sundial of Raebareli was made by a mechanic.

Sextile faces

तुलादेः षडशीत्यंशैः षडशीतिमुखं दिनम् ।

Translation—(4) From the tulā solstice, sixty days of the sextile face occur in sequence. There are four and they are in the dual signs. (5) Up to the 26th degree of Sagittarius, 22nd degree of Pisces, 18th degree of Gemini, and 14th degree of Virgo.

Scientific Commentary—The meaning of day in these verses is not Sawan day, but the time when the sun moves by one degree. Such a year of 360 days is more than 365 days and 6 hours according to Sawan. But the motion of the sun is not always the same, so the values of the four sextile faces are also not the same in Sawan days. Starting from the Libra sign, and adding thirty-thirty degrees of Libra and Scorpio signs and 26 degrees of Sagittarius, they become 86 degrees, so it ends at the 26 degrees of Sagittarius. The second sextile face starts from the 27th degree of Sagittarius and ends at the 22nd degree of Pisces. Similarly, it ends at the 18th degree of Gemini and the 14th degree of Virgo. The four signs in which the sextile faces end are those of the dual signs, which have been discussed in predictive astrology.

In some texts, the place of Timina is written as Nimisha, which seems incorrect because Nimisha does not mean the Pisces sign.

Uttarayana and Dakshinayana and seasons—

तयोर्मकरसङ्क्रान्तेः षण्मासेषूत्तरायणम् ।
कर्क्यादेस्तु तथैव स्यात् षण्मासा दक्षिणायनम् ॥६॥
द्विराशिमानादृतवः षडुक्ताशिशिरादयः ।
मेषादयो द्वादशैते मासास्तैरेव वत्सरः ॥१०॥

Translation—(6) The time from which the sun enters the Capricorn sign for 6 months is Uttarayana, and the time from which it enters the Cancer sign for 6 months is Dakshinayana. (10) The seasons experience two signs; the cycle of seasons like Shishir begins with the Capricorn solstice; the beginning of 12 solar months begins with the Aries solstice, which is one year.

Scientific Commentary—These verses show the mutual relationship between the signs, solstices, and seasons. The signs are considered fixed, and their beginning is from the beginning point of Ashwini according to Sūrya Siddhānta, according to which the portion of the celestial star is 180. However, the order of the seasons follows according to the equinoxes, which is moving, so the relationship between the signs, ayanas, and seasons is gradually slipping. There was a time when the beginning of Uttarayana occurred at the same time when the sun's motion also began in the north and it moved towards the north for 6 months. Similarly, the beginning of Dakshinayana occurred at the time when the sun's motion was towards the south in the Cancer sign. But now these two events do not happen together; the sun's northward motion begins 23 days before the Capricorn solstice. In five hundred years, this difference will be about one month. Special discussion has been made on this subject in Triprashnādhikāra. It is an established view of Sūrya Siddhānta that the equinox remains at the 27 degrees of Ashwini, there is no more difference, but this is neither proven by modern science nor accepted by Bhaskaracharya etc. The positions of the Nakshatras mentioned in Brahmanic texts, such as Krittika, prove that the view of Sūrya Siddhānta is not correct (Triprashnādhikāra page 240).

Some scholars also have the opinion, which is well supported on the basis of Brahmanic texts, that the commencement of Uttarayana is not considered from that time.

Source page 823

When the tendency of the sun is towards the north, it was considered that time when the sun comes into the north in the North latitude from the equator. This also resolves the days and nights of the gods well because the gods are considered to reside in the North Pole and the beginning of the day or sunrise on the North Pole occurs at the same time when the sun starts moving north from the equator. Therefore, the Uttaraayana is considered the day of the gods and Dakshinayana their night. This is also logical. If Bhaskaraacharya ji were to consider this, he would not have to make this imagination regarding Uttaraayana.1

Auspicious Period of Sankranti

अर्कमानकलाषष्ट्या गुणिता भुक्तिभाजिताः ।

Translation - The auspicious period of Sankranti is half an hour before and after the Sankranti when the result of dividing the art of the image of the sun by the art of the value of the sun is multiplied by sixty of its daily motion.

Scientific Commentary—Sankranti occurs at the time when the center of the sun's image enters the zodiac, but the value of the sun's image is approximately 32 arts, so the auspicious period of Sankranti begins at the time when the eastern edge of the sun's image touches the zodiac while entering and remains until the western edge of the image does not cross the beginning point of the zodiac. This time is approximately 32 hours, which is half 16 hours. Therefore, the auspicious period begins approximately 16 hours before Sankranti and lasts until 16 hours after. For fine calculation, one should use the ratio shown in the shlokas. If the daily motion of the sun during the Sankranti period is 60 hours, then how many hours will be the motion of the sun's image? The names of the lunar months are kept on the names of the constellations on which the moon remains during the full moon. The alliance made by this principle of tithi, month, and constellations is unparalleled in the history of world astrology. This proves well that the Hindu astrologers in ancient times were very talented and the accusation of copying the astrology of other countries by them is very shameless and biased. Now, by sūkṣma gaṇanā (subtle calculation), it is certainly proven that this mutual relationship between constellations and months is sometimes missed, but here it must also be considered that the fact that the rule which has been running for more than three thousand years has become loose somewhere is not a wonder and is proof of the ignorance of the rule makers. It can be easily seen from the table given on pages 557-58 how much difference has occurred at this time.

The constellations of the remaining three years are taken from the ordinary Panchangs of Lucknow and Kashi. Those constellations on which the sign of wealth is marked have become somewhat different according to the above rule. (just as the names of the Nakshatras of the full moon of the moon are named after the names of the lunar months) by the combination of the setting and rising of Jupiter on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the months of Vaishakha, etc., names of the years of Kartik, etc., were given.

Source page 828

Chapter 803

Science commentary—at the time when Jupiter comes very close to the Sun, because of the sunlight, it cannot be seen, so it is considered set. Then when it moves so far away from the Sun that it becomes visible, it is considered risen. (See Udaya-stadhikar p. 656-57). This event happens approximately when there is conjunction of the Sun and Jupiter, which used to occur at an interval of about 366 days or 13 months. This period is called 'Varhaspati year'. The names of such years are kept according to the constellations on which the Sun and the Moon are both present at the time of Jupiter's rising or setting. It is stated in the 16th verse that the names of the lunar months are based on the names of those constellations on which the Moon remains in the full moon period, therefore it is proven that the Sun is in the 14th constellation of those lunar months' full moon constellations. For example, in the month of Vaishakh, the full moon falls on the Vishakha or Anuradha constellations, so in this month, the Sun will remain in the 14th constellation of Vishakha or Anuradha, which is Krittika or Rohini. If Jupiter rises or sets at this time, then it is certain that it will also remain on these constellations or one or two constellations ahead or behind, and the new moon will also be on these constellations, therefore Jupiter's 'Kartika year' will begin from this time. That is, if Jupiter rises or sets in the month of Vaishakh, then Jupiter's 'Kartika year' will be applicable, if it rises in the month of Jyeshtha, then 'Varhaspati marg shirsh' year will be applicable, etc. To remove the dilemma between the lunar months and the Varhaspati years, this difference is also made that a 'Maha' is added before the names of the Varhaspati years. However, these Kartik etc. years are not promoted nowadays.

Upon careful observation, it will be apparent that this rule of Sūrya Siddhānta is very loose. The difference between the setting time and the rising time of Jupiter is approximately one month, during which the sun moves more than two constellations. It is possible that at the time of setting, the sun is in the constellation Swati, and at the time of rising, it is in Anuradha. In such a situation, which Varahaspati year should be considered, 'Maha Chaitra' or 'Maha Vaishakh'? Perhaps to resolve this dilemma, Acharya Varahamihira has given this rule in the Brihat Samhita that the name of Jupiter's year should be the name of the constellation in which Jupiter is at the time of rising. Varahamihira has discussed the different results of these years.

Some scholars draw the conclusion that this text was received from the Yavanas astrologers. In this regard, some thoughts will be written in detail in the introduction without further discussion here.

Thus the Sūrya Siddhānta, Chapter on Scientific Commentary, Chapter on Mean Motions, Chapter on True Positions, Chapter on the Three Problems

In some texts, a short chapter of 21 shlokas named Vijopanayanadhyāya is found, on which commentators have not commented that the need for Vija-samskara might not have been necessary during the time of the text's composition, so this chapter has been added from the back. In my short opinion, it is possible that what has been written so far has been combined from Suryansh Purusha to Mayasura in this form, but after that Mayasura must have lived for many years and found some difference from his experience, according to which he finally added Vijopanayanadhyāya. Or perhaps some other astrologer after Mayasura extended it. An effort will be made to shed light on this in the introduction. At this time, I also dare to add this chapter.

यथा शिखा मयूराणां नागानां मणयो यथा
तद्वद्वेदाङ्ग शास्त्राणां गणितं मूर्धनि स्थितम् ॥१॥
न देयं तत् कृतघ्नाय वेदविप्लवकाय च ।
अर्थलुब्धाय मूर्खाय साहङ्काराय पापिने ॥२॥
एवं विधाय पुत्त्रायाप्यदेयं सहजाय च ।
दत्तेन वेद मार्गस्य समुच्छेदः कृतो भवेत् ॥३॥

Chapter 807

ब्रजेतामन्धतामिस्रं गुरु शिष्यौ सुदारुणम् ।
ततः शान्ताय शुचये ब्राह्मणायैव दापयेत् ॥४॥
चक्रानुपातजो मध्यो मध्यवृत्तांशजः स्फुटः ।
कालेन दृक्समो न स्यात् ततो बीजक्रियोच्यते ।।५।।
राश्यादिरिन्दुरङ्कघ्नो भक्तो नक्षत्रकक्षया ।
शेषं नक्षत्रकक्षायास्त्यजेच्छेषकयोस्तयोः ॥६॥
यदल्पं तद्भजेद्वानां कक्षया तिथिनिघ्नया ।
बीजं भागादिकं तत् स्यात् कारयेत् तद्धनं रवौ ॥७॥
त्रिगुणं शोधयेदिन्दौ जिनघ्नं भूमिजे क्षिपेत् ।
दृग्यमघ्नऋणं ज्ञोच्चे खरामघ्नं गुरावृणम् ।।८।।
ऋणं व्योमनवघ्नं स्याद्दानवेज्यचलोच्चके ।
धनं सप्ताहतं मन्दे परिधीनामथोच्यते ॥६॥
युग्मान्तोक्ताः परिधयो ये ते नित्यं परिस्फुटाः ।
ओजान्तोक्तास्तु ते ज्ञेयाः परबीजेन संस्कृताः ॥१०॥
वच्मि निर्वीजकानोजपदान्ते वृत्त भागकान् ।
सूर्येन्द्वोर्मनवो दन्ता धृतितत्वकलोनिताः ॥११॥
बाणतर्का महीजस्य सौम्यस्याचल बाहवः ।
वाक्पतेरष्टनेत्राणि व्योमशीतांशवो भृगोः ॥१२॥
शून्यर्त्तवोऽर्कं पुत्रस्य बीजमेतेषु कारयेत् ।
बीजं खाग्न्युद्धृतं शोध्यं परिध्यंशेषु भास्वतः ॥१३॥
इनाप्तं योजयेदिन्दोः कुजस्याश्वहृतं क्षिपेत् ।
विदश्चन्द्रहृतं योज्यं सूरेरिन्द्रहतं धनम् ॥१४॥
धनं भृगोर्भुवा निघ्नं रविघ्नं शोधयेच्छने ।
एवं मान्दाः परिध्यंशाः स्फुटाः स्युर्वच्मि शीघ्रकान् ।।१५।।
भौमस्याभ्रगुणाक्षीणि बुधस्याब्धि गुणेन्दवः ।
बाणाक्षा देव पूज्यस्य भार्गवस्येन्दु षड्यमाः ॥१६॥
शनिश्चन्द्राब्धयः शीघ्रा ओजान्ते वीजवर्जिताः ।
द्विघ्नं स्वं कुज भागेषु बीजं द्विघ्नमृणं विदः ॥१७॥
अत्यष्टिघ्नं धनं सूरेरिन्दुघ्नं शोधयेत्कवेः ।
चन्द्रघनमृणमार्कस्य स्यूरेभिर्दृक्समा ग्रहाः ॥१८॥
‘एतद्वोजं मया ख्यातं प्रीत्या परमया तव ।
गोपनीयमिदं नित्यं नोपदेश्यं यतस्ततः ॥१९॥

परीक्षिताय शिष्याय गुरुभक्ताय साधवे ।
देयं विप्राय नान्यस्मै प्रतिकञ्चुककारिणे ॥२०॥
बीजं निःशेष सिद्धान्त रहस्यं परमं स्फुटम् ।
यात्नापाणिग्रहादीनां कार्याणां शुभसिद्धिदम् ॥२१॥

Scientific Commentary—these are found after the 23rd verse and the first 4 verses of the last chapter of the mānādhyāya and are at least 400 years old because Ranganath ji has mentioned it in his gūḍhārtha prakāśikā ṭīkā written in 1525. This proves that the need to perform seed correction in Sūrya Siddhānta also existed, and our old Acharyas were in favor of making the astrology flawless and comprehensive, not like some pundits nowadays, not the fakirs of the line.

No commentator from here has commented on these verses, so I also consider it useless to translate it because these old seeds are no longer useful. Now it is necessary to fix all calculations with new observations.

Thus, the Scientific Commentary of the fourteenth and last chapter named mānādhyāya of Sūrya Siddhānta has ended.
